children.translated_text: Of him whose flawless qualities are an unfathomable ocean of knowledge and compassion,

children.text: sevyatām akṣayo dhīrāḥ sa śriye cāmṛtāya ca ||
children.translated_text: let the wise serve that inexhaustible one, for prosperity and for immortality.
Having gathered other treatises and recast them in concise form,
the complete instruction on names and genders is stated by sections.
For the most part gender is to be known from difference of form, and sometimes from association;
the feminine, masculine, and neuter are to be understood where there is a special rule for that case.

children.text: bhedākhyānāya na dvaṃdvo naikaśeṣo na saṃkaraḥ
children.translated_text: To indicate distinctions, no dvandva compound, no single-remainder form, and no mixture
has been made here for words of different genders, apart from the order of those not explicitly stated.

children.text: triliṅgyāṃ triṣv iti padaṃ mithune tu dvayoriti
children.translated_text: In words of three genders, the expression "in the three" is used; in a pair, "in the two" is used.
A prohibited gender implies the remaining sense; endings and expressions beginning with such particles do not apply to what precedes.
The indeclinable svar, and svarga, nāka, tridiva, and tridaśālaya, denote heaven;

children.text: suraloko dyodivau dve striyāṃ klībe triviṣṭapam ||
children.translated_text: suraloka, the two feminine forms dyau and div, and the neuter triviṣṭapa also denote it.
Amara, nirjara, deva, tridaśa, vibudha, and sura are names for the gods;
so too are suparvan, sumanas, tridiveśa, and divaukas.
Āditeya, diviṣad, lekha, and aditinandana are also names for them;
so are āditya, ṛbhu, asvapna, martya, and amṛtāndhas.
Barhirmukha, ṛtubhuj, gīrvāṇa, and dānavāraya are further names for the gods;

children.text: vṛndārakā daivatāni puṃsi vā devatāḥ striyām ||
children.translated_text: vṛndāraka and daivata are masculine, while devatā is feminine.
The Ādityas, Viśvas, Vasus, Tuṣitas, Ābhāsvaras, and Anilas,
together with the Mahārājikas, Sādhyas, and Rudras, are classes of deities.
Vidyādharas, apsarases, yakṣas, rakṣases, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras,
as well as piśācas, guhyakas, siddhas, and bhūtas, are these divine-born classes.
Asura, daitya, daiteya, danuja, enemy of Indra, and dānava
mean the disciples of <s>Śukra</s>, the sons of <s>Diti</s>, the former gods, and the enemies of the gods.
<s>Sarvajña</s>, <s>Sugata</s>, <s>Buddha</s>, <s>Dharmarāja</s>, and <s>Tathāgata</s>
<s>Samantabhadra</s>, <s>Bhagavān</s>, <s>Mārajit</s>, <s>Lokajit</s>, and <s>Jina</s> are names of the Buddha.
<s>Ṣaḍabhijña</s>, <s>Daśabala</s>, <s>Advayavādin</s>, and <s>Vināyaka</s>

children.text: munīndraḥ śrīghanaḥ śāstā muniḥ śākyamunistu yaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Munīndra</s>, <s>Śrīghana</s>, <s>Śāstā</s>, <s>Muni</s>, and <s>Śākyamuni</s> are also his names.
He is <s>Śākyasiṃha</s>, <s>Sarvārthasiddha</s>, and <s>Śauddhodani</s>;
he is also <s>Gautama</s>, <s>Arkabandhu</s>, and the son of <s>Māyādevī</s>.
<s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Ātmabhū</s>, <s>Surajyeṣṭha</s>, <s>Parameṣṭhin</s>, and <s>Pitāmaha</s>
<s>Hiraṇyagarbha</s>, <s>Lokeśa</s>, <s>Svayaṃbhū</s>, and <s>Caturānana</s> are names of <s>Brahmā</s>.
<s>Dhātṛ</s>, <s>Abjayoni</s>, <s>Druhiṇa</s>, <s>Viriñci</s>, and <s>Kamalāsana</s>
<s>Sraṣṭṛ</s>, <s>Prajāpati</s>, <s>Vedhas</s>, <s>Vidhātṛ</s>, <s>Viśvasṛj</s>, and <s>Vidhi</s> are further names of him.
<s>Nābhijanman</s>, <s>Aṇḍaja</s>, <s>Pūrva</s>, <s>Nidhana</s>, and <s>Kamalodbhava</s>
<s>Sadānanda</s>, <s>Rajomūrti</s>, <s>Satyaka</s>, and <s>Haṃsavāhana</s> are also names of <s>Brahmā</s>.
<s>Viṣṇu</s>, <s>Nārāyaṇa</s>, <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>, <s>Vaikuṇṭha</s>, and <s>Viṣṭaraśravas</s>
<s>Dāmodara</s>, <s>Hṛṣīkeśa</s>, <s>Keśava</s>, <s>Mādhava</s>, and <s>Svabhū</s> are names of <s>Viṣṇu</s>.
<s>Daityāri</s>, <s>Puṇḍarīkākṣa</s>, <s>Govinda</s>, and <s>Garuḍadhvaja</s>
<s>Pītāmbara</s>, <s>Acyuta</s>, <s>Śārṅgin</s>, <s>Viṣvaksena</s>, and <s>Janārdana</s> are further names.
<s>Upendra</s>, the younger brother of <s>Indra</s>, <s>Cakrapāṇi</s>, and <s>Caturbhuja</s>
<s>Padmanābha</s>, <s>Madhuripu</s>, <s>Vāsudeva</s>, and <s>Trivikrama</s> are also names of him.
<s>Devakīnandana</s>, <s>Śauri</s>, <s>Śrīpati</s>, and <s>Puruṣottama</s>
<s>Vanamālin</s>, <s>Balidhvaṃsin</s>, <s>Kaṃsārāti</s>, and <s>Adhokṣaja</s> are names of <s>Viṣṇu</s>.
<s>Viśvambhara</s>, <s>Kaiṭabhajit</s>, <s>Vidhu</s>, and <s>Śrīvatsalāñchana</s>
<s>Purāṇapuruṣa</s>, <s>Yajñapuruṣa</s>, and <s>Narakāntaka</s> are further names.
<s>Jalaśāyin</s>, <s>Viśvarūpa</s>, <s>Mukunda</s>, and <s>Muramardana</s> are names of him.
<s>Vasudeva</s> is his father, and he is also called <s>Ānakadundubhi</s>.
<s>Balabhadra</s>, <s>Pralambaghna</s>, <s>Baladeva</s>, and elder brother of <s>Acyuta</s>
<s>Revatīramaṇa</s>, <s>Rāma</s>, <s>Kāmapāla</s>, and <s>Halāyudha</s> are names of <s>Balarāma</s>.
<s>Nīlāmbara</s>, <s>Rauhiṇeya</s>, <s>Tālāṅka</s>, <s>Musalin</s>, and <s>Halin</s>
<s>Saṃkarṣaṇa</s>, <s>Sīrapāṇi</s>, <s>Kālindībhedana</s>, and <s>Bala</s> are also his names.
<s>Madana</s>, <s>Manmatha</s>, <s>Māra</s>, <s>Pradyumna</s>, and <s>Mīnaketana</s>
<s>Kandarpa</s>, <s>Darpaka</s>, <s>Anaṅga</s>, <s>Kāma</s>, <s>Pañcaśara</s>, and <s>Smara</s> are names of <s>Kāma</s>.
<s>Śambarāri</s>, <s>Manasija</s>, <s>Kusumeṣu</s>, <s>Ananyaja</s>,
<s>Puṣpadhanvan</s>, <s>Ratipati</s>, <s>Makaradhvaja</s>, and <s>Ātmabhū</s> are further names.
The lotus, the aśoka blossom, the mango flower, and the fresh jasmine,
together with the blue lotus, are the five arrows of the five-arrowed god.
Unmādana, Tāpana, Śoṣaṇa, and Stambhana,

children.text: sammohanaś ca kāmaś ca pañca bāṇāḥ prakīrtitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: as well as Sammohana, are proclaimed to be the five arrows of <s>Kāma</s>.
<s>Brahmasū</s> and <s>Viśvaketu</s> are names for <s>Aniruddha</s>, the husband of <s>Uṣā</s>.

children.text: lakṣmīḥ padmālayā padmā kamalā śrīr haripriyā ||
children.translated_text: <s>Lakṣmī</s>, <s>Padmālayā</s>, <s>Padmā</s>, <s>Kamalā</s>, <s>Śrī</s>, and beloved of <s>Hari</s>
<s>Indirā</s>, mother of the world, <s>Mā</s>, daughter of the milk-ocean, and <s>Ramā</s>
<s>Bhārgavī</s>, mother of the world, and daughter of the milk-ocean are names of <s>Lakṣmī</s>.
The conch of <s>Lakṣmīpati</s> is <s>Pāñcajanya</s>, and the discus is <s>Sudarśana</s>;

children.text: kaumodakī gadā khaḍgo nandakaḥ kaustubho maṇiḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Kaumodakī</s> is the mace, <s>Nandaka</s> the sword, and <s>Kaustubha</s> the jewel.

children.text: cāpaḥ śārṅgaṃ murāres tu śrīvatso lāñchanaṃ smṛtam
children.translated_text: The bow of <s>Murāri</s> is <s>Śārṅga</s>, and <s>Śrīvatsa</s> is remembered as the mark;
his horses are <s>Śaibya</s>, <s>Sugrīva</s>, <s>Meghapuṣpa</s>, and <s>Balāhaka</s>.

children.text: sārathirdāruko mantrī hy uddhavaś cānujo gadaḥ
children.translated_text: His charioteer is <s>Dāruka</s>, his minister is <s>Uddhava</s>, and his younger brother is <s>Gada</s>.
<s>Garutmān</s>, <s>Garuḍa</s>, <s>Tārkṣya</s>, <s>Vainateya</s>, and lord of birds
<s>Nāgāntaka</s>, chariot of <s>Viṣṇu</s>, <s>Suparṇa</s>, and eater of serpents are names of <s>Garuḍa</s>.
<s>Śambhu</s>, <s>Īśa</s>, <s>Paśupati</s>, <s>Śiva</s>, <s>Śūlin</s>, and <s>Maheśvara</s>
<s>Īśvara</s>, <s>Śarva</s>, <s>Īśāna</s>, <s>Śaṃkara</s>, and <s>Candraśekhara</s>
<s>Bhūteśa</s>, <s>Khaṇḍaparaśu</s>, <s>Girīśa</s>, <s>Giriśa</s>, and <s>Mṛḍa</s> are names of <s>Śiva</s>.
<s>Mṛtyuṃjaya</s>, <s>Kṛttivāsas</s>, <s>Pinākin</s>, and lord of the Pramathas,
<s>Ugra</s>, <s>Kapardin</s>, <s>Śrīkaṇṭha</s>, <s>Śitikaṇṭha</s>, and skull-bearer are further names.
<s>Vāmadeva</s>, <s>Mahādeva</s>, <s>Virūpākṣa</s>, and <s>Trilocana</s>,
<s>Kṛśānuretas</s>, <s>Sarvajña</s>, <s>Dhūrjaṭi</s>, and <s>Nīlalohita</s> are also names of <s>Śiva</s>.
<s>Hara</s>, <s>Smarahara</s>, <s>Bharga</s>, <s>Tryambaka</s>, and <s>Tripurāntaka</s> are names of <s>Śiva</s>.
<s>Gaṅgādhara</s>, <s>Andhakaripu</s>, <s>Kratudhvaṃsī</s>, and <s>Vṛṣadhvaja</s> are also names of <s>Śiva</s>.

children.text: vyomakeśo bhavo bhīmaḥ sthāṇū rudra umāpatiḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Vyomakeśa</s>, <s>Bhava</s>, <s>Bhīma</s>, <s>Sthāṇu</s>, <s>Rudra</s>, and <s>Umāpati</s> are further names of him.
<s>Ahirbudhnya</s>, <s>Aṣṭamūrti</s>, <s>Gajāri</s>, and <s>Mahānaṭa</s> too are names of <s>Śiva</s>.
His matted crest is called <s>Kaparda</s> or <s>Jaṭājūṭa</s>; his bow is <s>Pināka</s> or <s>Ajagava</s>.

children.text: pramathāḥ syuḥ pāriṣadā brāhmītyādyās tu mātaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: His attendants are called <s>Pramathas</s> or <s>Pāriṣadas</s>; <s>Brāhmī</s> and the others are the <s>Mātṛs</s> (Mother goddesses).
<s>Vibhūti</s>, <s>bhūti</s>, and <s>aiśvarya</s> denote supernatural power, eightfold beginning with <s>aṇimā</s>.

children.text: aṇimā mahimā caiva garimā laghimā tathā ||
children.translated_text: The first four are <s>aṇimā</s> (minuteness), <s>mahimā</s> (greatness), <s>garimā</s> (heaviness), and <s>laghimā</s> (lightness).

children.text: prāptiḥ prākāmyam īśitvaṃ vaśitvaṃ cāṣṭa siddhayaḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Prāpti</s> (attainment), <s>prākāmya</s> (irresistible will), <s>īśitva</s> (lordship), and <s>vaśitva</s> (control) make up the eight <s>siddhis</s>.
<s>Umā</s>, <s>Kātyāyanī</s>, <s>Gaurī</s>, <s>Kālī</s>, <s>Haimavatī</s>, and <s>Īśvarī</s> are names of the goddess.
<s>Śivā</s>, <s>Bhavānī</s>, <s>Rudrāṇī</s>, <s>Śarvāṇī</s>, and <s>Sarvamaṅgalā</s> are likewise her names.
<s>Aparṇā</s>, <s>Pārvatī</s>, <s>Durgā</s>, <s>Mṛḍānī</s>, <s>Caṇḍikā</s>, and <s>Ambikā</s> are also names of her.
<s>Āryā</s>, <s>Dākṣāyaṇī</s>, <s>Girijā</s>, and <s>Menakātmajā</s> are further names of <s>Pārvatī</s>.

children.text: karmamoṭī tu cāmuṇḍā carmamuṇḍā tu carcikā ||
children.translated_text: <s>Karmamoṭī</s> is <s>Cāmuṇḍā</s>; <s>Carmamuṇḍā</s> is <s>Carcikā</s>.
<s>Vināyaka</s>, <s>Vighnarāja</s>, <s>Dvaimātura</s>, and <s>Gaṇādhipa</s> are names of <s>Gaṇeśa</s>.
<s>Ekadanta</s>, <s>Heramba</s>, <s>Lambodara</s>, and <s>Gajānana</s> are also names of him.
<s>Kārttikeya</s>, <s>Mahāsena</s>, <s>Śarajanmā</s>, and <s>Ṣaḍānana</s> are names of <s>Skanda</s>.
<s>Pārvatīnandana</s>, <s>Skanda</s>, <s>Senānī</s>, <s>Agnibhū</s>, and <s>Guha</s> are further names of him.
<s>Bāhuleya</s>, <s>Tārakajit</s>, <s>Viśākha</s>, and <s>Śikhivāhana</s> are also names of <s>Kārttikeya</s>.
<s>Ṣāṇmātura</s>, <s>Śaktidhara</s>, <s>Kumāra</s>, and <s>Krauñcadāraṇa</s> are likewise names of him.

children.text: śṛṅgī bhṛṅgī riṭis tuṇḍī nandiko nandikeśvaraḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Śṛṅgī</s>, <s>Bhṛṅgī</s>, <s>Riṭi</s>, <s>Tuṇḍī</s>, <s>Nandika</s>, and <s>Nandikeśvara</s> are attendant names.
<s>Indra</s>, <s>Marutvān</s>, <s>Maghavā</s>, <s>Biḍaujas</s>, and <s>Pākaśāsana</s> are names of <s>Indra</s>.
<s>Vṛddhaśravas</s>, <s>Sunāsīra</s>, <s>Puruhūta</s>, and <s>Purandara</s> are also names of <s>Indra</s>.
<s>Jiṣṇu</s>, <s>Lekharṣabha</s>, <s>Śakra</s>, <s>Śatamanyu</s>, and <s>Divaspati</s> are further names of him.

children.text: sutrāmā gotrabhid vajrī vāsavo vṛtrahā vṛṣā
children.translated_text: <s>Sutrāmā</s>, <s>Gotrabhid</s>, <s>Vajrī</s>, <s>Vāsava</s>, <s>Vṛtrahā</s>, and <s>Vṛṣā</s> are names of <s>Indra</s>.
<s>Vāstoṣpati</s>, <s>Surapati</s>, <s>Balārāti</s>, and <s>Śacīpati</s> are also his names.
<s>Jambhabhedin</s>, <s>Harihaya</s>, <s>Svarāṭ</s>, and <s>Namucisādana</s> are further names of <s>Indra</s>.
<s>Saṃkrandana</s>, <s>Duścyavana</s>, <s>Turāṣāṭ</s>, and <s>Meghavāhana</s> are likewise names of him.
<s>Ākhaṇḍala</s>, <s>Sahasrākṣa</s>, and <s>Ṛbhukṣas</s> are names of <s>Indra</s>; his beloved is named next.
His beloved wife is <s>Pulomajā</s>, <s>Śacī</s>, or <s>Indrāṇī</s>; his city is <s>Amarāvatī</s>.
His horse is <s>Uccaiḥśravas</s>, his charioteer is <s>Mātali</s>, and his grove is <s>Nandana</s>.
His palace is <s>Vaijayanta</s>, and <s>Jayanta</s> is the son of <s>Pākaśāsana</s>.
<s>Airāvata</s>, <s>Abhramātaṅga</s>, <s>Airāvaṇa</s>, and <s>Abhramuvallabha</s> are names of <s>Indra</s>'s elephant.

children.text: hrādinī vajramastrī syāt kuliśaṃ bhiduraṃ paviḥ ||
children.translated_text: The thunderbolt is called <s>Hrādinī</s>, <s>Vajra</s>, <s>Kuliśa</s>, <s>Bhidura</s>, and <s>Pavi</s>.
<s>Śatakoṭi</s>, <s>Svaru</s>, <s>Śamba</s>, <s>Dambholi</s>, and <s>Aśani</s> are additional terms for the thunderbolt.
A sky-going vehicle is a <s>vimāna</s>; <s>Nārada</s> and others are divine seers.

children.text: syāt sudharmā devasabhā pīyūṣam amṛtaṃ sudhā
children.translated_text: <s>Sudharmā</s> is the gods' assembly hall; <s>pīyūṣa</s>, <s>amṛta</s>, and <s>sudhā</s> mean nectar.
<s>Mandākinī</s>, <s>Viyadgaṅgā</s>, <s>Svarṇadī</s>, and <s>Suradīrghikā</s> are names of the heavenly Gaṅgā.
<s>Meru</s>, <s>Sumeru</s>, <s>Hemādri</s>, <s>Ratnasānu</s>, and <s>Surālaya</s> are names of the divine mountain.
The five trees of the gods include <s>Mandāra</s> and <s>Pārijātaka</s>.
<s>Saṃtāna</s>, <s>Kalpavṛkṣa</s>, and <s>Haricandana</s> are the remaining divine trees.
<s>Sanatkumāra</s> is called <s>Vaidhātra</s>; the heavenly physicians are the two sons of <s>Aśvinī</s>.

children.text: nāsatyāv aśvinau dasrāv āśvineyau ca tāv ubhau
children.translated_text: They are called <s>Nāsatyas</s>, <s>Aśvins</s>, <s>Dasras</s>, and <s>Āśvineyas</s>.
In the feminine plural, <s>apsarases</s> are heavenly courtesans, beginning with <s>Urvaśī</s>.
<s>Hāhā</s>, <s>Hūhū</s>, and the like are <s>Gandharvas</s> among the heaven-dwellers.
<s>Agni</s>, <s>Vaiśvānara</s>, <s>Vahni</s>, <s>Vītihotra</s>, and <s>Dhanaṃjaya</s> are names of fire.
<s>Kṛpīṭayoni</s>, <s>Jvalana</s>, <s>Jātavedas</s>, and <s>Tanūnapāt</s> are also names of fire.
<s>Barhiṣ</s>, <s>Śuṣmā</s>, <s>Kṛṣṇavartman</s>, <s>Śociṣkeśa</s>, and <s>Uṣarbudha</s> are further names of fire.
<s>Āśrayāśa</s>, <s>Bṛhadbhānu</s>, <s>Kṛśānu</s>, <s>Pāvaka</s>, and <s>Anala</s> are likewise names of fire.
<s>Rohitāśva</s>, <s>Vāyusakha</s>, <s>Śikhāvān</s>, and <s>Āśuśukṣaṇi</s> are additional names of fire.
<s>Hiraṇyaretas</s>, <s>Hutabhuj</s>, <s>Dahana</s>, and <s>Havyavāhana</s> are also names of fire.
<s>Saptārci</s>, <s>Damunā</s>, <s>Śukra</s>, <s>Citrabhānu</s>, and <s>Vibhāvasu</s> are further names of fire.
<s>Śuci</s> is another name of fire; the submarine fire is <s>Aurva</s>, <s>Vāḍaba</s>, or <s>Vaḍabānala</s>.

children.text: vahner dvayor jvālakīlāv arcir hetiḥ śikhāḥ striyām ||
children.translated_text: The flame of fire is called <s>Jvālā</s> or <s>Kīlā</s>; <s>Arci</s>, <s>Heti</s>, and <s>Śikhā</s> are feminine terms for flame.
<s>Sphuliṅga</s> and <s>agnikaṇa</s> mean a spark; <s>saṃtāpa</s> and <s>saṃjvara</s> both mean burning heat.
<s>Ulkā</s> is a flame that has shot forth; <s>bhasita</s> and <s>bhasman</s> mean ash.

children.text: kṣāro rakṣā ca dāvastu davo vanahutāśanaḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Kṣāra</s> and <s>rakṣā</s> are ash-like residues; <s>dāva</s>, <s>dava</s>, and <s>vanahutāśana</s> mean forest fire.
<s>Dharmarāja</s>, <s>Pitṛpati</s>, <s>Samavartin</s>, and <s>Paretarāṭ</s> are names of <s>Yama</s>.
<s>Kṛtānta</s>, <s>Yamunābhrātā</s>, <s>Śamana</s>, <s>Yamarāṭ</s>, and <s>Yama</s> are also his names.
<s>Kāla</s>, <s>Daṇḍadhara</s>, <s>Śrāddhadeva</s>, <s>Vaivasvata</s>, and <s>Antaka</s> are further names of <s>Yama</s>.
<s>Rākṣasa</s>, <s>Koṇapa</s>, <s>Kravyāt</s>, <s>Kravyāda</s>, <s>Asrapa</s>, and <s>Āśara</s> denote a demon or flesh-eater.
<s>Rātriṃcara</s>, <s>Rātricara</s>, <s>Karbura</s>, and <s>Nikaṣātmaja</s> are also terms for a rākṣasa.
<s>Yātudhāna</s>, <s>Puṇyajana</s>, <s>Nairṛta</s>, <s>Yātu</s>, and <s>Rākṣasa</s> are further terms for such beings.
<s>Pracetas</s>, <s>Varuṇa</s>, <s>Pāśin</s>, lord of aquatic beings, and lord of waters are names of <s>Varuṇa</s>.
<s>Śvasana</s>, <s>Sparśana</s>, <s>Vāyu</s>, <s>Mātariśvan</s>, and <s>Sadāgati</s> are names of wind.
<s>Pṛṣadaśva</s>, <s>Gandhavaha</s>, <s>Gandhavāha</s>, <s>Anila</s>, and <s>Āśuga</s> are also names of wind.
<s>Samīra</s>, <s>Māruta</s>, <s>Marut</s>, <s>Jagatprāṇa</s>, and <s>Samīraṇa</s> are further names of wind.
<s>Nabhasvat</s>, <s>Vāta</s>, <s>Pavana</s>, <s>Pavamāna</s>, and <s>Prabhañjana</s> are likewise names of wind.
<s>Prakampana</s> means a great wind; <s>Jhañjhāvāta</s> is a great wind accompanied by rain.
<s>Prāṇa</s>, <s>Apāna</s>, <s>Samāna</s>, <s>Udāna</s>, and <s>Vyāna</s> are the bodily winds.

children.text: śarīrasthā ime raṃhastarasī tu rayaḥ syadaḥ
children.translated_text: These are located in the body; <s>raṃhas</s>, <s>taras</s>, <s>raya</s>, and <s>syada</s> denote speed or force.

children.text: javo 'tha śīghraṃ tvaritaṃ laghu kṣipramaraṃ drutam ||
children.translated_text: <s>Java</s> means speed; quickness is expressed by <s>śīghra</s>, <s>tvarita</s>, <s>laghu</s>, <s>kṣipra</s>, <s>aram</s>, and <s>druta</s>.

children.text: satvaraṃ capalaṃ tūrṇam avilambitam āśu ca
children.translated_text: <s>Satvara</s>, <s>capala</s>, <s>tūrṇa</s>, <s>avilambita</s>, and <s>āśu</s> also mean quick or prompt.
For constancy, the words are <s>satata</s>, <s>anārata</s>, <s>aśrānta</s>, <s>saṃtata</s>, <s>avirata</s>, and <s>aniśam</s>.
<s>Nitya</s>, <s>anavarata</s>, and <s>ajasra</s> also mean continual; <s>atiśaya</s> and <s>bhara</s> mean excess.
<s>Ativela</s>, <s>bhṛśa</s>, <s>atyartha</s>, <s>atimātra</s>, <s>udgāḍha</s>, and <s>nirbhara</s> mean very great or excessive.
<s>Tīvra</s>, <s>ekānta</s>, <s>nitānta</s>, <s>gāḍha</s>, <s>bāḍha</s>, and <s>dṛḍha</s> also express intensity or firmness.

children.text: klībe śīghrādyasattve syāt triṣveṣāṃ sattvagāmi yat ||
children.translated_text: Words such as <s>śīghra</s> are neuter when used abstractly; when they qualify a concrete thing, they take all three genders.
For <s>Kubera</s>: <s>Kubera</s>, friend of <s>Tryambaka</s>, king of the yakṣas, and lord of the guhyakas are names of him.
<s>Manuṣyadharman</s>, <s>Dhanada</s>, <s>Rājarāja</s>, and <s>Dhanādhipa</s> are further names for him.
<s>Kiṃnareśa</s>, <s>Vaiśravaṇa</s>, <s>Paulastya</s>, and <s>Naravāhana</s> are also names of <s>Kubera</s>.
<s>Yakṣa</s>, <s>Ekapiṅga</s>, <s>Ailavila</s>, <s>Śrīda</s>, and <s>Puṇyajaneśvara</s> are additional names for him.
His pleasure-garden is <s>Caitraratha</s>, and his son is <s>Nalakūbara</s>.

children.text: kailāsaḥ sthānamalakā pūr vimānaṃ tu puṣpakam ||
children.translated_text: His abode is <s>Kailāsa</s>, his city is <s>Alakā</s>, and his aerial car is <s>Puṣpaka</s>.
A <s>Kiṃnara</s> is also called a <s>Kimpuruṣa</s>, horse-faced, and <s>Mayu</s>.
Nidhi and śevadhi are masculine words for treasure; the kinds of treasure begin with <s>Padma</s> and <s>Śaṅkha</s>.
The nine treasures include <s>Mahāpadma</s>, <s>Padma</s>, <s>Śaṅkha</s>, <s>Makara</s>, and <s>Kacchapa</s>,
and <s>Mukunda</s>, <s>Kunda</s>, <s>Nīla</s>, and <s>Kharva</s>; these are the nine nidhis.
Dyo and div are two feminine words; abhra, vyoman, puṣkara, and ambara denote the sky.
Nabhas, antarikṣa, gagana, ananta, suravartman, and kha are also words for the sky.
Viyat and <s>Viṣṇupada</s> may also denote it; ākāśa and vihāyas are masculine.

children.text: vihāsayo 'pi nāko 'pi dyur api syāt tadavyam ||
children.translated_text: Vihāsa, nāka, and dyu may also be used for that sky, with indeclinable usage noted.
Tārāpatha, antarikṣa, meghādhvan, and mahābila are further words for the firmament.
Vihāyas is masculine when it means a bird; when it means the sky, it is masculine or neuter.

children.text: diśastu kakubhaḥ kāṣṭhā āśāśca haritaśca tāḥ
children.translated_text: The directions are called kakubh, kāṣṭhā, āśā, and harit, all feminine.
The eastern, southern, and western directions are prācī, avācī, and pratīcī respectively.

children.text: uttarā dig udīcī syād diśyaṃ tu triṣu digbhave
children.translated_text: The northern direction is udīcī; diśya, meaning produced in a direction, is used in all three genders.
Avāgbhava and avācīna mean southern; udīcīna and udagbhava mean northern.
Pratyagbhava and pratīcīna mean western, while prācīna and prāgbhava mean eastern; these are used in all three genders.
For the directions in order, the lords are <s>Indra</s>, <s>Vahni</s>, <s>Pitṛpati</s>, <s>Nairṛta</s>, <s>Varuṇa</s>, and <s>Marut</s>,

children.text: kubera īśaḥ patayaḥ pūrvādīnāṃ diśāṃ kramāt
children.translated_text: <s>Kubera</s> and <s>Īśa</s>; these are the rulers of the directions beginning with the east.
In the same directional order the planets are <s>Ravi</s>, <s>Śukra</s>, <s>Mahīsānu</s>, <s>Svarbhānu</s>, <s>Bhānuja</s>, and <s>Vidhu</s>,

children.text: budho bṛhaspatiś ceti diśāṃ caiva tathā grahāḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Budha</s> and <s>Bṛhaspati</s>; these likewise are the planets of the directions.
The elephants of the directions are <s>Airāvata</s>, <s>Puṇḍarīka</s>, <s>Vāmana</s>, <s>Kumuda</s>, and <s>Añjana</s>,
<s>Puṣpadanta</s>, <s>Sārvabhauma</s>, and <s>Supratīka</s>.
Their female elephants, in order, are <s>Abhramu</s>, <s>Kapilā</s>, <s>Piṅgalā</s>, and <s>Anupamā</s>,
<s>Tāmrakarṇī</s>, <s>Śubhradantī</s>, <s>Aṅganā</s>, and <s>Añjanāvatī</s>.

children.text: klībāvyayaṃ tv apadiśaṃ diśormadhye vidik striyām ||
children.translated_text: Apadiś is a neuter indeclinable; vidik, feminine, is the intermediate direction between two directions.

children.text: abhyantaraṃ tv antarālaṃ cakravālaṃ tu maṇḍalam
children.translated_text: Abhyantara and antarāla mean an inside space; cakravāla means a circular boundary or ring.
Abhra, megha, vārivāha, stanayitnu, and balāhaka are words for cloud.
Dhārādhara, jaladhara, taḍitvat, vārida, and ambubhṛt also denote a cloud.
Ghana, jīmūta, mudira, jalamuc, and dhūmayoni are further cloud names.
Kādambinī and meghamālā mean a mass or row of clouds; abhriya, in all three genders, means cloud-born.
Stanita and garjita, and rasita and the like, denote the sound of clouds, thunder.
Śampā, śatahradā, hrādinī, airāvatī, and kṣaṇaprabhā are names of lightning.

children.text: taḍit saudāmanī vidyuc cañcalā capalā api ||
children.translated_text: Taḍit, saudāmanī, vidyut, cañcalā, and capalā also denote lightning.
Sphūrjathu and vajranirghoṣa denote the thunderous crash; meghajyotis and iraṃmada denote lightning.
<s>Indrāyudha</s> and <s>Śakradhanus</s> are the rainbow; the same, when straight and red, is called ṛjurohita.
Vṛṣṭi and varṣa mean rain; when rain is checked, avagrāha and avagraha are equivalent terms.
Dhārāsampāta is āsāra, a torrent of rain; śīkara means drops of water.
A hailstone is varṣopala or karakā; a day covered by clouds is durdina.

children.text: antardhā vyavadhā puṃsi tv antardhir apavāraṇam ||
children.translated_text: Antardhā and vyavadhā are masculine terms for concealment or obstruction; antardhi and apavāraṇa also mean covering.
Apidhāna, tirodhāna, pidhāna, and ācchādana likewise mean covering or concealment.
Names of the moon include <s>Himāṃśu</s>, <s>Candramas</s>, <s>Candra</s>, <s>Indu</s>, and <s>Kumudabāndhava</s>.
They also include <s>Vidhu</s>, <s>Sudhāṃśu</s>, <s>Śubhrāṃśu</s>, <s>Oṣadhīśa</s>, and <s>Niśāpati</s>.

children.text: abjo jaivātṛkaḥ somo glaur mṛgāṅkaḥ kalānidhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Abja</s>, <s>Jaivātṛka</s>, <s>Soma</s>, <s>Glau</s>, <s>Mṛgāṅka</s>, and <s>Kalānidhi</s> are further names of the moon.
<s>Dvijarāja</s>, <s>Śaśadhara</s>, <s>Nakṣatreśa</s>, and <s>Kṣapākara</s> are also moon names.

children.text: kalā tu ṣoḍaśo bhāgo bimbo 'strī maṇḍalaṃ triṣu ||
children.translated_text: Kalā means a sixteenth part; bimba and maṇḍala denote a disk, with maṇḍala used in all three genders.
Bhitta means a fragment or piece; ardha, masculine, and ardham, neuter, mean half or equal share.

children.text: candrikā kaumudī jyotsnā prasādas tu prasannatā ||
children.translated_text: Candrikā, kaumudī, and jyotsnā mean moonlight; prasāda means clearness or serenity.

children.text: kalaṅkāṅkau lāñchanaṃ ca cihnaṃ lakṣma ca lakṣaṇam
children.translated_text: Kalaṅka, aṅka, lāñchana, cihna, lakṣma, and lakṣaṇa mean a mark or characteristic sign.

children.text: suṣamā paramā śobhā śobhā kāntir dyutiś chaviḥ ||
children.translated_text: Suṣamā is surpassing beauty; śobhā, kānti, dyuti, and chavi mean splendor or radiance.
Avaśyāya, nīhāra, tuṣāra, tuhina, and hima are words for dew, frost, or snow.
Prāleya and mihikā are also such words; himānī means a mass of snow.

children.text: śītaṃ guṇe tadvadarthāḥ suṣīmaḥ śiśiro jaḍaḥ
children.translated_text: Śīta means cold as a quality; words meaning possessed of cold are suṣīma, śiśira, and jaḍa,
tuṣāra, śītala, śīta, and hima; these seven adjectives take other genders.
<s>Dhruva</s> is called <s>Auttānapādi</s>; <s>Agastya</s> is <s>Kumbhasambhava</s>.
He is also <s>Maitrāvaruṇi</s>; <s>Lopāmudrā</s> is his lawful wife.

children.text: nakṣatramṛkṣaṃ bhaṃ tārā tārakāpyuḍu vā striyām
children.translated_text: Nakṣatra, ṛkṣa, bha, tārā, tārakā, and also uḍu in the feminine denote a star or lunar mansion.
The stars beginning with <s>Aśvinī</s> are the <s>Dākṣāyiṇīs</s>; <s>Aśvayuj</s> and <s>Aśvinī</s> name the first mansion.
<s>Rādhā</s> is <s>Viśākhā</s>; for <s>Puṣya</s> the names are <s>Sidhya</s> and <s>Tiṣya</s>; with <s>Śraviṣṭhā</s>,

children.text: samā dhaniṣṭhāḥ syuḥ proṣṭhapadā bhādrapadāḥ striyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Dhaniṣṭhā</s> is synonymous; <s>Proṣṭhapadā</s> and <s>Bhādrapadā</s> are feminine names.
<s>Mṛgaśīrṣa</s> and <s>Mṛgaśiras</s> are the same; <s>Āgrahāyaṇī</s> also belongs to that mansion.
<s>Ilvalās</s> are the stars that occupy the region of its head.
Names of <s>Bṛhaspati</s> are <s>Bṛhaspati</s>, <s>Surācārya</s>, <s>Gīṣpati</s>, <s>Dhiṣaṇa</s>, and <s>Guru</s>.
<s>Jīva</s>, <s>Āṅgirasa</s>, <s>Vācaspati</s>, and <s>Citraśikhaṇḍija</s> are also names of <s>Bṛhaspati</s>.

children.text: śukro daityaguruḥ kāvya uśanā bhārgavaḥ kaviḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Śukra</s>, <s>Daityaguru</s>, <s>Kāvya</s>, <s>Uśanas</s>, <s>Bhārgava</s>, and <s>Kavi</s> are names of <s>Śukra</s>.
<s>Aṅgāraka</s>, <s>Kuja</s>, <s>Bhauma</s>, <s>Lohitāṅga</s>, and <s>Mahīsuta</s> are names of the planet Mars.
<s>Rauhiṇeya</s>, <s>Budha</s>, and <s>Saumya</s> name Mercury; <s>Sauri</s> and <s>Śanaiścara</s> are equivalent names for Saturn.

children.text: tamas tu rāhuḥ svarbhānuḥ saiṃhikeyo vidhuṃtudaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Rāhu</s>, <s>Svarbhānu</s>, <s>Saiṃhikeya</s>, and <s>Vidhuṃtuda</s> are names of the dark eclipse-being.
The Seven Seers, beginning with <s>Marīci</s> and <s>Atri</s>, are called <s>Citraśikhaṇḍins</s>.

children.text: rāśīnām udayo lagnaṃ te tu meṣavṛṣādayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The rising of a zodiac sign is lagna; those signs begin with <s>Meṣa</s> and <s>Vṛṣa</s>.
Names of the sun include <s>Sūra</s>, <s>Sūrya</s>, <s>Āryaman</s>, <s>Āditya</s>, <s>Dvādaśātman</s>, and <s>Divākara</s>,
<s>Bhāskara</s>, <s>Ahaskara</s>, <s>Bradhna</s>, <s>Prabhākara</s>, and <s>Vibhākara</s>.
Names of the Sun include <s>Bhāsvat</s>, <s>Vivasvat</s>, <s>Saptāśva</s>, <s>Haridaśva</s>, and <s>Uṣṇaraśmi</s>.
Also <s>Vikartana</s>, <s>Arka</s>, <s>Mārtaṇḍa</s>, <s>Mihira</s>, <s>Aruṇa</s>, and <s>Pūṣan</s> are names of the Sun.
<s>Dyumaṇi</s>, <s>Taraṇi</s>, <s>Mitra</s>, <s>Citrabhānu</s>, and <s>Virocana</s> are further names of the Sun.
So too are <s>Vibhāvasu</s>, <s>Grahapati</s>, <s>Tviṣāmpati</s>, and <s>Aharpati</s>.
<s>Bhānu</s>, <s>Haṃsa</s>, <s>Sahasrāṃśu</s>, <s>Tapana</s>, <s>Savitṛ</s>, and <s>Ravi</s> are names of the Sun.
<s>Padmākṣa</s>, <s>Tejasāṃrāśi</s>, <s>Chāyānātha</s>, and <s>Tamisrahā</s> are also names of the Sun.
<s>Karmasākṣin</s>, <s>Jagaccakṣus</s>, <s>Lokabandhu</s>, and <s>Trayītanu</s> are likewise names of the Sun.
<s>Pradyotana</s>, <s>Dinamaṇi</s>, <s>Khadyota</s>, and <s>Lokabāndhava</s> are names of the Sun.
<s>Ina</s>, <s>Bhaga</s>, <s>Bhāmanidhi</s>, <s>Aṃśumālin</s>, and <s>Añjinīpati</s> are further solar names.
<s>Māṭhara</s>, <s>Piṅgala</s>, and <s>Daṇḍa</s> are the attendants of the fierce-rayed Sun.
The Sun's charioteer is called <s>Sūrasūta</s>, <s>Aruṇa</s>, <s>Anūru</s>, <s>Kāśyapi</s>, and <s>Garuḍāgraja</s>.
A halo around the solar or lunar orb is called pariveṣa, paridhi, or upasūryaka-maṇḍala.
Kiraṇa, usra, mayūkha, aṃśu, gabhasti, ghṛṇi, and raśmi are words for a ray.
Bhānu, kara, and marīci also mean ray; dīdhiti is used in both masculine and feminine, especially as feminine.

children.text: syuḥ prabhā rug rucis tviḍ bhābhāś chavidyutidīptayaḥ
children.translated_text: Prabhā, rug, ruci, tviṣ, bhā, bhās, chavi, dyuti, and dīpti are words for radiance or light.

children.text: rociḥ śocir ubhe klībe prakāśo dyota ātapaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Rocis and śocis are both neuter words for light; prakāśa, dyota, and ātapa mean brightness or heat.

children.text: koṣṇaṃ kavoṣṇaṃ mandoṣṇaṃ kaduṣṇaṃ triṣu tadvati
children.translated_text: Koṣṇa, kavoṣṇa, mandoṣṇa, and kaduṣṇa mean lukewarm, and are used in all three genders for something of that quality.

children.text: tigmaṃ tīkṣṇaṃ kharaṃ tadvan mṛgatṛṣṇā marīcikā ||
children.translated_text: Tigma, tīkṣṇa, and khara mean sharp or intense; mṛgatṛṣṇā and marīcikā mean a mirage.

children.text: kālo diṣṭo 'py anehāpi samayo 'py atha pakṣatiḥ
children.translated_text: Kāla, diṣṭa, anehas, and samaya are words for time; next, pakṣati is mentioned.

children.text: pratipad dve ime strītve tadādyāstithayo dvayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: Pakṣati and pratipad are feminine words; the lunar days beginning with pratipad are called tithis, in either of two genders.

children.text: ghasro dināhanī vā tu klībe divasavāsarau
children.translated_text: Ghasra, dina, and ahan are words for day; divasa and vāsara are also neuter words for day.
Pratyūṣa, aharmukha, and kalya mean dawn; uṣas and pratyuṣas also mean dawn.

children.text: vyuṣṭaṃ vibhātaṃ dve klībe puṃsi gosarga iṣyate
children.translated_text: Vyuṣṭa and vibhāta are two neuter words for daybreak; gosarga is accepted as masculine.

children.text: prabhātaṃ ca dinānte tu sāyaṃ saṃdhyā pitṛprasūḥ ||
children.translated_text: Prabhāta too means morning; at the end of the day, sāyam, saṃdhyā, and pitṛprasū mean evening twilight.
Prāhṇa, aparāhṇa, and madhyāhna denote forenoon, afternoon, and midday; trisaṃdhya denotes the three twilights, and then come terms for night.
Śarvarī, niśā, niśīthinī, rātri, triyāmā, kṣaṇadā, and kṣapā are feminine words for night.
Vibhāvarī, tamasvinī, rajanī, yāminī, and tamī are also words for night.
Tamisrā and tāmasī mean a dark night; jyautsnī is a moonlit night, one furnished with moonlight.
A night joined to both the coming and the present day is called pakṣiṇī.
Many nights together are called gaṇarātra; pradoṣa is the opening of night.
Ardharātra and niśītha both mean midnight; yāma and prahara are equivalent words for a watch of the night or day.
The interval between the first lunar day and the fifteenth is called a parvasaṃdhi, a junction of the fortnight.

children.text: pakṣāntau pañcadaśyau dve paurṇamāsī tu paurṇimā
children.translated_text: The two fifteenth lunar days are the ends of the fortnights; paurṇamāsī is the same as paurṇimā, the full-moon day.
When the Moon lacks a digit that full-moon day is anumati; when the Moon is complete it is rākā.
Amāvāsyā, also amāvasyā, is called darśa, the conjunction of Sun and Moon.

children.text: sā dṛṣṭenduḥ sinīvālī sā naṣṭendukalā kuhūḥ ||
children.translated_text: That new-moon day is sinīvālī when the Moon is seen, and kuhū when its lunar digit has disappeared.

children.text: uparāgo graho rāhugraste tv indau ca pūṣṇi ca
children.translated_text: Uparāga and graha denote an eclipse, when the Moon or the Sun is seized by <s>Rāhu</s>.
Sopaplava and uparakta both mean eclipsed or afflicted; an upāhita is a fiery portent.
By a single expression, the Sun and Moon, the makers of day and night, are called puṣpavantau.

children.text: aṣṭādaśa nimeṣāstu kāṣṭhā triṃśat tu tāḥ kalā ||
children.translated_text: Eighteen nimeṣas make a kāṣṭhā, and thirty kāṣṭhās make a kalā.

children.text: tāstu triṃśat kṣaṇaste tu muhūrto dvādaśāstriyām
children.translated_text: Thirty kalās make a kṣaṇa, and twelve kṣaṇas make a muhūrta, a word not feminine.

children.text: te tu triṃśadahorātraḥ pakṣaste daśapañca ca ||
children.translated_text: Thirty muhūrtas make an ahorātra, a day and night; fifteen of these make a pakṣa, a fortnight.

children.text: pakṣau pūrvāparau śuklakṛṣṇau māsastu tāv ubhau
children.translated_text: The two fortnights are the earlier and later, the bright and dark; the two together make a month.

children.text: dvau dvau mārgādi māsau syādṛtustairayanaṃ tribhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Two months each, beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, make a season, and three such seasons make an ayana.
The two ayanas are the Sun's northern and southern courses; together they make a year.
The time when night and day are equal is called viṣuvat or viṣuva.

children.text: puṣpayuktā paurṇamāsī pauṣī māse tu yatra sā
children.translated_text: The full-moon day joined with Puṣya gives the month in which it occurs the name Pauṣa.

children.text: nāmnā sa pauṣo māghādyāś caivam ekādaśāpare ||
children.translated_text: In the same way the other eleven months, beginning with Māgha, are named from their corresponding full-moon asterisms.
Mārgaśīrṣa is also called Saha, Mārga, and Āgrahāyaṇika.

children.text: pauṣe taiṣasahasyau dvau tapā māghe 'tha phālgune ||
children.translated_text: Pauṣa has the two names Taiṣa and Sahasya; Māgha is called Tapas.
Phālguna is called Tapasya and Phālgunika; Caitra is called Caitrika and Madhu.

children.text: vaiśākhe mādhavo rādho jyeṣṭhe śukraḥ śucistvayam ||
children.translated_text: Vaiśākha is called Mādhava and Rādha; Jyeṣṭha is called Śukra, and Śuci denotes the next month.

children.text: āṣāḍhe śrāvaṇe tu syānnabhāḥ śrāvaṇikaśca saḥ
children.translated_text: Śuci is Āṣāḍha; Śrāvaṇa is called Nabhas and Śrāvaṇika.
Nabhasya, Prauṣṭhapada, Bhādra, and Bhādrapada are equivalent names for the following month.
Āśvina is also called Iṣa and Āśvayuja; next comes Kārtika.
Bāhula and Ūrja are names of Kārtika; Hemanta and Śiśira are non-feminine names of seasons.
In spring, Vasanta is called Puṣpasamaya and Surabhi; Grīṣma is called Ūṣmaka.
Grīṣma is also Nidāgha, Uṣṇopagama, Uṣṇa, Ūṣmāgama, and Tapas.

children.text: striyāṃ prāvṛṭ striyāṃ bhūmni varṣā atha śaratstriyām
children.translated_text: Prāvṛṭ is feminine; Varṣā, in common usage, is feminine; then Śarad is feminine.

children.text: ṣaḍamī ṛtavaḥ puṃsi mārgādīnāṃ yugaiḥ kramāt ||
children.translated_text: These six seasons are masculine, arranged in order by pairs of months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa.
Saṃvatsara, vatsara, abda, hāyana, śarat, and samā are words for year, with varying gender.
For the ancestors, a day and night is made by a month; for the gods, by a year.

children.text: daive yugasahasre dve brāhmaḥ kalpau tu tau nṝṇām
children.translated_text: In divine reckoning, two thousand yugas constitute the two kalpas of <s>Brahmā</s>, while for human beings they are kalpas.
A manvantara is seventy-one divine yugas.

children.text: saṃvartaḥ pralayaḥ kalpaḥ kṣayaḥ kalpānta ityapi
children.translated_text: Saṃvarta, pralaya, kalpa, kṣaya, and kalpānta are words for dissolution or the end of a kalpa.
Paṅka is neuter, pāpmā is masculine, and pāpa, kilbiṣa, and kalmaṣa are words for sin or evil.
Kaluṣa, vṛjina, enas, agha, aṃhas, durita, and duṣkṛta are also words for sin or wrongdoing.
Dharma, used in neuter as well, puṇya, śreyas, sukṛta, and vṛṣa are words for merit or righteousness.
Mut, prīti, pramada, harṣa, pramoda, āmoda, and saṃmada are words for joy or delight.
Ānandathu and ānanda mean happiness; śarman, śāta, and sukha also mean happiness or ease.

children.text: śvaḥ śreyasaṃ śivaṃ bhadraṃ kalyāṇaṃ maṅgalaṃ śubham
children.translated_text: Śvas, śreyas, śiva, bhadra, kalyāṇa, maṅgala, and śubha are words for what is auspicious or good.
Bhāvuka, bhavika, bhavya, kuśala, and kṣema are also non-feminine words for welfare or good fortune.

children.text: śastaṃ cātha triṣu dravye pāpaṃ puṇyaṃ sukhādi ca
children.translated_text: Śasta is another such word; when qualifying a thing, pāpa, puṇya, sukha, and the like are used in all three genders.
Matallikā, macarcikā, prakāṇḍa, uddha, and tallaja are terms expressing excellence.
These words denote what is praised or excellent; ayaḥ and vidhi mean an auspicious, welfare-bringing destiny.

children.text: daivaṃ diṣṭaṃ bhāgadheyaṃ bhāgyaṃ strī niyatirvidhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Daiva, diṣṭa, bhāgadheya, and bhāgya mean fate or fortune; niyati and vidhi are feminine terms for it.

children.text: hetur nā kāraṇaṃ bījaṃ nidānaṃ tv ādikāraṇam
children.translated_text: Hetu, kāraṇa, and bīja mean cause; nidāna is an original or primary cause.

children.text: kṣetrajña ātmā puruṣaḥ pradhānaṃ prakṛtiḥ striyām ||
children.translated_text: Kṣetrajña, ātman, and puruṣa denote the self; pradhāna and the feminine prakṛti denote primordial nature.
A temporally conditioned distinction is an avasthā, a state; the guṇas are sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Januḥ, janana, and janman mean birth; jani, utpatti, and udbhava mean arising or origin.
Prāṇin, cetana, janmin, jantu, janyu, and śarīrin are terms for a living embodied being.
Jāti and jāta mean class or generality; vyakti is separate individuality.

children.text: cittaṃ tu ceto hṛdayaṃ svāntaṃ hṛnmānasaṃ manaḥ
children.translated_text: Citta, cetas, hṛdaya, svānta, hṛd, mānasa, and manas are terms for the mind or inner heart.

children.text: buddhirmanīṣā dhiṣaṇā dhīḥ prajñā śemuṣī matiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Buddhi, manīṣā, dhiṣaṇā, dhī, prajñā, śemuṣī, and mati mean intelligence or understanding.
Prekṣā, upalabdhi, cit, saṃvit, pratipatti, jñapti, and cetanā are terms for awareness or cognition.

children.text: dhīr dhāraṇāvatī medhā saṃkalpaḥ karma mānasam ||
children.translated_text: Medhā is dhī endowed with retention; saṃkalpa is a mental act or resolve.
Avadhāna, samādhāna, and likewise praṇidhāna mean attention or concentrated application.
Cittābhoga, manaskāra, carcā, saṃkhyā, and vicāraṇā denote consideration or reflection.

children.text: vimarśo bhāvanā caiva vāsanā ca nigadyate
children.translated_text: Vimarśa, bhāvanā, and vāsanā are likewise named as modes of reflection, cultivation, or mental impression.
Adhyāhāra, tarka, and ūha mean supposition or reasoning; vicikitsā means doubt.
Saṃdeha and dvāpara also mean doubt; nirṇaya and niścaya are equivalent terms for determination.
Mithyādṛṣṭi is nāstikatā, false or unbelieving view; vyāpāda is thought of hostility or harm.
Siddhānta and rāddhānta are equivalent terms for established doctrine; bhrānti, mithyāmati, and bhrama mean error or delusion.
Saṃvid, āgūḥ, pratijñāna, niyama, āśrava, and saṃśrava mean agreement, promise, or undertaking.
Aṅgīkāra, abhyupagama, pratiśrava, and samādhi are also terms for acceptance or assent.

children.text: mokṣe dhīr jñānam anyatra vijñānaṃ śilpaśāstrayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: With reference to liberation, dhī is jñāna, knowledge; elsewhere vijñāna denotes skill in arts and sciences.
Mukti, kaivalya, nirvāṇa, śreyas, niḥśreyasa, and amṛta are names of liberation.
Mokṣa and apavarga also mean liberation; ajñāna, avidyā, and the feminine ahaṃmati mean ignorance or ego-notion.
Form, sound, smell, taste, and touch are these viṣayas, the sense-objects.
They are also called gocara and indriyārtha; hṛṣīka and indriya denote the sense faculty that has an object.
The organs of action are those beginning with the anus; the cognitive senses are mind, eye, and the like.

children.text: tuvaras tu kaṣāyo 'strī madhuro lavaṇaḥ kaṭuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Tuvara or kaṣāya denotes the astringent taste; sweet, salty, and pungent are also listed among tastes.

children.text: tikto 'mlaśca rasāḥ puṃsi tadvatsu ṣaḍamī triṣu
children.translated_text: Together with bitter and sour, these are the six rasas, named in the masculine; when applied to things possessing them, they take all three genders.
Parimala is fragrance produced by rubbing, a scent that delights people.
When that scent carries very far it is āmoda; as a quality-word, its grammatical gender follows the thing qualified.
Samākarṣin and nirhārin describe a far-drawing fragrance; surabhi and ghrāṇatarpaṇa mean pleasing to the nose.
Iṣṭagandha, sugandhi, āmodin, and mukhavāsana mean sweet-smelling or perfumed.
Pūtigandha and durgandha mean foul-smelling; what smells raw or fetid is visra or āmagandhi.
Śukla, śubhra, śuci, śveta, viśada, śyeta, and pāṇḍara are terms for white.
Avadāta, sita, gaura, avalakṣa, dhavala, and arjuna also mean white or bright.
Hariṇa, pāṇḍura, and pāṇḍu mean pale; slightly pale or greyish is dhūsara.
For black, the terms are nīla, asita, śyāma, kāla, śyāmala, and mecaka.

children.text: pīto gauro haridrābhaḥ palāśo harito harit
children.translated_text: Pīta, gaura, haridrābha, and palāśa mean yellow; harita and harit mean green or yellow-green.
Lohita, rohita, rakta, śoṇa, and kokanadacchavi mean red, lotus-colored.
Aruṇa means faintly red; pāṭala means white mixed with red, that is, pink.
Śyāva and kapiśa denote dark brown or tawny; dhūmra and dhūmala denote smoky black-red.
Kaḍāra, kapila, piṅga, piśaṅga, kadru, and piṅgala are tawny or brown color terms.
Citra, kirmīra, kalmāṣa, śabala, and karbura mean variegated, mottled, or spotted.
When denoting the quality, words such as śukla are masculine; when denoting a thing possessing that quality, they take that thing's gender.

children.text: brāhmī tu bhāratī bhāṣā gīr vāg vāṇī sarasvatī ||
children.translated_text: Brāhmī, <s>Bhāratī</s>, bhāṣā, gīr, vāk, vāṇī, and <s>Sarasvatī</s> are terms for speech or language.

children.text: vyāhāra uktir lapitaṃ bhāṣitaṃ vacanaṃ vacaḥ
children.translated_text: Vyāhāra, ukti, lapita, bhāṣita, vacana, and vacas mean utterance or spoken expression.
Apabhraṃśa and apaśabda mean a corrupt or improper word; in śāstra, śabda is a signifying expression.

children.text: tiṅ subantacayo vākyaṃ kriyā vā kārakānvitā
children.translated_text: A vākya, sentence, is a collection of finite verb forms and nominal forms, or an action furnished with its kārakas.

children.text: śrutiḥ strī veda āmnāyastrayī dharmastu tadvidhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Śruti is feminine; Veda, āmnāya, and trayī denote sacred revelation, while dharma is its injunction.
Ṛk, Sāman, and Yajus are the three Vedas, collectively called the Trayī.
Śikṣā and the rest are limbs of śruti; oṃkāra and praṇava are equivalent terms.
Itihāsa is an account of ancient events; the three accents are udātta and the others.
Ānvīkṣikī is the science of reasoning, and daṇḍanīti is arthaśāstra, the science of polity.
An ākhyāyikā is a narrative of an attested matter; a purāṇa is marked by the five characteristics.
Kathā is a composed or imagined narrative; pravahlikā and prahelikā mean a riddle.
Smṛti is a dharma-compendium; samāhṛti and saṃgraha mean collection.
Samasyā has a condensed or compound meaning; kiṃvadantī and janaśruti mean rumor or popular report.
Vārttā, pravṛtti, vṛttānta, and udanta mean news or an account; then āhvaya means a name.

children.text: ākhyāhve abhidhānaṃ ca nāmadheyaṃ ca nāma ca ||
children.translated_text: Ākhyā, āhvā, abhidhāna, nāmadheya, and nāman all mean name or designation.
Hūti, ākāraṇa, and āhvāna mean calling or summoning; saṃhūti is a summons made by many.
Vivāda and vyavahāra mean dispute or litigation; upanyāsa is the opening of speech.
Upodghāta is an introduction, and udāhāra an example; śapana and the masculine śapatha mean an oath or imprecation.
Praśna, anuyoga, and pṛcchā mean a question; prativākya and uttara are equivalent terms for an answer.
Mithyābhiyoga, abhyākhyāna, and mithyābhiśaṃsana mean false accusation.
Abhiśāpa means a curse; praṇāda is a sound arising from affection or passion.

children.text: yaśaḥ kīrtiḥ samajñā ca stavaḥ stotraṃ stutirnutiḥ
children.translated_text: Yaśas, kīrti, and samajñā mean fame; stava, stotra, stuti, and nuti mean praise.
Āmreḍita is something said twice or three times; what is loudly proclaimed is ghoṣaṇā.
Kāku, feminine, is the alteration of voice caused by grief, fear, and the like.
Avarṇa, ākṣepa, nirvāda, parīvāda, and apavāda are terms connected with disparagement.

children.text: upakrośo jugupsā ca kutsā nindā ca garhaṇe
children.translated_text: Upakrośa, jugupsā, kutsā, and nindā likewise mean blame or censure.
Pāruṣya and ativāda mean harsh speech; bhartsana is speech threatening harm.
An upālambha accompanied by blame is called paribhāṣaṇa.

children.text: tatra tv ākṣāraṇā yaḥ syādākrośo maithunaṃ prati ||
children.translated_text: In that sphere, abuse referring to sexual intercourse is ākṣāraṇā, a form of ākrośa.
Ābhāṣaṇa and ālāpa mean address or conversation; pralāpa is meaningless speech.
Anulāpa is repeated speaking; vilāpa is lamentation.
Vipralāpa is contradictory speech; saṃlāpa is mutual conversation.
Supralāpa and suvacana mean good or pleasant speech; apalāpa means denial or disavowal.
Codya, ākṣepa, and abhiyoga denote an accusation or charge; śāpa and ākrośa denote cursing and abusive reviling.

children.text: astrī cāṭu caṭu ślāghā premṇā mithyāvikatthanam ||
children.translated_text: Cāṭu, also caṭu, is non-feminine and means flattery: false exaggeration or praise made out of affection.
Saṃdeśavāk and vācika denote an oral message; the following varieties of speech are used in all three genders.

children.text: ruśatī vāg akalyāṇī syātkalyā tu śubhātmikā ||
children.translated_text: Ruśatī is inauspicious or hurtful speech, while kalyā is speech of an auspicious nature.
Sāntva is speech that is exceedingly sweet; saṃgata and hṛdayaṃgama mean agreeable, going to the heart.
Niṣṭhura and paruṣa mean harsh; grāmya and aślīla mean vulgar or obscene; sūnṛta means pleasing, kindly speech.
Sūnṛta is also used of truthful speech; saṃkula and kliṣṭa mean confused speech whose parts strike against one another.
Grasta is speech in which letters or words are lost; nirasta is speech uttered hastily.
Jambūkṛta is speech accompanied by spitting; abaddha is meaningless speech.
Anakṣara and avācya mean inarticulate or unutterable speech; āhata is speech with a false meaning.
Sotprāsa is speech with mocking or playful derision; maṇita is the cooing sound of love-play.
Śrāvya, hṛdya, and manohāri mean pleasant to hear, pleasing, and charming; vispaṣṭa is speech clearly and openly uttered.

children.text: atha mliṣṭamavispaṣṭaṃ vitathaṃ tv anṛtaṃ vacaḥ
children.translated_text: Mliṣṭa and avispaṣṭa mean indistinct speech; vitatha and anṛta mean false speech.
Satya, tathya, ṛta, and samyak mean true or correct; when they qualify something possessing that quality, they are used in all three genders.
Śabda, nināda, ninada, dhvani, dhvāna, rava, and svana are words for sound.
Svāna, nirghoṣa, nirhrāda, nāda, nisvāna, and nisvana are also words for sound or resonance.
Ārava, ārāva, saṃrāva, and virāva are further words for sound; marmara denotes a rustling noise.
Marmara is used for the rustling of garments and leaves, while śiñjita denotes the jingling of ornaments.
Nikvāṇa, nikvaṇa, kvāṇa, kvaṇa, and kvaṇana are words for ringing or twanging.
For the twanging of a vīṇā, prefixed forms such as prakvāṇa and prakvaṇa are used.
Kolāhala and kalakala mean clamor or uproar; vāśita and ruta denote the cries of animals.
Pratiśrut, feminine, and pratidhvāna mean echo; gīta and gāna are equivalent words for song.
Niṣāda, Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, and Dhaivata are musical notes.

children.text: pañcamaś cety amī sapta tantrīkaṇṭhotthitāḥ svarāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Together with Pañcama, these are the seven notes produced from strings and the throat.

children.text: kākalī tu kale sūkṣme dhvanī tu madhurāsphuṭe
children.translated_text: Kākalī denotes a fine, delicate tone; dhvani denotes a sweet but indistinct sound.
Kala is a soft tone, mandra a deep one, and tāra a very high one; these three are used in all three genders.
In human beings, musical sound is twenty-twofold; the voice situated in the chest is the low register.
The voice situated in the throat is sung as the middle register, and that in the head as the high register.
A rhythm joined with proper time is ekatāla; vīṇā is also called vallakī.

children.text: tripañcī sā tu tantrībhiḥ saptabhiḥ parivādinī ||
children.translated_text: Tripañcī is a kind of vīṇā; when furnished with seven strings, it is called parivādinī.
Stringed instruments such as the vīṇā are tata; covered drums such as the muraja are ānaddha.
Hollow instruments such as the vaṃśa flute are suṣira; solid instruments such as bronze cymbals are ghana.
This fourfold class of instruments is called vādya, vāditra, and ātodya.

children.text: mṛdaṅgā murajā bhedās tv aṅkyāliṅgyordhvakās trayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Mṛdaṅgas are muraja drums; their three varieties are aṅkya, āliṅgya, and ūrdhvaka.

children.text: syād yaśaḥpaṭaho ḍhakkā bherī strī dundubhiḥ pumān
children.translated_text: Yaśaḥpaṭaha and ḍhakkā are drum terms; bherī is feminine, and dundubhi is masculine.

children.text: ānakaḥ paṭaho 'strī syāt koṇo vīṇādi vādanam ||
children.translated_text: Ānaka and paṭaha are also drum names and are not feminine; koṇa denotes the playing of the vīṇā and similar instruments.
The staff of a vīṇā is called pravāla, and its kakubha is called prasevaka.
The kolambaka is its body, and upanāha means its binding or fastening.
Ḍamaru, maḍḍu, ḍiṇḍima, and jharjhara are varieties of musical instruments.
Mardala, paṇava, and others are additional varieties; nartakī and lāsikā are equivalent words for a female dancer.

children.text: vilambitaṃ drutaṃ madhyaṃ tattvamogho ghanaṃ kramāt
children.translated_text: Vilambita, druta, and madhya are, respectively, the slow, fast, and middle tempos, with the terms tattva, ogha, and ghana in order.
Tāla is the measure of time-units in performance; laya is evenness or keeping time, and it is not feminine.

children.text: tāṇḍavaṃ naṭanaṃ nāṭyaṃ lāsyaṃ nṛtyaṃ ca nartane
children.translated_text: Tāṇḍava, naṭana, nāṭya, lāsya, and nṛtya are words connected with dancing or performance.
Tauryatrika is the triad of dance, song, and instrumental music; nāṭya consists of this threefold performance.

children.text: bhrakuṃsaś ca bhrukuṃsaś ca bhrūkuṃsaśceti nartakaḥ
children.translated_text: Bhrakuṃsa, bhrukuṃsa, and bhrūkuṃsa are words for a dancer.
In theatrical usage, a man wearing women's dress is called gaṇikājjukā.
Ābutta denotes a sister's husband; bhāva denotes a learned man, and āvuka is another dramatic term of address.
Janaka means father; yuvarāja, kumāra, and bhartṛdāraka denote a prince or royal son.
A king is called bhaṭṭāraka or deva, and his daughter is called bhartṛdārikā.
A consecrated queen is devī, while other royal women are called bhaṭṭinī.
Abrahmaṇya is an exclamation used to declare that someone must not be killed; the king's brother-in-law is called rāṣṭriya.
Ambā means mother; bālā and vāsū are terms for a young girl; ārya is equivalent to māriṣa as an address.
Attikā denotes an elder sister; niṣṭhā and nirvahaṇa are equivalent words for completion or conclusion.

children.text: haṇḍe hañje halāhvāne nīcāṃ ceṭīṃ sakhīṃ prati ||
children.translated_text: Haṇḍe, hañje, and halā are calls addressed to a low woman, a maidservant, or a female friend.
Aṅgahāra is movement of the limbs; vyañjaka and abhinaya are equivalent terms for expressive acting.
When expression is produced through bodily movement and inner disposition, the two kinds are called aṅgika and sāttvika, used in all three genders.
Śṛṅgāra, vīra, karuṇa, adbhuta, hāsya, and bhayānaka are dramatic rasas.
Bībhatsa and raudra are also rasas; śṛṅgāra is described as pure and radiant.
Vīra is the rasa that increases energy; kāruṇya, karuṇā, and ghṛṇā mean pity or compassion.
Kṛpā, dayā, anukampā, and anukrośa are also words for compassion; next comes laughter.

children.text: hāso hāsyaṃ ca bībhatsaṃ vikṛtaṃ triṣvidaṃ dvayam
children.translated_text: Hasa, hāsa, and hāsya mean laughter or the comic; bībhatsa and vikṛta mean the disgusting or deformed, and the pair is used in all three genders.
Vismaya, adbhuta, āścarya, and citra mean wonder; then come words for the frightening.

children.text: dāruṇaṃ bhīṣaṇaṃ bhīṣmaṃ ghoraṃ bhīmaṃ bhayānakam
children.translated_text: Dāruṇa, bhīṣaṇa, bhīṣma, ghora, bhīma, and bhayānaka mean terrible or fearsome.
Bhayaṅkara, pratibhaya, raudra, and ugra are further words for the fearsome; these are used in all three genders.

children.text: caturdaśa daras trāso bhītir bhīḥ sādhvasaṃ bhayam
children.translated_text: The fourteen terms just given are used in all three genders; dara, trāsa, bhīti, bhī, sādhvasa, and bhaya mean fear.
Bhāva is a mental modification or state; anubhāva is that which makes a bhāva known.
Garva, abhimāna, ahaṃkāra, and māna mean pride, an elevation of the mind.
Darpa, avaloka, avaṣṭambha, cittodreka, smaya, and mada are further words for arrogance or pride.
Anādara, paribhava, parībhāva, and tiraskriyā mean disrespect or contempt.
Rīḍhā, avamānanā, avajñā, avahelana, and asūrkṣaṇa are also words for slighting or contempt.
Mandākṣa, hrī, trapā, vrīḍā, lajjā, and sāpatrapā are words for shame or modesty.
Kṣānti and titikṣā mean forbearance; abhidhyā is desire directed toward another's possession.
Akṣānti means intolerance; īrṣyā and asūyā mean envy, with asūyā being the imputing of faults even to virtues.

children.text: vairaṃ virodho vidveṣo manyuśokau tu śuk striyām ||
children.translated_text: Vaira, virodha, and vidveṣa mean enmity; manyu is anger, while śoka and the feminine śuk mean sorrow.
Paścāttāpa, anutāpa, and vipratīsāra all mean remorse or regret.
Kopa, krodha, amarṣa, roṣa, pratigha, and the feminine words ruṭ and krudh are words for anger.
Śīla denotes good conduct; unmāda is derangement of the mind.

children.text: premā nā priyatā hārdaṃ premasneho 'tha dohadam ||
children.translated_text: Preman, priyatā, hārda, prema, and sneha are words for love or affection; then dohada denotes longing.

children.text: icchā kāṅkṣā spṛhehā tṛḍ vāñchā lipsā manorathaḥ
children.translated_text: Icchā, kāṅkṣā, spṛhā, īhā, tṛṭ, vāñchā, lipsā, and manoratha are words for desire.
Kāma, abhilāṣa, and tarṣa are also words for that desire; when it is excessive, it is called lālasā, used in two genders.
Upādhi, masculine, means concern over <s>dharma</s> (normative duty); ādhi, masculine, is mental pain.
Cintā, smṛti, and ādhyāna denote anxious thought or recollection; utkaṇṭhā and utkalikā are equivalent words for yearning.
Utsāha is adhyavasāya, firm resolve; when that possesses very great power, it is vīrya.
Kapaṭa, a non-feminine word, together with vyāja, dambha, upadhi, chadman, and kaitava, denotes deceit.
Kusṛti, nikṛti, and śāṭhya mean crookedness or fraud; pramāda is inattentiveness.

children.text: kautūhalaṃ kautukaṃ ca kutukaṃ ca kutūhalam ||
children.translated_text: Kautūhala, kautuka, kutuka, and kutūhala are words for curiosity or wonder.
For women, vilāsa, bibboka, vibhrama, and also lalita are terms for graceful amorous expression.
Helā and līlā likewise are hāvas, actions born from the feeling of erotic love.

children.text: dravakeliparīhāsāḥ krīḍā līlā ca narma ca
children.translated_text: Drava, keli, parīhāsa, krīḍā, līlā, and narma are words for play, sport, or jesting.

children.text: vyājo 'padeśo lakṣyaṃ ca krīḍā khelā ca kūrdanam ||
children.translated_text: Vyāja, apadeśa, and lakṣya mean pretext; krīḍā, khelā, and kūrdana mean play or sport.
Gharma and nidāgha mean heat; sveda is sweat; pralaya is loss of activity or consciousness.
Avahitthā is concealment of one's outward expression; saṃvega and sambhrama are equivalent words for agitation or alarm.

children.text: syādācchuritakaṃ hāsaḥ sotprāsaḥ sa manāk smitam
children.translated_text: Ācchuritaka is laughter with mockery; when that laughter is slight, it is smita, a smile.
The middle degree of laughter is vihasita; romāñca and romaharṣaṇa mean horripilation.

children.text: kranditaṃ ruditam kruṣṭaṃ jṛmbhastu triṣu jṛmbhaṇam
children.translated_text: Krandita, rudita, and kruṣṭa mean crying or wailing; jṛmbhaṇa is yawning, with jṛmbha used in all three genders.
Vipralambha and visaṃvāda are words for deception or breach; riṅgaṇa and skhalana are equivalent words for stumbling.

children.text: syān nidrā śayanaṃ svāpaḥ svapnaḥ saṃveśa ityapi
children.translated_text: Nidrā, śayana, svāpa, svapna, and saṃveśa are words for sleep.

children.text: tandrī pramīlā bhrakuṭir bhrukuṭir bhrūkuṭiḥ striyām ||
children.translated_text: Tandrī and pramīlā mean drowsiness; bhrakuṭi, bhrukuṭi, and bhrūkuṭi are feminine words for a frown.
Adṛṣṭi is said of an unlovely eye; saṃsiddhi and prakṛti are words for inherent nature.
Svarūpa, svabhāva, and nisarga are also words for inherent nature; next comes vepathu, trembling.

children.text: kampo 'tha kṣaṇa uddharṣo maha uddhava utsavaḥ
children.translated_text: Vepathu and kampa mean trembling; kṣaṇa, uddharṣa, maha, uddhava, and utsava are words for a festival or celebration.
Adhobhuvana, pātāla, balisadma, the abode of <s>Bali</s>, and rasātala are names for the underworld.
Nāgaloka is also a subterranean serpent-world; next, kuhara, suṣira, vivara, and bila are words for a cavity or hole.

children.text: chidraṃ nirvyathanaṃ rokaṃ randhraṃ śvabhraṃ vapā suṣiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Chidra, nirvyathana, roka, randhra, śvabhra, vapā, and suṣi are words for a hole, cleft, or cavity.

children.text: gartāvaṭau bhuvi śvabhre sarandhre suṣiraṃ triṣu
children.translated_text: Garta and avaṭa mean a pit in the ground; suṣira, meaning perforated or hollow, is used in all three genders.
Andhakāra, a non-feminine word, together with dhvānta, tamisra, timira, and tamas, denotes darkness.
Dense darkness is andhatamasa, while diminished darkness is avatamasa.
Saṃtamasa is darkness on all sides; the nāgas are called Kādraveyas, and their lord is named next.
Their lord is <s>Śeṣa</s> or <s>Ananta</s>; <s>Vāsuki</s>, however, is the serpent-king. Next, for gonasa,
the word tilitsa is used; for ajagara, a great python, śayu and vāhasa are both used.
Alagarda and jalavyāla mean a water-snake; rājila and ḍuṇḍubha are equivalent snake names.
Māludhāna is the same as mātulāhi; nirmukta and muktakañcuka mean a snake that has shed its slough.
Sarpa, pṛdāku, bhujaga, bhujaṃga, ahi, and bhujaṃgama are words for snake.
Āśīviṣa, viṣadhara, cakrī, vyāla, and sarīsṛpa are also words for snake.
Kuṇḍalī, gūḍhapāt, cakṣuḥśravas, kākodara, and phaṇin are further words for snake.
Darvīkara, dīrghapṛṣṭha, dandaśūka, and bileśaya are likewise words for snake.
Uraga, pannaga, bhogin, jihmaga, and pavanāśana are also names for snake.
Lelihāna, dvirasana, gokarṇa, and kañcukin likewise denote a snake.
Kumbhīnasa, phaṇadhara, hari, and bhogadhara are also words for snake.

children.text: aheḥ śarīraṃ bhogaḥ syād āśīr apy ahidaṃṣṭrikā ||
children.translated_text: Bhoga denotes a snake's body or coil; āśī also means a snake's fang.

children.text: triṣvāheyaṃ viṣāsthyādi sphaṭāyāṃ tu phaṇā dvayoḥ
children.translated_text: Āheya is used in all three genders for what belongs to a snake, such as its poison or bones; phaṇā, used in two genders, denotes the expanded hood.
Kañcuka and nirmoka are equivalent words for a cast-off slough; kṣveḍa, garala, and viṣa mean poison.
Kākola, kālakūṭa, and halāhala are poison names used in the masculine and neuter genders.
Saurāṣṭrika, śauklikeya, brahmaputra, and pradīpana are additional varieties of poison.
Dārada and vatsanābha as well: these are the nine varieties of poison.
A poison-physician is a jāṅgulika; a snake-catcher is a vyālagrāhin or ahituṇḍika.

children.text: syān nārakas tu narako nirayo durgatiḥ striyām
children.translated_text: Nāraka, naraka, niraya, and the feminine word durgati are words for hell.
Its varieties include <s>Tapana</s>, <s>Avīci</s>, <s>Mahāraurava</s>, and <s>Raurava</s>.
<s>Saṃghāta</s>, <s>Kālasūtra</s>, and others are further hells; the beings there are nārakas, hell-beings.
Pretas are departed spirits; <s>Vaitaraṇī</s> is the river of hell; alakṣmī is nirṛti, misfortune or ruin.
Viṣṭi and ājū denote forced service; kāraṇā and yātanā mean intense pain or torment.
Pīḍā, bādhā, vyathā, duḥkha, and āmanasya are words for suffering, including pain born of childbirth.
Kaṣṭa, kṛcchra, and ābhīla are used in all three genders for something painful or difficult, according to such distinctions.
Samudra, abdhi, akūpāra, pārāvāra, and saritpati are words for ocean.
Udanvat, udadhi, sindhu, sarasvat, sāgara, and arṇava are also words for ocean.
Ratnākara, jalanidhi, yādaḥpati, and apāmpati are likewise words for ocean.
Its subdivisions include kṣīroda, the milk ocean, lavaṇoda, the salt ocean, and others.

children.text: āpaḥ strī bhūmni vārvāri salilaṃ kamalaṃ jalam ||
children.translated_text: Āpas is a feminine plural word; vār, vāri, salila, kamala, and jala are words for water.
Payaḥ, kīlāla, amṛta, jīvana, bhuvana, and vana are also words for water.
Kabandha, udaka, pāthaḥ, puṣkara, and sarvatomukha are likewise words for water.
Ambhas, arṇas, toya, pānīya, nīra, kṣīra, ambu, and śambara are also words for water.
Meghapuṣpa and ghanarasa are words for water; āpya and ammaya are two adjectives, used in all three genders, meaning watery.
Bhaṅga, taraṅga, and ūrmi are words for wave, while vīci is feminine.
Among waves, a great one is called ullola or kallola; āvarta is the swirling of water, a whirlpool.
Pṛṣanti, bindu, and pṛṣata are masculine words for a drop; vipruṣ is feminine.

children.text: cakrāṇi puṭabhedāḥ syur bhramāś ca jalanirgamāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Cakras are bursts of bubbles, and bhramas are outflows or whirling movements of water.

children.text: kūlaṃ rodhaś ca tīraṃ ca pratīraṃ ca taṭaṃ triṣu
children.translated_text: Kūla, rodhas, tīra, pratīra, and taṭa, used in all three genders, are words for a bank or shore.
The far and near shores are parārvācī; pātra is the space between those banks.
Dvīpa, a non-feminine word, is antarīpa, land whose shore lies within surrounding water.
That which rises out of water is pulina, a sandbank; saikata means made of sand.
Niṣadvara and jambāla denote mud; paṅka is not feminine, and śāda and kardama also mean mud.
Jalocchvāsa and parīvāha are overflows or outflows of water; kūpaka and vidāraka denote fissures or openings.
Nāvya, in all three genders, means navigable by boat; nau, taraṇi, and tari are feminine terms for a boat.

children.text: uḍupaṃ tu plavaḥ kolaḥ sroto 'mbusaraṇaṃ svataḥ ||
children.translated_text: Uḍupa, plava, and kola mean a raft or float; srotas is the natural flowing course of water.
Ātara and tarapaṇya denote the fare for crossing by boat; droṇī is a wooden trough that carries water.
A sāṃyātrika is a ship-merchant, and karṇadhāra or nāvika means a helmsman or boatman.
Niyāmaka and potavāha mean pilots or boatmen; kūpaka and guṇavṛkṣaka denote the mast.
Naukādaṇḍa, kṣepaṇī, aritra, and kenipātaka are terms for an oar or paddle.

children.text: abhriḥ strī kāṣṭhakuddālaḥ sekapātraṃ tu secanam
children.translated_text: Abhri, feminine, is a wooden hoe or spade; sekapātra and secana mean a vessel for bailing or sprinkling water.
Ardhanāva, neuter, denotes half of a boat; atinu, in all three genders, describes one who has gone beyond or past a boat.
Prasanna and accha, in all three genders, mean clear; kaluṣa, anaccha, and āvila mean turbid or muddy.
Nimna, gabhīra, and gambhīra mean deep or low; uttāna means the opposite, shallow or raised.
Agādha means bottomless or not touched at the bottom; dāśa and dhīvara denote a fisherman, a Kaivarta.
Ānāya, masculine, and jāla mean a net; śaṇasūtra and pavitraka denote hempen cord or netting.
Matsyādhānī and kuveṇī mean a fish-basket; baḍiśa and matsyavedhana mean a fish-hook.
Pṛthuroman, jhaṣa, matsya, mīna, vaisāriṇa, and aṇḍaja are names for fish.
Visāra and śakulī are also fish names; gaḍaka denotes the young of a śakula fish.
Sahasradaṃṣṭra and pāṭhīna are fish names; ulūpī and śiśuka are equivalent terms.
Nalamīna and cilicima denote a reed-fish; proṣṭhī and śapharī are two names for a small fish.
A mass of tiny fish-eggs or small fish is called potādhāna; next come the fish species.
Rohita, madgura, śāla, rājīva, śakula, and timi are names of fish.
Timiṅgala and the like are also fish; yādāṃsi means aquatic creatures.
Their varieties include śiśumāra, udra, śaṅku, makara, and others.
Kulīra and karkaṭaka mean crab; kamaṭha and kacchapa mean tortoise.
Grāha and avahāra denote a seizing aquatic creature; nakra and kumbhīra mean crocodile, and then comes mahīlatā.
Mahīlatā, gaṇḍūpada, kiñculaka, nihākā, and godhikā are equivalent names for an earthworm-like creature.

children.text: raktapā tu jalaukāyāṃ striyāṃ bhūmni jalaukasaḥ
children.translated_text: Raktapā and the feminine jalaukā mean leech; jalaukasaḥ in the plural means water-dwellers.
Muktāsphoṭa and the feminine śukti mean a pearl-shell or oyster; śaṅkha and kambu, not feminine, mean conch.
Small conches are śaṅkhanakhas; śambūka and jalaśukti denote water-shells or aquatic mollusks.
For frog, the terms are maṇḍūka, varṣābhū, śālūra, plava, and dardura.

children.text: śilī gaṇḍūpadī bhekī varṣābhvī kamaṭhī ḍuliḥ
children.translated_text: Śilī, gaṇḍūpadī, bhekī, varṣābhvī, kamaṭhī, and ḍuli are feminine frog names.
Śṛṅgī, durnāmā, and dīrghakośikā are names connected with the female or mate of the madgura fish.
Jalāśaya and jalādhāra mean a reservoir of water; among them, one with deep water is a hrada.
Āhāva and nipāna denote a watering-place or reservoir near a well.

children.text: puṃsyevāndhuḥ prahiḥ kūpa udapānaṃ tu puṃsi vā
children.translated_text: Andhu, prahi, and kūpa are masculine terms for a well; udapāna may also be masculine.
Nemi, trikā, and vīnāha mean the rim or binding that forms the mouth of that well.
In the case of a puṣkariṇī, khāta means dug out, while an undug natural basin is devakhātaka.
Padmākara, taḍāga, kāsāra, sarasī, and saraḥ are terms for a pond or lake.

children.text: veśantaḥ palvalaṃ cālpasaro vāpī tu dīrghikā
children.translated_text: Veśanta and palvala mean a small lake or pool; vāpī and dīrghikā denote a long pond or reservoir.
Kheya and parikhā mean a moat or ditch; an ādhāra is a place where waters are held.
Ālavāla, āvāla, and āvāpa denote a water-basin or reservoir; then nadī and sarit mean river.
A river is also called taraṅgiṇī, śaivalinī, taṭinī, hrādinī, and dhunī.
It is also called srotasvinī, dvīpavatī, sravantī, nimnagā, and āpagā.
Other river terms are kūlaṃkaṣā, nirjhariṇī, rodhovakrā, and <s>Sarasvatī</s>.
The <s>Gaṅgā</s> is called <s>Viṣṇupadī</s>, <s>Jahnutanayā</s>, and <s>Suranimnagā</s>.
It is also called <s>Bhāgīrathī</s>, <s>Tripathagā</s>, <s>Trisrotā</s>, and <s>Bhīṣmasū</s>.
<s>Kālindī</s>, <s>Sūryatanayā</s>, <s>Yamunā</s>, and <s>Śamanasvasā</s> are names of the <s>Yamunā</s>.
<s>Revā</s>, <s>Narmadā</s>, <s>Somodbhavā</s>, and <s>Mekalakanyakā</s> are names of the <s>Narmadā</s>.
<s>Karatoyā</s>, <s>Sadānīrā</s>, <s>Bāhudā</s>, and <s>Saitavāhinī</s> are river names.

children.text: śatadrustu śutudriḥ syādvipāśā tu vipāṭ striyām ||
children.translated_text: <s>Śatadru</s> is called <s>Śutudrī</s>; the feminine <s>Vipāśā</s> is also called <s>Vipāṭ</s>.
<s>Śoṇa</s> is called <s>Hiraṇyavāha</s>; kulyā denotes a small artificial river or channel.
<s>Śarāvatī</s>, <s>Vetravatī</s>, <s>Candrabhāgā</s>, and <s>Sarasvatī</s> are river names.
<s>Kāverī</s> and others are rivers; sambheda means the confluence of rivers.

children.text: dvayoḥ praṇālī payasaḥ padavyāṃ triṣu tūttarau ||
children.translated_text: Praṇālī and payasaḥ padavī denote a channel for water; the latter terms take all three genders.
For what belongs to the <s>Devikā</s> and the <s>Sarayū</s>, the forms are dāvika and sārava respectively.
Saugandhika, kalhāra, hallaka, and raktasaṃdhyaka denote a fragrant red water-lily.
Utpala, kuvalaya, and nīlāmbujanma denote the blue water-lily.
Indīvara too is used for this blue flower; for the white one, the names are kumuda and kairava.
The tuber of these plants is śālūka; vāriparṇī and kumbhikā denote an aquatic leaf-plant.
Jalanīlī, śaivāla, and śaivala mean water-moss or algae; then comes kumudvatī.
Kumudvatī means a place full of kumudas; for nalinī, terms such as bisinī and padminī are used.
Padma, nalina, aravinda, and mahotpala, optionally masculine, are names for the lotus.
Sahasrapattra, kamala, śatapattra, and kuśeśaya are also lotus names.
Paṅkeruha, tāmarasa, sārasa, and sarasīruha likewise mean lotus.
Bisa, prasūna, rājīva, puṣkara, and ambhoruha are further lotus terms.
Puṇḍarīka and sitāmbhoja denote the white lotus; next, for the red water-born flower:
Raktotpala and kokanada mean red lotus; nāla or nāla, not feminine, denotes the lotus-stalk.
Mṛṇāla and bisa denote the lotus fiber or stalk; khaṇḍa, not feminine, means a cluster of lotuses and the like.
Karahāṭa and śiphākanda mean the root or tuber; kiñjalka and kesara, not feminine, mean the filament or stamen.
Saṃvartikā means a new petal or folded young leaf; bījakośa and varāṭaka mean the seed-capsule.
The topics of heaven, sky, directions, time, intellect, speech, and the like, together with drama, have been stated.
The underworld, serpents, hell, water, and what is connected with these have also been set forth.
Thus, in the <s>Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana</s> composed by <s>Amarasiṃha</s>,
the first kāṇḍa, beginning with heaven and complete with its divisions, is finished.
Here the sections beginning with earth, city, mountain, forest, herbs, animals, and the like are declared,
together with humans, Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, along with their main and subsidiary divisions.

children.text: bhūr bhūmir acalānantā rasā viśvambharā sthitā
children.translated_text: Bhū, bhūmi, acalā, anantā, rasā, viśvambharā, and sthitā are names for the earth.

children.text: dharā dharitrī dharaṇiḥ kṣoṇirjyā kāśyapī kṣitiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Dharā, dharitrī, dharaṇi, kṣoṇi, jyā, kāśyapī, and kṣiti are also names for the earth.
Sarvaṃsahā, vasumatī, vasudhā, urvī, and vasuṃdharā are names of the earth.

children.text: gotrā kuḥ pṛthivī pṛthvī kṣmāvanirmedinī mahī ||
children.translated_text: Gotrā, ku, pṛthivī, pṛthvī, kṣmā, avani, medinī, and mahī are likewise names of the earth.

children.text: vipulā gahvarī dhātrī gaurilā kumbhinī kṣamā
children.translated_text: Vipulā, gahvarī, dhātrī, gaurilā, kumbhinī, and kṣamā are further names of the earth.
Bhūtadhātrī, ratnagarbhā, jagatī, and sāgarāmbarā also denote the earth.

children.text: mṛnmṛttikā praśastā tu mṛtsā mṛtsnā ca mṛttikā
children.translated_text: Mṛd and mṛttikā mean soil or clay; good clay is called mṛtsā, mṛtsnā, and mṛttikā.
Urvarā is land rich in every crop; ūṣa is saline soil.

children.text: ūṣavān ūṣaro dvāv apy anyaliṅgau sthalaṃ sthalī
children.translated_text: Ūṣavān and ūṣara also denote saline ground, with variable gender; sthala and sthalī mean dry ground.
Maru and dhanvan are equivalent terms for desert; khila and aprahata are the same, meaning untilled waste land.

children.text: triṣvatho jagatī loko viṣṭapaṃ bhuvanaṃ jagat
children.translated_text: For the world there are the terms jagatī, loka, viṣṭapa, bhuvana, and jagat, with some used in all three genders.
This world is the <s>Bhārata</s> region, extending to the boundary of <s>Śarāvatī</s>.
For regions, prāg and prācya denote the east, dakṣiṇa the south, udīcya the north, and paścima and uttara the west and north.

children.text: pratyanto mlecchadeśaḥ syān madhyadeśas tu madhyamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Pratyanta is a frontier or foreign land; <s>Madhyadeśa</s> is the middle country.
<s>Āryāvarta</s>, the holy land, is the middle region between <s>Vindhya</s> and <s>Himālaya</s>.
Nīvṛt and janapada denote an inhabited district; deśa, viṣaya, and upavartana are terms for a territory.

children.text: triṣv āgoṣṭhān naḍaprāye naḍvān naḍvala ityapi
children.translated_text: Naḍvān and naḍvala, used in the three genders, describe a place mostly covered with reeds.
Kumudvān describes a place mostly full of water lilies, and vetasvān one abounding in cane or rattan.
Śādvala is ground green with grass, while paṅkila is ground with mud.
Anūpa is a place mostly made up of water or marsh; kaccha, in the masculine, has the same sense.
Śarkarā is feminine for gravel; śarkarila, śārkara, and śarkarāvat mean gravelly.
When such adjectives qualify a country they are to be inferred in this way, as also with sikatāvat, sandy.
A country whose rice is sustained by river water or by rainwater
is called nadīmātṛka and devamātṛka respectively.
In a well-ruled country the word is rājanvān, having a king; elsewhere the form is rājavān.
Goṣṭha and gosthānaka mean a cattle-station; gauṣṭhīna means something that formerly was such a place.
Paryantabhū and parisara mean bordering ground; setu and āli denote a dike or embankment, the former masculine and the latter feminine.
Vāmalūra and nāku are terms for an anthill; valmīka is masculine or neuter.
Ayana, vartman, mārga, adhvan, panthāna, padavī, and sṛti are terms for a road or path.

children.text: saraṇiḥ paddhatiḥ padyā vartany ekapadīti ca ||
children.translated_text: Saraṇi, paddhati, padyā, vartanī, and ekapadī also mean a path or track.
Atipanthā, supanthā, and satpatha denote an excellent or honored road.

children.text: vyadhvo duradhvo vipathaḥ kadadhvā kāpathaḥ samāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Vyadhvan, duradhvan, vipatha, kadadhvan, and kāpatha are equivalent terms for a bad road.
Apanthā and apatha are equivalent; śṛṅgāṭaka and catuṣpatha denote a crossroads.
Prāntara is a road that is distant and empty; kāntāra is a difficult road.
Gavyūti is feminine and equals two krośas; nalva is a measure of four hundred kiṣkus.
Ghaṇṭāpatha and saṃsaraṇa mean a thoroughfare; for a city, that is its upaniṣkara.
Dyāvāpṛthivī, rodasī, and dyāvābhūmī are paired terms for heaven and earth.

children.text: divaspṛthivyau gañjā tu rumā syāl lavaṇākaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: Divaspṛthivī is another such pair; gañjā or rumā denotes a salt source or salt mine.

children.text: pūḥ strī purīnagaryau vā pattanaṃ puṭabhedanam
children.translated_text: Pūḥ, feminine, and purī or nagarī mean a city; pattana and puṭabhedana mean a town or port.
Sthānīya and nigama are settlement terms; a town distinct from its root city
is a śākhānagara, a branch-town, while veśa is a quarter inhabited by courtesans.
Āpaṇa, niṣadyā, vipaṇi, and paṇyavīthikā are terms for a market or street of merchandise.

children.text: rathyā pratolī viśikhā syāc cayo vapramastriyām
children.translated_text: Rathyā, pratolī, and viśikhā mean a street; caya and vapra denote a rampart or bank and are not feminine.

children.text: prākāro varaṇaḥ sālaḥ prācīnaṃ prātanto vṛtiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Prākāra, varaṇa, sāla, prācīna, prātanta, and vṛti are terms for an enclosure or wall.
Bhitti, feminine, kuḍya, and eḍūka denote a wall, especially one with internal brickwork or inserted supports.
Gṛha, geha, udavasita, veśman, sadman, and niketana mean a house or dwelling.
Niśānta, pastya, sadana, bhavana, agāra, and mandira are also words for a house.
Gṛhāḥ is masculine and used only in the plural; nikāya, nilaya, and ālaya denote abodes.

children.text: vāsaḥ kuṭī dvayoḥ śālā sabhā saṃjavanaṃ tv idam
children.translated_text: Vāsa means residence; kuṭī is of two genders, while śālā, sabhā, and saṃjavana denote a hall or shelter.
Catuḥśāla is a four-halled building; for sages, parṇaśālā and uṭaja mean a leaf-hut, with uṭaja not feminine.
Caitya and āyatana are equivalent terms for a shrine; a horse-stable is mandurā.
Āveśana is an artisan's workshop; prapā is a hall or shed for drinking water.
A maṭha is a residence for students and the like; gañjā is a liquor-house.
Garbhāgāra and vāsagṛha denote an inner living chamber; ariṣṭa is a maternity room.
Kuṭṭima, not feminine, means a paved floor; nibaddhā bhūḥ is fixed or paved ground, and candraśālā or śirogṛha is an upper room.
Vātāyana and gavākṣa mean a window; maṇḍapa, not feminine, is a public hall or shelter.
Harmya and similar words denote the residences of the wealthy; prāsāda is the residence of gods and kings.
Saudha, not feminine, is a royal residence; upakāryā and upakārikā denote an auxiliary building or pavilion.
Svastika, sarvatobhadra, nandyāvarta, and the like,
as well as vicchandaka, are distinct types of the mansions of rulers.
The women's house of kings is called antaḥpura or avarodhana.
Śuddhānta and avarodha have the same meaning; aṭṭa and kṣauma, not feminine, denote a raised structure or tower.
Praghāṇa, praghaṇa, and ālinda denote the chamber or portico at the outer doorway.
Gṛhāvagrahaṇī and dehalī mean the threshold; aṅgaṇa, catvara, and ajira mean a courtyard.

children.text: adhastād dāruṇi śilā nāsā dārūpari sthitam
children.translated_text: A stone placed below a wooden door-frame is called nāsā; what is set above the timber
is a covered inner doorway, while a side-door is called pakṣadvāra or pakṣaka.
Valīka and nīdhra denote the edge of a roof-panel; paṭala means a covering or roof.
Gopānasī and valabhī denote the curved timber used in roofing.
Viṭaṅka, masculine or neuter, denotes the projecting eaves called kapotapālikā.

children.text: strī dvār dvāraṃ pratīhāraḥ syādvitardis tu vedikā ||
children.translated_text: Dvār is feminine, while dvāra and pratīhāra mean a door; vitardi is a vedikā, a raised platform.
Toraṇa, not feminine, is an outer gateway; a city gate is a gopura.

children.text: kūṭaṃ pūrdvāri yaddhastinakhas tasmin atha triṣu ||
children.translated_text: At a city gate, the projection called hastinakha is a kūṭa; then, in all three genders,
kapāṭa and arara are equivalent terms for a door-leaf, and its crossbar is argala, not masculine.
Ārohaṇa and sopāna mean stairs; niśreṇi and adhirohiṇī mean a ladder.
Sammārjanī and śodhanī mean a broom; saṃkara and avakara likewise mean sweepings or refuse.
When refuse has been thrown out, mukha and niḥsaraṇa are terms for the outlet, while saṃniveśa and nikarṣaṇa denote disposal or removal.
Saṃvasatha and grāma are equivalent terms for a village; veśmabhū and vāstu, not feminine, mean a house-site.
Upaśalya is the edge of a village; sīmā and sīma are both feminine terms for a boundary.
Ghoṣa means a hamlet of the <s>Ābhīras</s>; pakkaṇa means a dwelling of the <s>Śabaras</s>.
For a mountain, the terms are mahīdhra, śikharin, kṣmābhṛt, ahāryadhara, and parvata.
Adri, gotra, giri, grāvā, acala, śaila, and śiloccaya also denote a mountain.
<s>Lokāloka</s> and <s>Cakravāla</s> are equivalent; <s>Trikūṭa</s> and <s>Trikakut</s> are likewise the same.
<s>Asta</s> is the western mountain, and <s>Udaya</s> is the eastern mountain.
<s>Himavān</s>, <s>Niṣadha</s>, <s>Vindhya</s>, <s>Mālyavān</s>, and <s>Pāriyātrika</s> are mountains.
<s>Gandhamādana</s> and other mountains, beginning with <s>Hemakūṭa</s>, are also called nagas.
Pāṣāṇa, prastara, grāvā, upala, aśman, śilā, and dṛṣad mean stone.
Kūṭa, śikhara, and śṛṅga denote a summit; prapāta, ataṭa, and bhṛgu denote a precipice or cliff.
Kaṭaka and nitamba denote a mountain's flank; snu, prastha, and sānu denote its tableland or ridge.
Utsa, prasravaṇa, vāripravāha, nirjhara, and jhara mean a spring or stream of water.

children.text: darī tu kandaro vā strī devakhātabile guhā ||
children.translated_text: Darī means a cave; kandara may be feminine, and guhā denotes a cave or hollow as if dug by the gods.
Gahvara means a deep cavern; gaṇḍaśailas are large stones fallen from a mountain.
