Dantakas are lateral projections jutting outward from a mountain.
Khani, feminine, and ākara mean a mine; pādas are outlying border-mountains.
Upatyakā is land near a mountain, while adhityakā is the higher ground above it.
Dhātu denotes mountain minerals such as manaḥśilā; gairika specifically denotes red ochre.
Nikuñja and kuñja, either neuter, mean an inner bower covered by creepers and the like.
Aṭavī, araṇya, vipina, gahana, kānana, and vana mean forest.
Mahāraṇya and araṇyānī mean a great forest; niṣkuṭas are house-gardens.
Ārāma and upavana denote an artificial or cultivated grove.
A vṛkṣavāṭikā is a garden beside the house of a minister or courtesan.
Ākrīḍa, masculine, and udyāna denote a public park of a king.
That same park, when suited to the inner palace, is a pramadavana, a women's pleasure-garden.
Vīthī, āli, āvali, paṅkti, śreṇī, lekhā, and rāji mean a row or line.
Vanyā denotes a tract or collection of forest; aṅkura means a newly sprouting shoot.
Vṛkṣa, mahīruha, śākhī, viṭapī, pādapa, and taru mean tree.
Anokaha, kuṭa, śāla, palāśin, dru, druma, and agama also mean tree.

children.text: vānaspatyaḥ phalaiḥ puṣpāt tair apuṣpād vanaspatiḥ
children.translated_text: A vānaspatya is a tree whose fruits arise from flowers; a vanaspati bears fruit without visible flowers.
Oṣadhis are plants that end with the ripening of their fruit; avandhya and phalegrahi mean fruit-bearing.
Vandhya, aphala, and avakeśin mean fruitless, while phalavān, phalin, and phalī mean fruitful.
Praphulla, utphulla, samphulla, vyākośa, vikaca, and sphuṭa are terms for something opened in bloom.
Phulla too means blossomed; terms beginning with avandhya are used in all three genders.

children.text: sthāṇurvā nā dhruvaḥ śaṅkur hrasvaśākhāśiphaḥ kṣupaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Sthāṇu, optionally masculine, together with dhruva and śaṅku denotes a stump; kṣupa is a shrub with short branches and roots.
Stamba and gulma denote a plant without a main trunk; vallī, vratati, and latā mean creeper.
Pratāninī, vīrudh, gulminī, and ulapa are also terms for a creeper.
The height or upward growth of a tree and the like is called āroha, ucchrāya, utsedha, or ucchraya.

children.text: astrī prakāṇḍaḥ skandhaḥ syān mūlācchākhāvadhis taroḥ ||
children.translated_text: Prakāṇḍa and skandha, not feminine, denote the trunk of a tree from the root up to the branches.
Śākhā and latā are paired as equivalent terms; skandhaśākhā and śālā are equivalent, and śiphā and jaṭā are equivalent.
A branch-root is called avaroha; a latā is a creeper that has gone from the root to the top.

children.text: śiro 'graṃ śikharaṃ vā nā mūlaṃ budhno 'ṅghrināmakaḥ
children.translated_text: Śiras, agra, and śikhara denote the top; mūla, budhna, and aṅghri denote the root or base.

children.text: sāro majjā nari tvakstrī valkaṃ valkalamastriyām ||
children.translated_text: Sāra and majjā mean heartwood or pith; tvac is feminine for bark, and valka and valkala are non-feminine bark terms.

children.text: kāṣṭhaṃ dārvindhanaṃ tv edha idhmamedhaḥ samitstriyām
children.translated_text: Kāṣṭha and dāru mean wood; indhana, edha, idhma, and edhas mean fuel, and samid is feminine.

children.text: niṣkuhaḥ koṭaraṃ vā nā vallarir mañjariḥ striyau ||
children.translated_text: Niṣkuha and koṭara, masculine or neuter, mean a tree-hollow; vallari and mañjarī are feminine terms for a spray or cluster.

children.text: pattraṃ palāśaṃ chadanaṃ dalaṃ parṇaṃ chadaḥ pumān
children.translated_text: Pattra, palāśa, chadana, dala, parṇa, and chada mean leaf.
Pallava, not feminine, and kisalaya mean a young shoot; vistāra and viṭapa, not feminine, denote a spreading branch.
The fruit of trees and the like is phala or sasya; the vṛnta is the stalk that holds the flower or fruit.

children.text: āme phale śalāṭuḥ syācchuṣke vānam ubhe triṣu ||
children.translated_text: Śalāṭu means unripe fruit, and vāna means dried fruit; both are used in all three genders.

children.text: kṣārako jālakaṃ klībe kalikā korakaḥ pumān
children.translated_text: Kṣāraka and jālaka are neuter terms, kalikā is feminine, and koraka is masculine for a bud.
Gucchaka and stabaka mean a cluster; kuḍmala and mukula, not feminine, mean a bud.

children.text: striyaḥ sumanasaḥ puṣpaṃ prasūnaṃ kusumaṃ sumam
children.translated_text: Sumanas, feminine, together with puṣpa, prasūna, kusuma, and suma, means flower.
Makaranda and puṣparasa mean flower-nectar; parāga and sumanorajas mean pollen.
For blossoms the general term is neuter when not otherwise specified; harītakī and similar names are feminine.
Āśvattha, vaiṇava, plākṣa, naiyagrodha, and aiṅguda are neuter when denoting fruit.

children.text: bārhataṃ ca phale jambvā jambūḥ strī jambu jāmbavam
children.translated_text: Bārhata too is neuter when denoting the fruit; for jambu, jambū is the feminine tree-name, while jambu and jāmbava denote the fruit.
Jāti and the like keep their own gender when denoting flowers, and vrīhi and the like when denoting grains.
Vidārī and the like keep their gender also when denoting roots; pāṭalā can also be neuter when denoting its flower.
Bodhidruma, caladala, pippala, and kuñjarāśana are terms for the aśvattha tree.
For aśvattha the preceding terms are used; now, for kapittha, the terms are dadhittha, grāhin, and manmatha.
For that same kapittha, dadhiphala, puṣpaphala, and dantaśaṭha are also names.
The udumbara is called jantuphala, yajñāṅga, and hemadugdhaka.
For kovidāra, the names are camarika, kuddāla, and yugapattraka.
The saptaparṇa is called viśālatvak, śārada, and viṣamacchada.
For āragvadha, the terms are rājavṛkṣa, śampāka, and caturaṅgula.
Ārevata, vyādhighātaka, kṛtamāla, and suvarṇaka are also names for āragvadha.
For jambīra, the names are dantaśaṭha, jambha, jambhīra, and jambhala.
Varuṇa is called varaṇa, setu, tiktaśāka, and kumāraka.
For puṃnāga, the terms are puruṣa, tuṅga, kesara, and devavallabha.
For pāribhadra, the terms are nimbataru, mandāra, and pārijātaka.
For tiniśa, syandana, nemī, and rathadru are names; atimuktaka begins the next set.
For atimuktaka, the terms are vañjula and citrakṛt; now pītanaka and pītana are two names for āmrātaka.
For āmrātaka the preceding two apply; for madhūka, the terms are guḍapuṣpa and madhudruma.
Vānaprastha and madhuṣṭhīla are also names for madhūka; for the water-born variety, the name here is madhūlaka.
For pīlu, the names are guḍaphala and sraṃsī; when it is mountain-born, another pair is used.
Akṣoṭa and kandarāla are the two names for that mountain-born pīlu; for aṅkoṭa, nikocaka is a name.
For palāśa, the names are kiṃśuka, parṇa, and vātapota; now vetasa begins the next entry.
Ratha, abhrapuṣpa, vidura, śītavānīra, and vañjula are names for the water-cane.
Parivyādha and vidula are two more names, and nādeyī and ambuvetasa also denote that plant.
For śobhāñjana, the names are śigru, tīkṣṇagandha, kākṣīva, and mocaka.
When that tree is red it is madhuśigru; ariṣṭa and phenila are equivalent names.
For bilva, the terms are śāṇḍilya and śailūṣa, as well as mālūra and śrīphala.

children.text: plakṣo jaṭī parkaṭī syān nyagrodho bahupādvaṭaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Plakṣa is called jaṭī and parkaṭī; nyagrodha is called bahupād and vaṭa.
Gālava, śābara, lodhra, tirīṭa, tilva, and mārjana are names for lodhra.
Āmra, cūta, and rasāla denote the mango; when it is very fragrant, it is sahakāra.
Kumbha and ulūkhalaka are neuter terms; kauśika, guggulu, and pura denote guggulu.
Śelu, śleṣmātaka, śīta, uddāla, and bahuvāraka are names of the śleṣmātaka tree.
Rājādana and priyāla denote the priyāla tree; sannakadru and dhanuḥpaṭa are another pair of names.
Gambhārī, sarvatobhadrā, kāśmarī, and madhuparṇikā form another synonym set.
Śrīparṇī, bhadraparṇī, and kāśmarya also denote the same tree; next, in two genders:
Karkandhū, badarī, koli, kola, kuvala, and phenila are names for the jujube.
Sauvīra, badara, and ghoṇṭā are further names; then svādukaṇṭaka is so called.
Vikaṅkata, suvāvṛkṣa, granthila, and vyāghrapād are names for svādukaṇṭaka.
Airāvata, nāgaraṅga, nādeyī, and bhūmijambukā denote the nāgaraṅga or citrus tree.
Tinduka, sphūrjaka, and kālaskandha are names for śitisāraka.
Kākendu, kulaka, and kākatinduka are names for kākapīluka.
Golīḍha, jhāṭala, ghaṇṭāpāṭali, mokṣa, and muṣkaka form another synonym set.
Tilaka is also kṣuraka and śrīmān; picula and jhāvuka are equivalent.
Śrīparṇikā, kumudikā, and kumbhī are names; kaiṭarya and kaṭphala are equivalent.
Kramuka is called paṭṭikā; paṭṭī is also called lākṣāprasādana.

children.text: tūdas tu yūpaḥ kramuko brahmaṇyo brahmadāru ca ||
children.translated_text: Tūda is yūpa, kramuka, brahmaṇya, and brahmadāru.
It is also tūla; nīpa, priyaka, and kadamba are names of haripriya.
Vīravṛkṣa, aruṣkara, agnimukhī, and bhallātakī are used in all three genders.
Kandarāla, kapītana, and supārśvaka are names for gardabhāṇḍa.
Plakṣa too is included; tintiḍī, ciñcā, and amlikā denote tamarind; next, for pītasāraka:
Sarjaka, āsana, bandhūkapuṣpa, priyaka, and jīvaka are its names.
For śāla, the terms are sarjaka, arśya, aśvakarṇaka, and sasyasaṃvara.
Nadīsarja, vīrataru, indradru, kakubha, and arjuna are names for the arjuna tree.
Rājādana and phalādhyakṣa denote kṣīrikā; next, in two genders:
Iṅgudī is also tāpasataru; for bhūrja, carmin and mṛdutvac are two names.

children.text: picchilā pūraṇī mocā sthirāyuḥ śālmalir dvayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: Picchilā, pūraṇī, mocā, and sthirāyuḥ are names for śālmalī, which is used in two genders.
Picchā denotes the resin or covering of śālmalī; rocana is called kūṭaśālmali.
Cirabilva, naktamāla, and karaja are names for karañjaka.
Prakīrya, pūtikaraja, pūtika, and kalimāraka are named...
...as varieties of karañja; ṣaḍgrantha, markaṭī, and aṅgāravallarī are included too.
Rohī, rohitaka, plīhaśatru, and dāḍimapuṣpaka are names for rohitaka.
Gāyatrī, bālatanaya, khadira, and dantadhāvana denote khadira.
Arimeda is the viṭkhadira; kadara is the white khadira.
Somavalka is another name for it; next come vyāghrapuccha and gandharvahastaka.
That plant is eraṇḍa, uruvūka, rucaka, and citraka.
Cañcu, pañcāṅgula, maṇḍa, vardhamāna, and vyaḍambaka are further names for it.

children.text: alpā śamī śamīraḥ syācchamī saktuphalā śivā
children.translated_text: Alpā, śamī, śamīra, saktuphalā, and śivā are names for śamī.
Piṇḍītaka, maruvaka, śvasana, and karahāṭaka...
...together with śalya, are names for madana; śakrapādapa and pāribhadraka begin the next set.

children.text: bhadradāru drukilimaṃ pītadāru ca dāru ca ||
children.translated_text: Bhadradāru, drukilima, pītadāru, and dāru...

children.text: pūtikāṣṭhaṃ ca sapta syur devadāruṇy atha dvayoḥ
children.translated_text: ...and pūtikāṣṭha make seven names for devadāru. Next, in two genders:
Pāṭali, pāṭalā, amoghā, kācasthālī, and phaleruhā are names for pāṭali.
Kṛṣṇavṛntā and kuberākṣī are also names; śyāmā is called mahilā.

children.text: latā govandanī gundrā priyaṅguḥ phalinī phalī ||
children.translated_text: Latā, govandanī, gundrā, priyaṅgu, phalinī, and phalī...
...as well as viṣvaksenā, gandhaphalī, kārambhā, and priyaka, are names for that plant.
Maṇḍūkaparṇa, pattrorṇa, naṭa, kaṭvaṅga, and ṭuṇṭuka...
...together with śyonāka, śukanāsa, ṛkṣa, dīrghavṛnta, and kuṭannaṭa, are names for śyonāka.

children.text: amṛtā ca vayaḥsthā ca triliṅgastu vibhītakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Amṛtā and vayaḥsthā are additional names; vibhītaka is used in all three genders.
Nākṣa, tuṣa, karṣaphala, bhūtāvāsa, and kalidruma are names for vibhītaka.

children.text: abhayā tv avyathā pathyā kāyasthā pūtanāmṛtā ||
children.translated_text: Abhayā, avyathā, pathyā, kāyasthā, pūtanā, and amṛtā...
...along with harītakī, haimavatī, cetakī, śreyasī, and śivā, are names for harītakī.
Pītadru, sarala, and pūtikāṣṭha are names for sarala; next, drumotpala...
...karṇikāra and parivyādha; lakuca, likuca, and ḍahu form another synonym set.
Panasa is kaṇṭakiphala; nicula, hijjala, and ambuja are another group of names.
Kākodumbarikā, phalgu, malayū, and jaghanephalā are names for the small fig.
For nimba, the names are ariṣṭa, sarvatobhadra, hiṅguniryāsa, and mālaka...
...and picumanda; next, picchilā, aguru, and śiṃśapā are a synonym group.
Kapilā and bhasmagarbhā are names for that śiṃśapā; śirīṣa is also kapītana.
Bhaṇḍila too is its name; next, cāmpeya, campaka, and hemapuṣpaka are names for campaka.
The bud of this tree is gandhaphalī; next, for kesara:
Bakula and vañjula are its names; for aśoka, karaka and dāḍima are equivalent.
Cāmpeya, kesara, nāgakesara, and kāñcanāhvaya are names for nāgakesara.
Jayā, jayantī, tarkārī, nādeyī, and vaijayantikā are names for jayantī.
Agnimantha is śrīparṇa; kaṇikā and gaṇikārikā are also listed.
Jaya is another name; next, kuṭaja, śakra, vatsaka, and girimallikā are names for kuṭaja.
The fruit of this very tree is called kaliṅga, indrayava, and bhadrayava.
Kṛṣṇapāka, phala, avigna, and suṣeṇā are names for karamardaka.
Kālaskandha, tamāla, and tāpiccha are names for tamāla; next, for sinduka:
Sinduvāra, indrasurasa, nirguṇḍī, and indrāṇikā are names for it.
Veṇī, garāgarī, devatāḍa, and jīmūta are also names for the same plant.

children.text: śrīhastinī tu bhūruṇḍī tṛṇaśūnyaṃ tu mallikā
children.translated_text: Śrīhastinī is called bhūruṇḍī; tṛṇaśūnya is mallikā.
Bhūpadī and śītabhīru are names, and the same plant when forest-grown is called āsphoṭā.

children.text: śephālikā tu suvahā nirguṇḍī nīlikā ca sā
children.translated_text: Śephālikā is called suvahā; nirguṇḍī and nīlikā too are names of it.
Its white variety is śvetasurasā; then bhūtaveśī and māgadhī are further plant names.
Gaṇikā, yūthikā, and ambaṣṭhā are names of that plant; when it is yellow, it is hemapuṣpikā.
Atimukta, puṇḍraka, vāsantī, and mādhavī-latā are names of the same vine.
Sumanā, mālatī, jāti, saptalā, and navamālikā are names of jasmine-like flowering plants.
Mādhya and kunda denote the kunda jasmine; the red one is bandhūka or bandhujīvaka.
Sahā, kumārī, and taraṇi are names; amlāna is called mahāsahā.
Among these, the red variety is kurabaka, and the yellow variety is kuraṇṭaka.

children.text: nīlī jhiṇṭī dvayorbāṇā dāsī cārtagalaśca sā
children.translated_text: Nīlī and jhiṇṭī are names; bāṇā is used in both genders, and dāsī and ārtagala also denote it.
Saireyaka is jhiṇṭī; when that plant is red, it is kurabaka.
When jhiṇṭī is yellow it is kuraṇṭaka; in both varieties, sahacarī is also a name.
The flower of sesame is called oḍrapuṣpa, japāpuṣpa, and vajrapuṣpa.
Pratihāsa, śataprāsa, caṇḍāta, and hayamāraka are names
of karavīra; but for karīra, krakara and granthila are both used.
Unmatta, kitava, dhūrta, dhattūra, and kanakāhvaya are names of dhattūra.
Mātula and madana also denote it, and its fruit is called mātulaputraka.
Phalapūra, bījapūra, and rucaka are names of mātuluṅga, the citron.
Samīraṇa, maruvaka, prasthapuṣpa, and phaṇijjaka are names of maruvaka.
Jambīra too is a citrus name; now for parṇāsa, kaṭhiñjara and kuṭheraka are used.
For the white variety here the name is arjaka; pāṭhī, citraka, and vahnisaṃjñaka denote citraka.
Arkāhva, vasuka, āsphoṭa, gaṇarūpa, and vikīraṇa are names
of arka, along with mandāra and arkaparṇa; for its white variety, alarka and pratāpasa are used.
Śivamallī, pāśupata, ekāṣṭhīla, buka, and vasu are plant names in this group.
Vandā, vṛkṣādanī, vṛkṣaruhā, and jīvantikā also denote the tree-growing parasitic plant.
Vatsādanī, chinnaruhā, guḍūcī, tantrikā, and amṛtā are names of guḍūcī.
Jīvantikā, somavallī, viśalyā, and madhuparṇī are also names of that plant.

children.text: mūrvā devī madhurasā moraṭā tejanī sravā
children.translated_text: Mūrvā, devī, madhurasā, moraṭā, tejanī, and sravā are names of mūrvā.
Madhūlikā, madhuśreṇī, gokarṇī, and pīluparṇī are also names for it.
Pāṭhā, ambaṣṭhā, viddhakarṇī, sthāpanī, śreyasī, and rasā are names of pāṭhā.
Ekāṣṭhīlā, pāpacelī, prācīnā, and vanatiktikā are also names for it.
Kaṭu, kaṭaṃbharā, aśokarohiṇī, and kaṭurohiṇī are names of a bitter medicinal plant.
Matsyapittā, kṛṣṇabhedī, cakrāṅgī, and śakulādanī also denote that plant.
Ātmaguptā, ajahā, vyaṇḍā, kaṇḍūrā, and prāvṛṣāyaṇī are names of kapikacchu.
Ṛṣyaproktā, śūkaśimbī, kapikacchu, and markaṭī are also names of cowhage.
Citrā, upacitrā, nyagrodhī, dravantī, śambarī, and vṛśā are names of dravantī.
Pratyakśreṇī, sutaśreṇī, raṇḍā, and mūṣikaparṇī are also names for it.
Apāmārga, śaikharika, dhāmārgava, and mayūraka are names of apāmārga.
Pratyakparṇī, keśaparṇī, kiṇihī, and kharamañjarī are also names of that plant.
Hañjikā, brāhmaṇī, padmā, bhārgī, and brāhmaṇayaṣṭikā are names of bhārgī.
Aṅgāravallī, bāleyaśāka, barbarā, and vardhaka are further names in this plant group.
Mañjiṣṭhā, vikasā, jiṅgī, samaṅgā, and kālameṣikā are names of mañjiṣṭhā.
Maṇḍūkaparṇī, bhaṇḍīrī, bhaṇḍī, and yojanavallī are also listed as names.
Yāsa, yavāsa, duḥsparśa, dhanvayāsa, and kunāśaka are names of yavāsa.
Rodanī, kacchurā, anantā, samudrāntā, and durālabhā are also names for it.
Pṛśniparṇī, pṛthakparṇī, citraparṇī, and aṅghrivallikā are names of pṛśniparṇī.
Kroṣṭuvinnā, siṃhapucchī, kalaśī, dhāvanī, and guhā are also names of that plant.
Nidigdhikā, spṛśī, vyāghrī, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā are names of bṛhatī.
Pracodanī, kulī, kṣudrā, duḥsparśā, and rāṣṭrikā are also names of that thorny plant.
Nīlī, kālā, klītakikā, grāmīṇā, and madhuparṇikā are names of indigo.

children.text: rañjanī śrīphalī tutthā droṇī dolā ca nīlinī ||
children.translated_text: Rañjanī, śrīphalī, tutthā, droṇī, dolā, and nīlinī are also names of it.
Avalguja, somarājī, suvalli, and somavallikā are names of bakucī.
Kālameṣī, kṛṣṇaphalī, vākucī, and pūtiphalī are also names of that plant.
Kṛṣṇopakulyā, vaidehī, māgadhī, capalā, and kaṇā are names of long pepper.
Uṣaṇā, pippalī, śauṇḍī, and kolā also denote pippalī; next comes karipippalī.
Karipippalī is called kapivallī, kolavallī, śreyasī, and vaśira, with vaśira masculine.

children.text: cavyaṃ tu cavikā kākaciñcīguñje tu kṛṣṇalā ||
children.translated_text: Cavya is also called cavikā; for kākaciñcī or guñjā, the name is kṛṣṇalā.
Palaṃkaṣā, ikṣugandhā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and svādukaṇṭaka are names of gokṣura.
Gokaṇṭaka, gokṣuraka, and vanaśṛṅgāṭa too are names of that plant.
Viśvā, viṣā, prativiṣā, ativiṣā, upaviṣā, and aruṇā are names of ativiṣā.

children.text: śṛṅgī mahauṣadhaṃ cātha kṣīrāvī dugdhikā same ||
children.translated_text: Śṛṅgī and mahauṣadha are also names for it; then kṣīrāvī and dugdhikā are equivalent.
Śatamūlī, bahusutā, abhīru, indīvarī, and varī are names of śatāvarī.
Ṛṣyaproktā, abhīrupattrī, nārāyaṇī, and śatāvarī are also names of that plant.
Aheru is a name; then pītadru, kālīyaka, and haridrava are names of dāruharidrā.
Dārvī, pacampacā, dāruharidrā, and parjanī too denote tree turmeric.
Vacā, ugragandhā, ṣaḍgranthā, golomī, and śataparvikā are names of vacā.
Śuklā and haimavatī are further names of it; vaidyamātṛ and siṃhī denote vāśikā.
Vṛṣa, aṭarūṣa, siṃhāsya, vāsaka, and vājidantaka are names of vāśikā.
Āsphoṭā and girikarṇī are names; viṣṇukrāntā is also called aparājitā.
Ikṣugandhā is called kāṇḍekṣu, kokilākṣa, ikṣuraka, and ikṣurā.

children.text: śāleyaḥ syāc chītaśivaś chattrā madhurikā misiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Śāleya is called śītaśiva; chattrā, madhurikā, and misi are additional names.

children.text: miśreyāpyatha sīhuṇḍo vajraḥ snukstrī snuhī guḍā
children.translated_text: Miśreyā too is a name; then sīhuṇḍa, vajra, snuk, snuhī, and guḍā denote the milky euphorbia.
Samantadugdhā also denotes it; next, vellā, amoghā, and citrataṇḍulā are names
as are taṇḍula and kṛmighna, of viḍaṅga, which may be masculine or neuter.
Balā and vāṭyālakā are names of balā; ghaṇṭāravā is also called śaṇapuṣpikā.

children.text: mṛdvīkā gostanī drākṣā svādvī madhuraseti ca
children.translated_text: Mṛdvīkā, gostanī, drākṣā, svādvī, and madhurasā are names of the grape or raisin.
Sarvānubhūti, saralā, tripuṭā, trivṛtā, and trivṛt are names of trivṛt.
Tribhaṇḍī and rocanī are also names; śyāmā and pālindhī denote suṣeṇikā.
Kālā, masūravidalā, ardhacandrā, and kālameṣikā are names of suṣeṇikā.
Madhuka, klītaka, yaṣṭimadhuka, and madhuyaṣṭikā are names of licorice.

children.text: vidārī kṣīraśuklekṣugandhā kroṣṭrī tu yā sitā ||
children.translated_text: Vidārī is also called kṣīraśuklā and ikṣugandhā; the white variety is kroṣṭrī.
Another variety is called kṣīravidārī, mahāśvetā, and ṛkṣagandhikā.
Lāṅgalī, śāradī, toyapippalī, and śakulādanī are names for a medicinal plant.
Kharāśvā, kāravī, dīpya, mayūra, and locamastaka are names in one synonym group.
Gopī, śyāmā, sārivā, anantā, and utpalasārivā denote sārivā.
Yogyā and ṛddhi, together with siddhi and lakṣmī, are names; these are also designations of vṛddhi.
Kadalī, vāraṇabusā, rambhā, mocā, aṃśumatī, and phalā are names of the banana plant.
Kāṣṭhīlā, mudgaparṇī, kākamudgā, and sahā are names of the same plant.
Vārttākī, hiṅgulī, siṃhī, bhaṇṭākī, and duṣpradharṣiṇī are names of the eggplant.
Nākulī, surasā, rāsnā, sugandhā, and gandhanākulī are equivalent plant names.

children.text: nakuleṣṭā bhujaṃgākṣī chattrākī suvahā ca sā ||
children.translated_text: Nakuleṣṭā, bhujaṃgākṣī, chattrākī, and suvahā are also names for that plant.
Vidārigandhā, aṃśumatī, śālaparṇī, sthirā, and dhruvā are synonyms.
Tuṇḍikerī, samudrāntā, kārpāsī, and badarā are also names in this plant group.

children.text: bhāradvājī tu sā vanyā śṛṅgī tu ṛṣabho vṛṣaḥ
children.translated_text: The wild form of that plant is bhāradvājī; śṛṅgī is also called ṛṣabha and vṛṣa.
Gāṅgerukī, nāgabalā, jhaṣā, and hrasvagavedhukā are plant names.
Dhāmārgava, ghoṣaka, mahājālī, and pītaka denote the same plant.
Jyotsnī, paṭolikā, jālī, nādeyī, and bhūmijambukā are synonyms.
Lāṅgalikī, agniśikhā, kākāṅgī, and kākanāsikā are names for a plant.
Godhāpadī, suvahā, musalī, and tālamūlikā are equivalent names.
Ajaśṛṅgī is called viṣāṇī; gojihvā and dārvikā are equivalent names.
Tāmbūlavallī, tāmbūlī, and nāgavallī are names of the betel vine; next comes the group beginning with dvijā.
Dvijā, hareṇu, reṇukā, kauntī, kapilā, and bhasmagandhinī are names in that group.
Elāvāluka, aileya, sugandhi, and harivāluka are synonyms.
Vāluka is another name; then, for pālaṅkī, the names are mukunda, kunda, and kunduru.
Bāla, hrīvera, barhiṣṭha, udīcya, and keśāmbu are names for the same fragrant root or grass.
Kālānusārī, vṛddha, aśmapuṣpa, śīta, and śiva are names in the next synonym set.

children.text: śaileyaṃ tālaparṇī tu daityā gandhakuṭī murā ||
children.translated_text: Śaileya is one name; tālaparṇī is also called daityā, gandhakuṭī, and murā.

children.text: gandhinī gajabhakṣyā tu suvahā surabhī rasā
children.translated_text: Gandhinī is one name; gajabhakṣyā is also called suvahā, surabhī, and rasā.
Maheraṇā, kundurukī, sallakī, and hlādinī are further names in that aromatic group.
Agnijvālā and subhikṣā are equivalent names; dhātakī is also called dhātupuṣpikā.
Pṛthvīkā, candrabālā, elā, niṣkuṭi, and bahulā are names of that plant or spice.
Sūkṣmā, upakuñcikā, tutthā, koraṅgī, tripuṭā, and truṭi are synonyms.
Vyādhi, kuṣṭha, pāribhāvya, vāpya, pākala, and utpala are names of a medicinal substance.
Śaṅkhinī is called corapuṣpī and keśinī; then comes vitunnaka.
Vitunnaka is also called jhaṭāmalā, ajjhaṭā, tālī, śivā, and tāmalakī.
Prapauṇḍarīka and pauṇḍarya are equivalent names; then tunna is also called kuberaka.
Kuṇi, kaccha, kāntalaka, and nandivṛkṣa are names; next comes rākṣasī.
Rākṣasī is also called caṇḍā, dhanaharī, kṣema, duṣpattra, and gaṇahāsaka.
Vyāḍāyudha, vyāghranakha, karaja, and cakrakāraka are synonyms.
Suṣirā, vidrumalatā, kapotāṅghri, naṭī, and nalī are further names.
Dhamanī, añjanakeśī, hanu, and haṭṭavilāsinī are also included in that synonym set.
Śukti, śaṅkha, khura, koladala, and nakha are equivalent names; then comes āḍhakī.
Āḍhakī, kākṣī, mṛtsnā, and tubarikā are names; mṛttālaka and surāṣṭraja are another pair.
Kuṭannaṭa, dāśapura, vāneya, and paripelava are names in one group.
Plava, gopura, gonarda, kaivartī, and mustaka are also names in that group.
Granthiparṇa, śuka, barha, and puṣpa are names; sthauṇeya and kukkura are another pair.

children.text: marunmālā tu piśunā spṛkkā devī latā laghuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Marunmālā, piśunā, spṛkkā, devī, latā, and laghu are synonyms.
Samudrāntā, vadhū, koṭivarṣā, and laṅkopikā are also names.
Tapasvinī, jaṭāmāṃsī, jaṭilā, lomaśā, and miṣī are names of jaṭāmāṃsī.

children.text: tvakpattram utkaṭaṃ bhṛṅgaṃ tvacaṃ cocaṃ varāṅgakam
children.translated_text: Tvakpattra, utkaṭa, bhṛṅga, tvac, coca, and varāṅgaka are names for aromatic bark.
Karcūraka, drāviḍaka, kālpaka, and vedhamukhyaka are equivalent names.
Oṣadhi applies to the class of herbs as such; when no specific class is meant, every medicinal substance is called auṣadha.
Leaves, flowers, and the like are called śāka; taṇḍulīya is also called alpamāriṣa.
Viśalyā, agniśikhā, anantā, phalinī, and śakrapuṣpikā are plant names.
It is also called ṛkṣagandhā, chagalāntrī, āvegī, and vṛddhadāraka.

children.text: juṅgo brāhmī tu matsyākṣī vayaḥsthā somavallarī
children.translated_text: Juṅga is one name; brāhmī is also called matsyākṣī, vayaḥsthā, and somavallarī.
Paṭuparṇī, haimavatī, svarṇakṣīrī, and himāvatī are synonyms.
Hayapucchī, kāmbojī, māṣaparṇī, and mahāsahā are names of a plant.
Tuṇḍikerī, raktaphalā, bimbikā, and pīluparṇī are also synonyms.
Barbarā, kavarī, tuṅgī, kharapuṣpā, and ajagandhikā are names in one group.

children.text: elāparṇī tu suvahā rāsnā yuktarasā ca sā ||
children.translated_text: Elāparṇī is also called suvahā, rāsnā, and yuktarasā.
Cāṅgerī, cukrikā, dantaśaṭhā, ambaṣṭhā, and amlaloṇikā are sour-herb names.
Sahasravedhī, cukra, amlavetasa, and śatavedhī are synonyms.
Namaskārī, gaṇḍakārī, samaṅgā, and khadirā are equivalent names.
Jīvantī, jīvanī, jīvā, jīvanīyā, and madhusravā are names of jīvantī.
Kūrcaśīrṣa, madhuraka, śṛṅga, hrasvāṅga, and jīvaka are names in this plant group.
Kirātatikta, bhūnimba, and anāryatikta are synonyms; next comes saptalā.
Saptalā is also called vimalā, sātalā, bhūriphenā, and carmakaṣā.
Vāyasolī, svādurasā, and vayaḥsthā are names; next comes makūlaka.
Makūlaka is also called nikumbha, dantikā, pratyakśreṇī, and udumbaraparṇī.
Ajamodā is called ugragandhā, brahmadarbhā, and yavānikā.
With respect to its root, pauṣkara has the names puṣkara, kāśmīra, and padmapattra.
Avyathā, aticarā, padmā, cāraṭī, and padmacāriṇī are plant names.
Kāmpilya, karkaśa, candra, raktāṅga, and rocanī are synonyms.
Prapunnāḍa is also called eḍagaja, dadrughna, and cakramardaka.
Padmāṭa is also called uraṇa; palāṇḍu is called sukandaka.
There, when it is green, the names are latārka and durdruma; next comes mahauṣadha.
Mahauṣadha, laśuna, gṛñjana, ariṣṭa, mahākanda, and rasona are names of garlic.
Punarnavā is called śothaghnī; vitunna is called suniṣaṇṇaka.
Vātaka, śītala, aparājitā, and śaṇaparṇī too are names of the same plant.
Pārāvatāṅghri, kaṭabhī, paṇyā, and jyotiṣmatī-latā are also names for it.
Vārṣika, trāyamāṇā, trāyantī, and balabhadrikā are equivalent names.
Viṣvaksenapriyā, gṛṣṭi, vārāhī, and badarā are likewise names.
Mārkava is bhṛṅgarāja; kākamācī is called vāyasī.
Śatapuṣpā, sitacchattrā, aticchattrā, madhurā, and misi are names of one plant.

children.text: avākpuṣpī kāravī ca saraṇā tu prasāriṇī
children.translated_text: Avākpuṣpī and kāravī are names; saraṇā is prasāriṇī.
For that same saraṇā, kaṭaṃbharā, rājabalā, and bhadrabalā are also used.
Janī, jatūkā, rajanī, jatukṛt, and cakravartinī are names in this group.
Saṃsparśā is another; then śaṭī is also called gandhamūlī and ṣaḍgranthikā.
Karcūra and palāśa are also names; then kāravella is called kaṭhillaka.

children.text: suṣavī cātha kulakaṃ paṭolas tiktakaḥ paṭuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Suṣavī is another name for kāravella; then kulaka, paṭola, tiktaka, and paṭu are equivalent.
Kūṣmāṇḍaka is karkāru; urvāru and karkaṭī are feminine names.
Ikṣvāku is kaṭutumbī; tumbī and alābū are both equivalent names.

children.text: citrā gavākṣī goḍumbā viśālā tv indravāruṇī
children.translated_text: Citrā, gavākṣī, goḍumbā, and viśālā are names for indravāruṇī.
Arśoghna, śūraṇa, and kanda are names; gaṇḍīra is called samaṣṭhilā.
Kalambī and upodikā are feminine vegetable names; mūlaka is also called hilamocikā.

children.text: vāstukaṃ śākabhedāḥ syur dūrvā tu śataparvikā ||
children.translated_text: Vāstuka and these others are kinds of greens; dūrvā is called śataparvikā.
Dūrvā is also sahasravīryā, bhārgavī, ruhā, and anantā; when white, it is called sitā.
That white variety is also called golomī, śatavīryā, gaṇḍālī, and śakulākṣakā.
Kuruvinda and meghanāman are names for mustā; mustaka is the non-feminine form.
Bhadramustaka, gundrā, cūḍālā, cakralā, and uccaṭā are also names.
For bamboo, the terms are tvaksāra, karmāra, tvacisāra, and tṛṇadhvaja.
Śataparvan, yavaphala, veṇu, maskara, and tejana are also names for bamboo.
Those bamboos that sound when stirred by the wind are called kīcakas.
Granthi is masculine; parvaparuṣī, gundra, tejanaka, and śara are reed names.
Naḍa is called dhamana and poṭagala; kāśa is a non-feminine grass name.

children.text: ikṣugandhā poṭagalaḥ puṃsi bhūmni tu balvajāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Ikṣugandhā and poṭagala are masculine terms; balvaja is used in the plural.
Rasāla is sugarcane; its varieties include puṇḍraka, kāntāraka, and others.
Vīraṇa or vīratara is the plant whose root is uśīra, a non-feminine word.
Abhaya, nalada, sevya, amṛṇāla, and jalāśaya are names for uśīra.
Lāmajjaka, laghulaya, avadāha, and iṣṭakāpatha are also names for uśīra.
Naḍa and the others, and also garmut, śyāmāka, and similar plants, are grasses.

children.text: astrī kuśaṃ kutho darbhaḥ pavitramatha kattṛṇam ||
children.translated_text: Kuśa, kutha, darbha, and pavitra are non-feminine names; then comes kattṛṇa.
Paurasa, augandhika, dhyāma, devajagdha, and rauhiṣa are names of kattṛṇa.
Chattra, aticchattra, pālaghna, mālātṛṇaka, and bhūstṛṇa are also names for it.
Śaṣpa is young grass; ghāsa, yavasa, tṛṇa, and arjuna mean grass.
A mass of grasses is tṛṇyā, while a mass of reeds is naḍyā.
The palm is called tṛṇarāja; coconut is nālikera and lāṅgalī.

children.text: ghoṇṭā tu pūgaḥ kramuko guvākaḥ khapuro 'sya tu ||
children.translated_text: Ghoṇṭā, pūga, kramuka, and guvāka are names for the areca; khapura is its fruit.
Udvega too is its fruit; these three, together with hintāla, are grass-trees.

children.text: kharjūraḥ ketakī tālī kharjūrī ca tṛṇadrumāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Kharjūra, ketakī, tālī, and kharjūrī are also grass-trees.

children.text: siṃho mṛgendraḥ pañcāsyo haryakṣaḥ kesarī hariḥ
children.translated_text: Siṃha, mṛgendra, pañcāsya, haryakṣa, kesarī, and hari are names for a lion.
Kaṇṭhīrava, mṛgāripu, mṛgadṛṣṭi, and mṛgāśana are also names for a lion.
Puṇḍarīka, pañcanakha, citrakāya, and mṛgadviṣ are further lion names.
Śārdūla and dvīpin denote a tiger; tarakṣu is called mṛgādana.

children.text: varāhaḥ sūkaro ghṛṣṭiḥ kolaḥ potrī kiriḥ kiṭiḥ
children.translated_text: Varāha, sūkara, ghṛṣṭi, kola, potrī, kiri, and kiṭi are names for a boar.

children.text: daṃṣṭrī ghoṇī stabdharomā kroḍo bhūdāra ityapi ||
children.translated_text: Daṃṣṭrin, ghoṇin, stabdharoman, kroḍa, and bhūdāra are also names for a boar.
Kapi, plavaṅga, plavaga, śākhāmṛga, and valīmukha are names for a monkey.

children.text: markaṭo vānaraḥ kīśo vanaukā atha bhalluke ||
children.translated_text: Markaṭa, vānara, kīśa, and vanaukas are also monkey names; next come the names for bear.
Ṛkṣa, accha, bhalla, and bhallūka are bear names; for the rhinoceros, khaḍga and khaḍgin are used.
Lulāya, mahiṣa, vāhadviṣat, kāsara, and sairibha are names for the buffalo.
Śivā is the feminine term; bhūrimāya, gomāyu, and mṛgadhūrtaka are jackal names.
Śṛgāla, vañcaka, kroṣṭu, pheru, pherava, and jambuka are also jackal names.
Otu, biḍāla, mārjāra, vṛṣadaṃśaka, and ākhubhuk are names for a cat.
Gaudhera, gaudhāra, and gaudheya are the three names for the offspring of the godhikā.
Śvāvit is called śalya; its quills or hairs are śalalī, śalala, and śala.
The wolf, vṛka, is called vātapramī, vātamṛga, koka, and īhāmṛga.
For deer, the terms are mṛga, kuraṅga, vātāyu, hariṇa, and ajinayoni.
Aiṇeya denotes the hide and the like of an eṇī; aiṇa denotes that of an eṇa, and both words are used in all three genders.
Kadalī, kandalī, cīna, camūru, and priyaka are also kinds of deer.
Samūru too is a deer; these hariṇas are sources of hides.
Kṛṣṇasāra, ruru, nyaṅku, raṅku, śambara, and rauhiṣa are deer.
Gokarṇa, pṛṣata, eṇa, ṛśya, rohita, and camara are also deer.

children.text: gandharvaḥ śarabho rāmaḥ sṛmaro gavayaḥ śaśaḥ
children.translated_text: Gandharva, śarabha, rāma, sṛmara, gavaya, and śaśa are animal names.
Thus these and others, beginning with the lion and beginning with cattle, are classes of animals.

children.text: adhogantā tu khanako vṛkaḥ pundhvaja unduraḥ
children.translated_text: Adhogantṛ, khanaka, vṛka, pundhvaja, and undura are names for a rat or mouse.
Unduru, mūṣaka, and ākhu are also mouse names; girikā is a young mouse.
Cucundarī and gandhamūṣī are shrew-like mouse names; dīrghadehī is a mouse.
Saraṭa is kṛkalāsa; musalī is the house-lizard.
Lūtā is feminine; tantuvāya, ūrṇanābha, and markaṭaka are equivalent names for a spider.
Nīlaṅgu is a worm; karṇajalaukā and śatpadī are both names in this group.
Vṛścika is śūkakīṭa; ali and druṇa are used for the scorpion.
Pārāvata, kalarava, and kapota denote a pigeon; next comes śaśādana.
Śaśādana, patrī, and śyena are names for a hawk; ulūka is called vāyasārāti and pecaka.
Divāndha, kauśika, ghūka, divābhīta, and niśāṭana are also names for the owl.
Vyāghrāṭa is bharadvāja; khañjarīṭa is khañjana.
Lohapṛṣṭha is kaṅka; then cāṣa is called kikīdivi.
Kaliṅga, bhṛṅga, and dhūmyāṭa are also names for the cāṣa; next śatapatraka begins the following entry.
Dārvāghāṭa is one bird-name; then sāraṅga, stokaka, and cātaka are equivalent names.
Kṛkavāku, tāmracūḍa, kukkuṭa, and caraṇāyudha are names for the cock.

children.text: caṭakaḥ kalaviṅkaḥ syāttasya strī caṭakā tayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: Caṭaka is kalaviṅka; the female of it is caṭakā.
For the male offspring the term is cāṭakaira, and for the female offspring she is likewise caṭakā.
Karkareṭu and kareṭu are equivalent; kṛkaṇa and krakara are also equivalent.
Vanapriya, parabhṛta, kokila, and pika are also names for the cuckoo.
For the crow, karaṭa, ariṣṭa, balipuṣṭa, and sakṛtprajā are terms.
Dhvāṅkṣa, ātmaghoṣa, parabhṛt, balibhuj, and vāyasa also denote the crow.

children.text: sa eva ca cirañjīvī caikadṛṣṭiśca maukuliḥ ||
children.translated_text: That same bird is also called cirañjīvin, ekadṛṣṭi, and maukuli.
The droṇakāka is kākola; dātyūha and kālakaṇṭhaka are equivalent.
Ātāpi and cilla are equivalent; dākṣāyya and gṛdhra are equivalent; kīra and śuka are equivalent.

children.text: kruḍ krauñco 'tha bakaḥ kahvaḥ puṣkarāhvastu sārasaḥ
children.translated_text: Kruḍ and krauñca are equivalent; baka and kahva are equivalent; puṣkarāhva is sārasa.
Koka, cakra, cakravāka, and rathāṅgāhvaya are names for the cakravāka bird.
Kādamba is kalahaṃsa; utkrośa and kurara are equivalent.
Haṃsas are also called śvetagarut, cakrāṅga, and mānasaukasa.
When those birds are white with red beaks and feet, they are rājahaṃsas.
With dusky beaks and feet they are mallikākṣas; when not white, they are dhārtarāṣṭras.
Śarāri, āṭi, āḍi, balākā, and bisakaṇṭhikā are bird-names.
The female of the haṃsa is varaṭā, while the female of the sārasa is lakṣmaṇā.
Jatukā, ajinapatrā, paroṣṇī, and tailapāyikā are names for the bat.
Varvaṇā, makṣikā, and nīlā are fly-names; saraghā and madhumakṣikā are names for the honeybee.
Pataṅgikā is puttikā; daṃśa is the forest-fly.
Daṃśī is a smaller variety of that; gandholī and varaṭā are used in both genders.

children.text: bhṛṅgārī jhīrukā cīrī jhillikā ca samā imāḥ
children.translated_text: Bhṛṅgārī, jhīrukā, cīrī, and jhillikā are all equivalent names.
Pataṅga and śalabha are equivalent; khadyota and jyotiriṅgaṇa are names for the firefly.
Madhuvrata, madhukara, madhuliṭ, and madhupālin are bee-names.
Dvirepha, puṣpaliṭ, bhṛṅga, ṣaṭpada, bhramara, and ali also denote the bee.
Mayūra, barhiṇa, barhī, nīlakaṇṭha, and bhujaṃgabhuj are names for the peacock.
Śikhāvala, śikhī, kekī, and meghanādānulāsin are also peacock-names.
Kekā is the voice of the peacock; candraka and mecaka are equivalent.

children.text: śikhā cūḍā śikhaṇḍas tu picchabarhe napuṃsake ||
children.translated_text: Śikhā and cūḍā mean crest; śikhaṇḍa, piccha, and barha are neuter terms for plumage.
For a bird, the terms are khaga, vihaṅga, vihaga, vihaṅgama, and vihāyasa.
Śakunti, pakṣin, śakuni, śakunta, śakuna, and dvija also denote a bird.
Patatrin, patrin, pataga, patat, patraratha, and aṇḍaja are further bird-names.
Nagaukas, vāji, vikira, viviṣkira, and patatraya are also names for birds.
Nīḍodbhava, garutmant, pitsant, and nabhasaṃgama likewise denote birds.

children.text: teṣāṃ viśeṣā hārīto madguḥ kāraṇḍavaḥ plavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Their particular kinds include hārīta, madgu, kāraṇḍava, and plava.
Tittiri, kukkubha, lāva, jīvañjīva, and koraka are also such species.
Koyaṣṭika, ṭiṭṭibhaka, vartaka, vartikā, and others are further varieties.
Garut, pakṣa, and chada mean wing; patra, patatra, and tanūruha mean feather.
Pakṣati is feminine and means the root of the wing; cañcu and troṭi, both feminine, mean beak.
Praḍīna, uḍḍīna, and saṃḍīna are actions of a bird's movement.
Peśī and kośa are terms connected with the egg; aṇḍa is neuter, while kulāya and nīḍa, not feminine, mean nest.

children.text: potaḥ pāko 'rbhako ḍimbhaḥ pṛthukaḥ śāvakaḥ śiśuḥ
children.translated_text: Pota, pāka, arbhaka, ḍimbha, pṛthuka, śāvaka, and śiśu mean a young one.

children.text: strīpuṃsau mithunaṃ dvandvaṃ yugmaṃ tu yugalaṃ yugam ||
children.translated_text: A female-and-male pair is mithuna; dvandva, yugma, yugala, and yuga mean a pair.
For a group, the terms are nivaha, vyūha, sandoha, visara, and vraja.
Stoma, ogha, nikara, trāta, vāra, saṃghāta, and saṃcaya also mean a collection.
Samudāya, samudaya, and samavāya too denote what is called a gaṇa, an aggregate.
In the feminine, saṃhati is used; vṛnda, nikuramba, and kadambaka also mean a collection.
As subdivisions of a vṛnda, varga is used for like members, while saṃgha and sārtha are used for living beings.
Kula is a group of the same kind; yūtha, masculine or neuter, is a herd of animals.
For cattle the term is samaja; for others, samāja; then, for those sharing the same property,
the term is nikāya, while puñja, rāśi, utkara, and kūṭa, not feminine, mean a heap.
Kāpota, śauka, māyūra, taittira, and the like denote the corresponding flock or group.
Birds and beasts attached to the household are cheka; they are also called gṛhyaka.

children.text: manuṣyā mānuṣā martyā manujā mānavā narāḥ
children.translated_text: Manuṣya, mānuṣa, martya, manuja, mānava, and nara are names for human beings.

children.text: syuḥ pumāṃsaḥ pañcajanāḥ puruṣāḥ pūruṣā naraḥ ||
children.translated_text: Pumāṃs, pañcajana, puruṣa, pūruṣa, and nara are also terms for a man or person.

children.text: strī yoṣidabalā yoṣā nārī sīmantinī vadhūḥ
children.translated_text: Strī, yoṣit, abalā, yoṣā, nārī, sīmantinī, and vadhū mean woman.
Pratīpadarśinī, vāmā, vanitā, and mahilā likewise mean woman.
Special terms for a woman include aṅganā, bhīru, kāminī, and vāmalocanā.

children.text: pramadā māninī kāntā lalanā ca nitambinī ||
children.translated_text: Pramadā, māninī, kāntā, lalanā, and nitambinī are also such special terms.

children.text: sundarī ramaṇī rāmā kopanā saiva bhāminī
children.translated_text: Sundarī, ramaṇī, and rāmā denote a beautiful woman; when she is angry, she is bhāminī.
Varārohā, mattakāśinī, uttamā, and varavarṇinī are further terms of this kind.
A consecrated queen is mahiṣī; the other women of a king are bhoginīs.
Patnī, pāṇigṛhītī, dvitīyā, and sahadharmiṇī are names for a wife.

children.text: bhāryā jāyātha puṃbhūmni dārāḥ syāttu kuṭumbinī
children.translated_text: Bhāryā and jāyā also mean wife; dāra is used in the masculine plural, and kuṭumbinī begins another set.

children.text: puraṃdhrī sucaritrā tu satī sādhvī pativratā ||
children.translated_text: Kuṭumbinī and puraṃdhrī denote a housewife; a woman of good conduct is satī, sādhvī, and pativratā.
A woman who has been given a co-wife is adhyūḍhā or adhivinnā; next, svayaṃvarā is one who chooses for herself.
Patiṃvarā is the same, while varyā means a marriageable woman; kulastrī and kulapālikā denote a woman of good family.
Kanyā and kumārī mean maiden; gaurī or nagnikā is a girl whose menstruation has not yet arrived.
Madhyamā is one whose menses have appeared; taruṇī and yuvati are equivalent terms for a young woman.
Snuṣā, janī, and vadhū are equivalent terms; ciriṇṭī is a married woman whose husband is living.

children.text: icchāvatī kāmukā syād vṛṣasyantī tu kāmukī ||
children.translated_text: Icchāvatī and kāmukā mean a desirous woman; vṛṣasyantī is kāmukī.

children.text: kāntārthinī tu yā yāti saṃketaṃ sābhisārikā
children.translated_text: A woman who, desiring her lover, goes to an assignation is an abhisārikā.
Puṃścalī, dharṣiṇī, bandhakī, asatī, kulaṭā, and itvarī are names for an unchaste woman.

children.text: svairiṇī pāṃsulā ca syādaśiśvī śiśunā vinā
children.translated_text: Svairiṇī and pāṃsulā are also such terms; aśiśvī means a woman without a child.
Avīrā is a woman without husband and son; viśvastā and avidhavā are equivalent.
Āli, sakhī, and vayasyā mean female friend; pativatnī and sabhartṛkā mean a woman whose husband is living.

children.text: vṛddhā paliknī prājñī tu prajñā prājñā tu dhīmatī ||
children.translated_text: Vṛddhā and paliknī mean an old woman; prājñī, prajñā, prājñā, and dhīmatī mean a wise woman.

children.text: śūdrī śūdrasya bhāryā syācchūdrā tajjātireva ca
children.translated_text: Śūdrī is the wife of a Śūdra; śūdrā is also simply a woman of that caste.
Ābhīrī and mahāśūdrī are equivalent, whether used for caste or for connection with a man.
Aryāṇī is a woman who is herself āryā; kṣatriyā and kṣatriyāṇī likewise denote a Kṣatriya woman.
Upādhyāyā and upādhyāyī may mean a female preceptor, and ācāryā also does so in its own right.

children.text: ācāryānī tu puṃyoge syādaryī kṣatriyī tathā
children.translated_text: Ācāryānī, however, is used in relation to a man; aryī and kṣatriyī are used in the same way.
Upādhyāyānī and upādhyāyī are similarly used; poṭā denotes one marked by both female and male characteristics.
Vīrapatnī and vīrabhāryā mean the wife of a hero; vīramātā and vīrasūḥ mean the mother of a hero.

children.text: jātāpatyā prajātā ca prasūtā ca prasūtikā ||
children.translated_text: Jātāpatyā, prajātā, prasūtā, and prasūtikā denote a woman who has borne a child.
A naked woman is nagnikā or koṭavī; dūtī and saṃcārikā are equivalent words for a female messenger or go-between.
Kātyāyanī is a half-aged, husbandless woman wearing ochre garments.
A sairandhrī is an independent craftswoman who lives in another person’s house.
Asiknī is a female servant, not old, who moves about within the women’s apartments.

children.text: vārastrī gaṇikā veśyā rūpājīvātha sā janaiḥ
children.translated_text: Vārastrī, gaṇikā, veśyā, and rūpājīvā denote a courtesan or woman living by her beauty.
When honored by people she is called vāramukhyā; kuṭṭanī and śambhalī are equivalent words for a bawd or procuress.
Vipraśnikā, īkṣaṇikā, and daivajñā denote a female diviner; then come the words for a menstruating woman.
Strīdharmiṇī, avirātreyī, malinī, and puṣpavatī are also words for a menstruating woman.
Ṛtumatī and udakyā are further such words; rajas, puṣpa, and ārtava denote menstrual discharge.
Śraddhālu and dohadavatī denote a woman with pregnancy longings; niṣkalā means one whose menstruation has ceased.
Āpannasattvā, gurviṇī, antarvatnī, and garbhiṇī denote a pregnant woman.
Gāṇikya denotes a group or class of courtesans; gārbhiṇa and yauvata likewise denote collective groups.
Punarbhū, didhiṣū, and rūḍhā denote a woman married again; her second husband is called didhiṣu.

children.text: sa tu dvijo 'gredidhiṣūḥ saiva yasya kuṭumbinī ||
children.translated_text: That twice-born man is called agredidhiṣū when she is the housewife in his household.
Kānīna is a son born from an unmarried girl; next, the son of a fortunate woman is named.
Such a son is saubhāgineya, while pārastraiṇeya is the son of another man’s wife.
Paitṛṣvaseya and paitṛṣvasrīya denote the son of a father’s sister.
The same formation applies to the son of a mother’s sister; vaimātreya and vimātṛja mean born from a stepmother.
Bāndhakineya and bandhula denote the son of an unchaste woman.

children.text: kaulaṭeraḥ kaulateyo bhikṣukī tu satī yadi ||
children.translated_text: Kaulaṭera and kaulateya are such terms; but if the woman is a chaste mendicant woman,
then her son is called kaulaṭineya, and also kaulateya.

children.text: ātmajastanayaḥ sūnuḥ sutaḥ putraḥ striyāṃ tvamī ||
children.translated_text: Ātmaja, tanaya, sūnu, suta, and putra mean son; in the feminine these words indicate daughter.
All authorities call the daughter duhitṛ; apatya and toka are common to both son and daughter.
Aurasa and orasya mean one born from oneself in one’s own line; tāta, janaka, and pitā mean father.
Janayitrī, prasū, mātā, and jananī mean mother; bhaginī and svasā mean sister.

children.text: nanāndā tu svasā patyur naptrī pautrī sutātmajā ||
children.translated_text: Nanāndā is a husband’s sister; naptrī, pautrī, and sutātmajā mean granddaughter.
The wives within a group of brothers are mutually called yātaraḥ.
Prajāvatī and bhrātṛjāyā denote a brother’s wife; mātulānī and mātulī denote a maternal uncle’s wife.

children.text: patipatnyoḥ prasūḥ śvaśrūḥ śvaśurastu pitā tayoḥ
children.translated_text: The mother of either husband or wife is śvaśrū, and their father is śvaśura.
A father’s brother is pitṛvya, while a mother’s brother is mātula.
A wife’s brothers are śyālas; a husband’s brothers are devṛ and devara.
Svasrīya and bhāgineya mean a sister’s son; jāmātā is a daughter’s husband.
Pitāmaha is the father’s father, and his father is the prapitāmaha.
The same pattern applies from the mother’s father onward; sapiṇḍas are sanābhayas, close kin.
Samānodarya, sodarya, sagarbhya, and sahaja are equivalent words for those born from the same womb.
Sagotra, bāndhava, jñāti, bandhu, sva, and svajana are equivalent terms for kinsmen or one’s own people.
Jñāteya and bandhutā denote, respectively, the state of kinship and the collective body of such relatives.
Dhava, priya, pati, and bhartṛ mean husband; jāra and upapati are equivalent words for a paramour.

children.text: amṛte jārajaḥ kuṇḍo mṛte bhartari golakaḥ
children.translated_text: A child born from a paramour is kuṇḍa while the husband is alive, and golaka when the husband is dead.
Bhrātrīya and bhrātṛja mean a brother’s son; a brother and sister together may be called bhrātarau.
Mother and father together are mātāpitarau, pitarau, mātarapitarau, or prasūjanayitārau.

children.text: śvaśrūśvaśurau śvaśurau putrau putraśca duhitā ca ||
children.translated_text: Mother-in-law and father-in-law together are śvaśrūśvaśurau or śvaśurau; a son and a daughter together are putrau.

children.text: daṃpatī jaṃpatī jāyāpatī bhāryāpatī ca tau
children.translated_text: The two, wife and husband, are called daṃpatī, jaṃpatī, jāyāpatī, and bhāryāpatī.
Garbhāśaya and jarāyu denote the womb or fetal envelope; ulba and kalala are non-feminine terms for embryonic matter.

children.text: sūtimāso vaijanano garbho bhrūṇa imau samau
children.translated_text: Sūtimāsa and vaijanana denote the month of birth; garbha and bhrūṇa are equivalent words for an embryo or fetus.
Tṛtīyāprakṛti, śaṇḍha, klība, paṇḍa, and napuṃsaka are terms for a person of the third sex or a eunuch.

children.text: śiśutvaṃ śaiśavaṃ bālyaṃ tāruṇyaṃ yauvanaṃ same
children.translated_text: Śiśutva, śaiśava, and bālya are equivalent words for childhood; tāruṇya and yauvana are equivalent words for youth.
Sthāvira means old age, vṛddhatva; vārdhaka also denotes a group of old people.

children.text: palitaṃ jarasā śauklyaṃ keśādau visrasā jarā
children.translated_text: Palita is whiteness in the hair and the like caused by age; jarā is decay through old age.
Uttānaśayā denotes a baby lying on its back; ḍimbhā, stanapā, and stanandhayī denote a suckling child.
A child is called bāla or māṇavaka; vayastha, taruṇa, and yuvā mean young.

children.text: pravayāḥ sthaviro vṛddho jīno jīrṇo jarannapi ||
children.translated_text: Pravayas, sthavira, vṛddha, jīna, jīrṇa, and jaran all denote an old person.
Varṣīyān, daśamī, and jyāyān mean older; pūrvaja, agriya, and agraja mean born earlier.
For one born later, the words are kaniṣṭha, yavīyas, avaraja, and anuja.
Amāṃsa, durbala, and chāta mean fleshless or weak; balavān, māṃsala, and aṃsala mean strong or fleshy.
Tundila, tundibha, tundī, bṛhatkukṣi, and picaṇḍila denote a pot-bellied person.
Avaṭīṭa, avanāṭa, and avabhraṭa denote one with a bent or flattened nose.

children.text: keśavaḥ keśikaḥ keśī valino valibhaḥ samau ||
children.translated_text: Keśava, keśika, and keśin mean hairy; valin and valibha are equivalent words for wrinkled.
Vikalāṅga and apogaṇḍa denote one with a defective limb; kharva, hrasva, and vāmana mean dwarf or short.
Kharaṇa and kharaṇasa denote one with a rough or defective nose; vigra denotes one whose nose is gone.
Khuraṇa and khuraṇasa are similar nasal terms; prajñu means one whose knees project forward.
Ūrdhvajñu and ūrdhvajānu mean one with raised knees; saṃjñu means one with contracted knees.

children.text: syādeḍe badhiraḥ kubje gaḍulaḥ kukare kuṇiḥ
children.translated_text: Eḍa means deaf; kubja and gaḍula mean hunchbacked; kukara and kuṇi denote one with a crooked or defective limb.
Pṛśni denotes one with a small body; śroṇa and paṅgu mean lame; muṇḍa means shaven-headed.
Valira and kekara denote a squinting person; khoḍa and khañja are used in all three genders for a lame person affected by age.
Jaḍula, kālaka, piplu, tilaka, and tilakālaka denote bodily spots or moles.
Anāmaya and ārogya mean health; cikitsā is the counteraction of illness.
Bheṣaja, auṣadha, bhaiṣajya, agada, and jāyu are words for medicine.
Ruk, rujā, upatāpa, roga, vyādhi, gada, and āmaya are feminine words for pain, affliction, or disease.

children.text: kṣayaḥ śoṣaśca yakṣmā ca pratiśyāyastu pīnasaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Kṣaya, śoṣa, and yakṣmā are names for wasting disease; pratiśyāya is pīnasa, catarrh.

children.text: strī kṣutkṣutaṃ kṣavaḥ puṃsi kāsastu kṣavathuḥ pumān
children.translated_text: Kṣut, kṣuta, and masculine kṣava denote sneezing; kāsa is cough, and kṣavathu is masculine.
Śopha, śvayathu, and śotha are words for swelling; pādasphoṭa and vipādikā denote fissures or eruptions of the feet.

children.text: kilāsasidhme kacchvāṃ tu pāma pāmā vicarcikā
children.translated_text: Kilāsa and sidhma are skin diseases; for kacchū, itch or scab, the words are pāma, pāmā, and vicarcikā.

children.text: kaṇḍūḥ kharjūśca kaṇḍūyā visphoṭaḥ piṭakaḥ striyām ||
children.translated_text: Kaṇḍū, kharjū, and kaṇḍūyā denote itching; visphoṭa is a blister, and piṭakā is feminine.
Vraṇa, wound, is non-feminine; īrma and maru are neuter, while nāḍīvraṇa, a sinus wound, is masculine.
Koṭha and maṇḍalaka denote eruptions; kuṣṭha and śvitra denote skin disease or white leprosy; durnāman and arśas denote piles.
Ānāha and nibandha denote obstruction or constipation; grahaṇī-ruk is intestinal disease, and pravāhikā is dysentery.

children.text: pracchardikā vamiśca strī pumāṃstu vamathuḥ samāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Pracchardikā and vamī are feminine words for vomiting, and masculine vamathu has the same meaning.
Among varieties of disease are feminine vidradhi, an abscess, and jvara, meha, and bhagandara.
Ślīpada and pādavalmīka denote elephantiasis of the foot; keśaghna and indraluptaka denote loss of hair.
Aśmarī is urinary stone, and mūtrakṛcchra is painful urination; the earlier terms up through śukrāvadhi are used in all three genders.
Rogahārin, agadaṃkāra, bhiṣaj, vaidya, and cikitsaka are words for a physician or healer.

children.text: vārto nirāmayaḥ kalya ullāgho nirgato gadāt
children.translated_text: Vārta, nirāmaya, kalya, and ullāgha describe one who has come out of disease and is free from illness.
Glāna and glāsnu mean languid; āmayāvī, vikṛta, vyādhita, and apaṭu describe one who is diseased or unwell.
Ātura, abhyamita, and abhyānta also denote an afflicted person; pāmanaka and kacchura are equivalent terms for one with scab or itch.
Dadruṇa means one suffering from dadru, ringworm; arśas means one afflicted with the disease of piles.
Vātakī means one with a vāta disorder, and vātarogin the same; sātisāra and atisārakī denote one with diarrhea.
For a person with moist eyes the words culla, cilla, and pilla are used; these same words also apply when the eye itself is wet.
Unmatta means mad or insane; unmādavat has the same sense. Śleṣmala, śleṣmaṇa, and kaphin denote one full of phlegm.
Nyubja denotes one bent over; tundila and tundibha denote one whose navel or belly is enlarged by disease.
Vilāsin and sidhmala denote one afflicted with sidhma; andha and adṛk mean blind; mūrta and mūrchita mean fainted or unconscious.
Śukra, tejas, retas, bīja, vīrya, and indriya are names for semen or generative power.

children.text: māyuḥ pittaṃ kaphaḥ śleṣmā striyāṃ tu tvagasṛgdharā
children.translated_text: Māyu and pitta denote bile; kapha and śleṣman denote phlegm; tvak and asṛgdharā are feminine words for skin.
Piśita, tarasa, māṃsa, palala, kravya, and āmiṣa are words for flesh or meat.
Uttapta denotes dried meat; likewise vallūra is used in all three genders for dried meat.
For blood the words are rudhira, asṛj, lohita, asra, rakta, kṣataja, and śoṇita.
Bukkā is the fore-flesh; hṛdaya and hṛt are the heart; medas, vapā, and vasā denote fat.

children.text: paścādgrīvāśirā manyā nāḍī tu dhamaniḥ śirā ||
children.translated_text: Manyā is the sinew at the back of the neck; nāḍī, dhamani, and śirā denote vessels or veins.

children.text: tilakaṃ kloma mastiṣkaṃ gordaṃ kiṭṭaṃ malo 'striyām
children.translated_text: Tilaka, kloma, and mastiṣka are bodily organ terms, with mastiṣka meaning brain; gorda, kiṭṭa, and mala are non-feminine terms for bodily waste or impurity.
Antra and purītat denote the intestines; gulma and masculine plīhā denote the spleen; next comes vasā.

children.text: snāyuḥ striyāṃ kālakhaṇḍayakṛtī tu same ime
children.translated_text: Snāyu, sinew, is feminine; kālakhaṇḍa and yakṛt are equivalent words for the liver.
Sṛṇikā, syandanī, and lālā denote saliva; dūṣikā is the discharge or dirt of the eyes.
The impurity of the nose is siṃghāṇa, nasal mucus; piñjūṣa is the impurity of the ears.
Mūtra and prasrāva denote urine; uccāra, avaskara, śamala, and śakṛt denote feces or excrement.
Purīṣa, gūtha, and varcas are non-feminine words for feces; viṣṭhā and viś are feminine words for the same.
Karpara and non-feminine kapāla denote skull or bone; kīkasa, kulya, and asthi are words for bone.
Kaṅkāla denotes the bones or skeleton of the body; kaśerukā denotes the bones of the back, the spine or vertebrae.

children.text: śiro'sthani karoṭiḥ strī pārśvāsthani tu parśukā ||
children.translated_text: Karoṭi, feminine, is the bone of the head, the skull; parśukā is the bone of the side, the rib.
Aṅga, pratīka, avayava, and apaghana are words for a limb or body part; then come words for the body as a whole.

children.text: gātraṃ vapuḥ saṃhananaṃ śarīraṃ varṣma vigrahaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Gātra, vapuḥ, saṃhanana, śarīra, varṣman, and vigraha are words for the body.
Kāya and deha are used in neuter and masculine; mūrti, tanu, and tanū are feminine words for the body or form.
The front of the foot is prapada; pāda, pada, aṅghri, and non-feminine caraṇa are words for the foot.
The joint or knob of the foot is ghuṭikā; the two gulpha, ankles, are masculine, and below them is pārṣṇi, the heel.
Jaṅghā and prasṛtā denote the shank; jānu, uparvan, and non-feminine aṣṭhīvat denote the knee.
Sakthi is neuter for thigh, and ūru is masculine; its joint, in the masculine, is vaṅkṣaṇa, the groin.
Guda, apāna, and masculine pāyu denote the anus; basti, below the navel, is used in two genders for the bladder or lower belly.

children.text: kaṭo nā śroṇiphalakaṃ kaṭiḥ śroṇiḥ kakudmatī
children.translated_text: Masculine kaṭa and śroṇiphalaka denote the pelvic plate; kaṭi, śroṇi, and kakudmatī denote the hip or waist.

children.text: paścānnitambaḥ strīkaṭyāḥ klībe tu jaghanaṃ puraḥ ||
children.translated_text: Behind, at a woman's waist, is nitamba; in front is neuter jaghana, the pubic region.
The two kūpaka are the hollows situated on the buttocks; where the pair is lacking or indistinct, the term is kakundara.
Feminine sphic in the dual and kaṭiprotha denote the buttocks; upastha is used for the two organs about to be mentioned.
Bhaga and yoni, in two genders, denote the female organ; śiśna, meḍhra, mehana, and śephas denote the penis.
Muṣka, aṇḍakośa, and vṛṣaṇa denote the testicle or scrotal sac; trika is the lower part at the base of the spine.
Picaṇḍa, kukṣi, jaṭhara, udara, and tunda denote the belly or abdomen; the two breasts are stana and kuca.

children.text: cūcukaṃ tu kucāgraṃ syānna nā kroḍaṃ bhujāntaram ||
children.translated_text: Cūcuka is the tip of the breast, the nipple; kroḍa, the space between the arms or the bosom, is neuter, not masculine.

children.text: uro vatsaṃ ca vakṣaśca pṛṣṭhaṃ tu caramaṃ tanoḥ
children.translated_text: Uras, vatsam, and vakṣas denote the chest or breast; pṛṣṭha is the back, the rear part of the body.
Skandha, bhujaśiras, and non-feminine aṃsa denote the shoulder; its two joints are the jatru, collarbones.
At the roots of the arms are the two kakṣa, armpits; below them is non-feminine pārśva, the side.

children.text: madhyamaṃ cāvalagnaṃ ca madhyo 'strī dvau parau dvayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: Madhyama, avalagna, and non-feminine madhya denote the middle of the body or waist; the two later terms are used in two genders.
Bhuja, bāhu, and praveṣṭa are words for the arm; kaphoṇi and kūrpara denote the elbow.
Above that is the pragaṇḍa, the upper arm; below it is the prakoṣṭha, the forearm.
On the outside of the hand, from the wrist to the little finger, is the karabha.
Śaya and pāṇi denote the hand with its five branches; tarjanī is also called pradeśinī, the index finger.
The aṅgulis are the branches of the hand; masculine aṅguṣṭha is the thumb, and pradeśinī is the index finger.

children.text: madhyamānāmikā cāpi kaniṣṭhā ceti tāḥ kramāt ||
children.translated_text: Madhyamā, anāmikā, and kaniṣṭhā are, in order, the middle finger, ring finger, and little finger.
Punarbhava, kararuha, non-feminine nakha, and non-feminine nakhara are words for the fingernail.
Prādeśa, tāla, and gokarṇa are hand-spans made on the stretched hand by joining the thumb with the index finger and the following fingers.
When the thumb is joined with the little finger, the measure is vitasti, a span of twelve aṅgulas.
On the hand, capeṭa, pratala, and prahasta denote the open palm with the fingers spread.
When the left and right hands are brought together, the terms are saṃhatatala and pratala for the joined palms.
A downward-turned or cupped hand is prasṛti; the two hands joined together are masculine añjali.

children.text: prakoṣṭhe vistṛtakare hasto muṣṭyā tu baddhayā
children.translated_text: With the hand extended from the forearm, the measure is hasta; with the fist closed, however,
that measure is ratni, while aratni is made with a fist excluding the little finger.
Vyāma is the interval between the two arms, including the hands, when they are stretched out sideways;
pauruṣa, used in all three genders, is the measure of a man when the arm and hand are stretched upward.
Kaṇṭha and gala denote the throat; for grīvā, the neck, śirodhi and kandharā are also used.
When that neck has three folds it is kambugrīvā; avaṭu, ghāṭā, and kṛkāṭikā are further neck terms.
Vaktra, āsya, vadana, tuṇḍa, ānana, lapana, and mukha are words for the mouth or face.

children.text: klībe ghrāṇaṃ gandhavahā ghoṇā nāsā ca nāsikā ||
children.translated_text: Ghrāṇa is neuter for the nose; gandhavahā, ghoṇā, nāsā, and nāsikā also denote the nose.
Oṣṭha and adhara denote the lips; radanacchada and daśanavāsas mean the coverings of the teeth, the lips.
Below them is the cibuka, the chin; gaṇḍa and kapola are the cheeks, and beyond them is hanu, the jaw.

children.text: radanā daśanā dantā radāstālu tu kākudam
children.translated_text: Radana, daśana, danta, and rada are words for teeth; tālu and kākuda denote the palate.
Rasajñā, rasanā, and jihvā denote the tongue; the two ends of the lips are called sṛkkiṇī.

children.text: lalāṭam alikaṃ godhirūrdhve dṛgbhyāṃ bhruvau striyau
children.translated_text: Lalāṭa, alika, and godhi denote the forehead; above the two eyes are the two feminine bhru, the eyebrows.
Kūrca, not feminine, is the space between the brows; tārakā and kanīnikā denote the pupil of the eye.
Locana, nayana, netra, īkṣaṇa, cakṣus, and akṣi are words for the eye.

children.text: dṛgdṛṣṭī cāsru netrāmbu rodanaṃ cāsramaśru ca ||
children.translated_text: Dṛk and dṛṣṭi are also eye or sight terms; asru, netrāmbu, rodana, asra, and aśru denote tears.
The two apāṅga are the ends of the eyes; kaṭākṣa is a glance from the corner of the eye.

children.text: karṇaśabdagrahau śrotraṃ śrutiḥ strī śravaṇaṃ śravaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Karṇa and śabdagraha denote the ear, the receiver of sound; śrotra, feminine śruti, śravaṇa, and śravas also denote the ear.

children.text: uttamāṅgaṃ śiraḥ śīrṣaṃ mūrdhā nā mastako 'striyām
children.translated_text: Uttamāṅga, śiras, śīrṣa, masculine mūrdhan, and non-feminine mastaka are words for the head.

children.text: cikuraḥ kuntalo vālaḥ kacaḥ keśaḥ śiroruhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Cikura, kuntala, vāla, kaca, keśa, and śiroruha are words for the hair of the head.
For a mass of that hair the words are kaiśika and kaiśya; alakā and cūrṇakuntala denote curls or ringlets.
When those curls are on the forehead they are bhramaraka; kākapakṣa and śikhaṇḍaka are particular side-lock or crest forms.
Kabarī is an arrangement of hair; dhammilla denotes hair that has been bound up.

children.text: śikhā cūḍā keśapāśī vratinastu saṭā jaṭā ||
children.translated_text: Śikhā, cūḍā, and keśapāśī denote a topknot or tied hair; for an ascetic, saṭā and jaṭā are matted locks.
Veṇī and praveṇī denote a braid; śīrṣaṇya and śirasya are terms applied to well-arranged hair on the head.
When they follow the word kaca, pāśa, pakṣa, and hasta have the sense of a cluster or mass of hair.

children.text: tanūruhaṃ roma loma tadvṛddhau śmaśru pummukhe
children.translated_text: Tanūruha, roma, and loman denote body hair; when that growth is on a man's face it is śmaśru, beard or moustache.
Ākalpa, veṣa, nepathya, pratikarma, and prasādhana are words for dress, toilet, or adornment.
The following ten words, used in all three genders, describe one who is adorned: alaṃkartṛ, alaṃkariṣṇu, and maṇḍita,
as well as prasādhita, alaṃkṛta, bhūṣita, and pariṣkṛta.
Vibhrāj, bhrājiṣṇu, and rociṣṇu complete the set; bhūṣaṇa and alaṃkriyā denote adornment or ornament.
Alaṃkāra, ābharaṇa, pariṣkāra, and vibhūṣaṇa are likewise words for ornament or decoration.
Maṇḍana is another such word; next, mukuṭa and kirīṭa, masculine and neuter, denote a crown or diadem.
Cūḍāmaṇi and śiroratna denote a crest-jewel; tarala is the jewel set in the middle of a necklace.
Vālapāśyā, pāritathyā, pattrapāśyā, and lalāṭikā are names of hair or forehead ornaments.
Karṇikā and tālapatra denote an ear ornament; kuṇḍala and karṇaveṣṭana are earrings.
Graiveyaka and kaṇṭhabhūṣā are ornaments for the neck; lambana is called lalantikā.
Prālambikā is made of gold, while uraḥsūtrikā is made of pearls.
Hāra, muktāvalī, devacchanda, and śatayaṣṭikā are words for a pearl necklace.
Varieties of necklace, distinguished by their strings, include guccha, gucchārdha, and gostana.
Ardhahāra and māṇavaka denote a half-necklace; ekāvalī and ekayaṣṭikā denote a single-string necklace.
That same single string, when it has twenty-seven pearls, is called nakṣatramālā.
Āvāpaka, pārihārya, kaṭaka, and non-feminine valaya are words for bracelets or bangles.
Keyūra and aṅgada are equivalent words for an armlet; aṅgulīyaka and ūrmikā denote a ring.
A ring bearing letters is an aṅgulimudrā; kaṅkaṇa is an ornament for the hand.

children.text: strīkaṭyāṃ mekhalā kāñcī saptakī raśanā tathā ||
children.translated_text: On a woman's waist, mekhalā, kāñcī, saptakī, and raśanā denote a girdle or belt.

children.text: klībe sārasanaṃ cātha puṃskaṭyāṃ śṛṅkhalaṃ triṣu
children.translated_text: Sārasana is neuter for the same; on a man's waist, śṛṅkhala is used in all three genders.
Pādāṅgada and tulākoṭi denote a foot ornament; mañjīra and non-feminine nūpura denote an anklet.
Haṃsaka and pādakaṭaka are foot bracelets; kiṅkiṇī is a small bell.
Bark, plant fiber or cotton, worm, and hair are the sources of garments; the ten related garment terms are used in all three genders.

children.text: vālkaṃ kṣaumādi phālaṃ tu kārpāsaṃ bādaraṃ ca tat
children.translated_text: Vālka is bark-cloth and the like; phāla, kārpāsa, and bādara denote cotton cloth.
Kauśeya is produced from the cocoon of a worm, that is silk; rāṅkava is made from animal hair.
Anāhata, niṣpravāṇi, and tantraka are terms for a new, unused garment.
A pair of washed garments is called udgamanīya.
Pattrorṇa is washed silk; bahumūlya and mahādhana mean very costly or highly valuable.

children.text: kṣaumaṃ dukūlaṃ syāddve tu nivītaṃ prāvṛtaṃ triṣu ||
children.translated_text: Kṣauma and dukūla are two words for fine linen or cloth; nivīta and prāvṛta are used in all three genders for something worn or wrapped.
Daśā, in the feminine plural, denotes the fringes or ends of a garment, especially the two ends of cloth.
Dairghya, āyāma, and āroha denote length; pariṇāha and viśālatā denote breadth or extent.
Paṭaccara is worn-out cloth; naktaka and karpaṭa are equivalent words for a rag.
Vastra, ācchādana, vāsa, caila, vasana, and aṃśuka are words for a garment or clothing.
Sucelaka and non-feminine paṭa denote cloth; varāśi and sthūlaśāṭaka denote coarse cloth.
Nicola is a covering cloth; rallaka and kambala are equivalent words for a blanket.
Antarīya, upasaṃvyāna, and paridhāna denote the lower garment.
Prāvāra and uttarāsaṅga are equivalent upper coverings, and bṛhatikā is the same.
Saṃvyāna and uttarīya also denote an upper garment; non-feminine cola and kūrpāsaka denote a tunic or jacket.
Nīśāra is a covering used to ward off cold and wind.
Ardhoruka is a garment of fine women; non-feminine caṇḍātaka is a related garment term.

children.text: syāt triṣvāprapadīnaṃ tat prāpnoty ā prapadaṃ hi yat ||
children.translated_text: Āprapadīna, used in all three genders, denotes that which reaches down to the forepart of the foot.
Vitāna and ulloca, non-feminine, denote a canopy or awning; dūṣya and related words denote a cloth house or tent.
Pratisīrā, javanikā, and tiraskariṇī denote a curtain or screen.
Parikarma and aṅgasaṃskāra denote body preparation or grooming; mārṣṭi, mārjanā, and mṛjā denote cleaning or wiping.
Udvartana and utsādana are equivalent words for rubbing the body with unguents; āplāva and āplava denote bathing or immersion.

children.text: snānaṃ carcā tu cārcikyaṃ sthāsako 'tha prabodhanam
children.translated_text: Snāna is bathing; carcā, cārcikya, and sthāsaka denote cosmetic application, and then prabodhana
and anubodha are equivalent to patralekhā and patrāṅguli, painted leaf-like decorative marks.
Tamālapatra, tilaka, and citraka are names for viśeṣaka, a distinctive cosmetic mark.

children.text: dvitīyaṃ ca turīyaṃ ca na striyāmatha kuṅkumam ||
children.translated_text: Dvitīya and turīya are also non-feminine names for such a mark; next comes kuṅkuma, saffron.
Kuṅkuma is born in <s>Kāśmīra</s>; agniśikha, vara, <s>Bāhlīka</s>, and pītana are also names for it.
Raktasaṃkoca, piśuna, dhīra, and lohitacandana are names for red sandalwood.

children.text: lākṣā rākṣā jatu klībe yāvo 'lakto drumāmayaḥ
children.translated_text: Lākṣā and rākṣā mean lac; jatu is neuter, and yāva, alakta, and drumāmaya are also names for lac dye or tree-resin coloring.
Lavaṅga, devakusuma, śrīsaṃjña, and jāyaka denote clove.
Kālīyaka and kālānusārya are names of a dark fragrant aloe-wood; next comes samārthaka.
Vaṃśika, aguru, rājārha, lohakṛmija, and joṅgaka are further names connected with fragrant aloe-wood.
Kālāguru and aguru are equivalent; the variety that is auspicious and jasmine-scented is called malligandhi.
Yakṣadhūpa, sarjarasa, rāla, and sarvarasa are names for resin used as incense.
Bahurūpa is another such name; then vṛkadhūpa and kṛtrimadhūpaka denote prepared incense.
Turuṣka, piṇḍaka, sihla, and yāvana also denote incense resin; next comes pāyasa.
Śrīvāsa, vṛkadhūpa, śrīveṣṭa, and saraladrava are names for fragrant resin or turpentine-like exudation.
Mṛganābhi, mṛgamada, and kastūrī denote musk; next comes kolaka.
Kolaka, kaṅkolaka, and kośaphala denote cubeb-like aromatic fruit; karpūra, camphor, is not feminine.
Tailaparṇika, gośīrṣa, and haricandana are non-feminine names for yellow sandalwood.
Tilaparṇī, pattrāṅga, rañjana, and raktacandana denote red sandalwood.
Kucandana is another name for it; jātīkośa and jātīphala are equivalent names for nutmeg or the fruit of jāti.
Yakṣakardama is a perfume mixture made with camphor, aguru, musk, and kakkola.
A stick or preparation for anointing the limbs is gātrānulepanī or varti; varṇaka is a cosmetic unguent, vilepana.
Fragrant powders are vāsayogas; bhāvita and vāsita, in all three genders, mean perfumed or scented.
The treatment produced with perfumes, garlands, and the like is called adhivāsana, perfuming or consecrating by scent.

children.text: mālyaṃ mālāsrajau mūrdhni keśamadhye tu garbhakaḥ
children.translated_text: Mālya, mālā, and sraj mean garland; one placed on the head among the hair is garbhaka.
A garland hanging from the topknot is prabhraṣṭaka; one placed forward on the forehead is lalāmaka.
A garland hanging straight down is prālamba; from the neck it is called vaikakṣika when it is arranged in a particular way.
That arrangement is when it is thrown crosswise over the breast; āpīḍa and śekhara are ornaments worn on the hair or crest.
Racanā means arrangement, parisyanda means flowing or dripping, and ābhoga means fullness or completeness.
Upadhāna and upabarha denote a pillow or bolster; śayyā, a bed, is like śayanīya.
Śayana, mañca, paryaṅka, and palyaṅka are equivalent to khaṭvā, a bed or cot.
Genduka and kanduka mean ball; dīpa and pradīpa mean lamp; pīṭha and āsana mean seat.
Samudgaka and saṃpuṭaka mean a small casket or box; pratigrāha and patadgraha mean a receptacle or catch-vessel.
Prasādhanī and kaṅkatikā denote a comb; paṭavāsaka is a scented powder made from ground material.
Mukura and ādarśa mean mirror; vyajana and tālavṛntaka mean fan.
Saṃtati, gotra, janana, kula, abhijana, and anvaya denote lineage, family, or descent.
Vaṃśa, anvavāya, and saṃtāna also mean lineage; the varṇas are the Brāhmaṇa and the other social classes.
Vipra, kṣatriya, viṭ, and śūdra are remembered as the fourfold varṇa system.
Rājabījī and rājavaṃśya denote one of royal lineage; bījya means one born from a family stock.
Mahākula, kulīna, ārya, sabhya, sajjana, and sādhu are terms for a noble, respectable, or good person.
Brahmacārī, gṛhī, vānaprastha, and bhikṣu make up the set of four life-stages.
That set is called āśrama, a non-feminine noun; dvijāti, agrajanman, bhūdeva, and vāḍava are terms for a Brāhmaṇa.
Vipra and brāhmaṇa also denote him; ṣaṭkarman is one occupied with the six duties such as sacrifice.
Vidvān, vipaścit, doṣajña, sudhī, kovida, and budha are words for a learned or intelligent person.

children.text: dhīro manīṣī jñaḥ prājñaḥ saṃkhyāvānpaṇḍitaḥ kaviḥ
children.translated_text: Dhīra, manīṣin, jña, prājña, saṃkhyāvān, paṇḍita, and kavi likewise denote a wise or learned person.
Dhīmān, sūri, kṛtin, kṛṣṭi, labdhavarṇa, and vicakṣaṇa are further words for an intelligent or accomplished person.
Dūradarśin and dīrghadarśin mean far-sighted; śrotriya and chāndasa are equivalent terms for a Vedic scholar.
A mīmāṃsaka is one belonging to the <s>Jaiminīya</s> tradition; a vedāntin is a brahmavādin, one who teaches brahman.
In the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> school one is called <s>Aulūkya</s>; a śūnyavādin is called <s>Saugata</s>.
A naiyāyika is associated with <s>Akṣapāda</s>; a syādvādika is an <s>Ārhaka</s>, that is, a Jain thinker.
Cārvāka and laukāyatika are equivalent; in the doctrine of satkārya, sāṃkhya and kāpila are equivalent.
Upādhyāya and adhyāpaka mean teacher; a guru is one who performs rites beginning with conception.
An ācārya is one who explains mantras; in a sacrifice the ādeṣṭṛ is the instructor, and vratin denotes one under a vow.

children.text: yaṣṭā ca yajamānaśca sa somavati dīkṣitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Yaṣṭṛ and yajamāna mean sacrificer; when connected with soma, he is dīkṣita, consecrated.
One habitually performing sacrifices is yāyajūka; a yajvā is one who has sacrificed according to rule.

children.text: sa gīrpatīṣṭayā sthapatiḥ somapīthī tu somapāḥ ||
children.translated_text: When he has performed the Gīrpati offering he is a sthapati; a somapīthin is a somapā, one who has drunk soma.
The sacrifice called sarvavedas is one in which the sacrificial fee is all of one's property.
An anūcāna is one who has learned, from a teacher, the Veda with its ancillary texts for recitation and teaching.
One who has received permission is samāvṛtta, a returned graduate; sutvā is said when the soma-pressing has been performed.
Chātra and antevāsin mean pupil; śaikṣa and prāthamakalpika denote a learner or beginner.
Those who practice the same brahma-vow are mutual sabrahmacārins.
Those who have the same teacher are satīrthyas; one who has piled the sacred fire is an agnicit.
Traditional instruction handed down in succession is aitihya; itihā is an indeclinable expression of tradition.
Upajñā is first or original knowledge; upakrama is the undertaking that begins after knowing.
Yajña, sava, adhvara, yāga, saptatantu, makha, and kratu are synonyms for sacrifice.
Recitation, oblation into fire, service to guests, libation to ancestors or beings, and bali-offering are the five rites.
These are the five great sacrifices, known by names beginning with brahmayajña.
Samajyā, pariṣad, goṣṭhī, sabhā, samiti, and saṃsad denote an assembly or council.
Āsthānī and the neuter āsthāna denote an assembly-place; sadas is used in both the feminine and the neuter.
Prāgvaṃśa is the structure east of the havis-house; sadasyas are those who know the ritual procedure.
Sabhāsad, sabhāstāra, sabhya, and sāmājika are terms for members of an assembly.
The adhvaryu, udgātṛ, and hotṛ are respectively knowers of the Yajus, Sāman, and Ṛc.
The āgnīdhra and the other priests, chosen with fees, are ṛtvijs and yājakas, officiating priests.
A vedi is prepared ground; on level ground, sthaṇḍila and catvara are equivalent terms.
Caṣāla and yūpakaṭaka denote the ring or fitting of a sacrificial post; kumbā, sugahanā, and vṛti denote an enclosure or fence.
Tarma means the top of a sacrificial post; araṇi, in either gender, is the wood used for producing fire by churning.
Dakṣiṇāgni, gārhapatya, and āhavanīya are the three sacred fires.
This triad of fires is called tretā; a properly prepared fire is called praṇīta or saṃskṛta anala.
Samūhya, paricāyya, and upacāyya are technical terms applied in connection with ritual fire operations.
The dakṣiṇāgni is the fire that is brought and led forth from the gārhapatya fire.
In that fire the term is ānāyya; agnāyī and svāhā are beloved of Hutabhuk, the fire-god.
A ṛc used for kindling the fire is called sāmidhenī and dhāyyā.
Chandas denotes metre, beginning with gāyatrī; caru, masculine, is a cooked oblation for the preparation of offerings.

children.text: āmikṣā sā śṛtoṣṇe yā kṣīre syāddadhiyogataḥ ||
children.translated_text: Āmikṣā is that which is produced when curd is added to boiled warm milk.
Dhavitra and vyajana are words for a fan, especially one fashioned from deer-skin.
Pṛṣadājya is ghee mixed with curd; paramānna and pāyasa mean milk-rice.
Havya and kavya are, respectively, food-offerings for the gods and for the ancestors; a vessel, such as a sruva, is used for them.

children.text: dhruvopabhṛjjuhūrnā tu sruvo bhedāḥ srucaḥ striyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Dhruvā, upabhṛt, juhū, and sruva are varieties of the sacrificial ladle called sruc, a feminine noun.
An upākṛta animal is one that has been consecrated with mantras and killed in a sacrifice.
Paramparāka, śamana, and prokṣaṇa are terms connected with killing for sacrificial slaughter.
Pramīta, upasaṃpanna, and prokṣita mean 'slain' and take the gender of what they describe.

children.text: sāṃnāyyaṃ haviragnau tu hutaṃ triṣu vaṣaṭ kṛtam ||
children.translated_text: Sāṃnāyya is an oblation; what has been offered in the fire is huta or vaṣaṭkṛta, used in all three genders.
Avabhṛtha is the concluding bath of consecration in a sacrifice; what is fit for that rite is yajñiya.

children.text: triṣvatha kratukarmeṣṭaṃ pūrtaṃ khātādi karma yat ||
children.translated_text: Yajñiya is used in all three genders; iṣṭa is sacrificial action, while pūrta is work such as digging tanks or wells.
Amṛta denotes the remnant of a sacrifice, and vighasa denotes the remnant of a meal.
Tyāga, vihāpita, and dāna are words for giving up or giving away; utsarjana and visarjana mean release or dismissal.
Viśrāṇana, vitaraṇa, sparśana, and pratipādana are words for bestowal or handing over.
Prādeśana, nirvapaṇa, apavarjana, and aṃhati likewise denote giving, assigning, or setting aside.
A gift made on that very day for the sake of the dead is called aurdhvadehika, in all three genders.
Nivāpa is an offering to the ancestors, and śrāddha is that rite as prescribed by śāstra.
Anvāhārya denotes the monthly rite; kutapa, a non-feminine noun, is the eighth portion of the day.
Paryeṣaṇā, parīṣṭi, anveṣaṇā, and gaveṣaṇā are words for searching or seeking.
Sani, adhyeṣaṇā, yācñā, abhiśasti, yācana, and arthanā are words for petitioning or asking.

children.text: ṣaṭ tu triṣvarghyamarghārthe pādyaṃ pādāya vāriṇi ||
children.translated_text: Arghya, used in all three genders, means what is fit for an argha offering; pādya is water for the feet.
Ātithya and ātitheya, in order, denote hospitality toward a guest and what is suitable for a guest.
Āveśika, āgantṛ, and atithi are words for a visitor who has come to the house; atithi is masculine.
Prāghūrṇika and prāghūṇaka are also words for such a guest; abhyutthāna means respectful rising.
Pūjā, namasyā, apaciti, saparyā, arcā, and arhaṇā are equivalent words for worship or honor.
Varivasyā, śuśrūṣā, paricaryā, and upāsanā denote service or attendance.
Vrajyā, aṭāṭyā, and paryaṭana mean wandering about; caryā is conduct, the manner of keeping to one's course of movement.
Upasparśa is ācamana, ritual sipping and rinsing; mauna is non-speaking, silence.
<s>Prācetasa</s>, <s>Ādikavi</s>, and <s>Maitrāvaruṇi</s> are names of that sage.
<s>Vālmīka</s> is another name; next, <s>Gādheya</s>, <s>Viśvāmitra</s>, and <s>Kauśika</s> are equivalent names for the same sage.
<s>Vyāsa</s>, <s>Dvaipāyana</s>, <s>Pārāśarya</s>, and <s>Satyavatīsuta</s> are equivalent names.
Ānupūrvī, a feminine noun, together with āvṛt, paripāṭī, and anukrama, denotes sequence or order.
