Paryāya also means succession or turn; atipāta, paryaya, and upātyaya mean a lapse or passing beyond.
Niyama and vrata, a non-feminine noun, denote a vow or observance, such as fasting and other meritorious acts.
Aupavasta and upavāsa mean fasting; viveka means separateness or distinctness of nature.
Brahmavarcas is the increase of sacred radiance through conduct and study; next comes añjali.
In recitation, the joined-hand gesture is brahmāñjali; drops connected with recitation are brahmabindus.
Brahmāsana is a posture for meditation and yoga; kalpa has the senses of rule and sequence.
Mukhya and prathama denote the primary form, the kalpa; anukalpa is the inferior form after it.
Upākaraṇa is the taking up of śruti, Vedic recitation, after a preparatory saṃskāra.
Pādagrahaṇa and abhivādana are both terms for the same respectful salutation, such as touching the feet.
Bhikṣu, parivrāj, karmandī, pārāśarī, and maskarī are words for a mendicant or wandering ascetic.
Tapasvī, tāpasa, pārikāṅkṣī, vācaṃyama, and muni are words for an ascetic or sage, especially one restrained in speech.
Dānta means one who endures the hardship of austerity; varṇin and brahmacārin denote religious students.
Ṛṣis are truth-speakers; snātaka means one who has bathed after completing the vow, and vratin means a vow-holder.
Those who have conquered the whole group of senses are called yatin or yati.
One who, because of a vow, sleeps on bare ground is called sthaṇḍilaśāyin.
Sthāṇḍila is another such term; virajas-tamas denotes one who has gone beyond both rajas and tamas.
Pavitra, prayata, and pūta mean pure; pāṣaṇḍas are sarvaliṅgins, wearers of every religious mark.

children.text: pālāśo daṇḍa āṣāḍho vrate rāmbhastu vaiṇavaḥ
children.translated_text: In a vow, a staff of palāśa wood is called āṣāḍha; one made of bamboo is rāmbha or vaiṇava.
Kamaṇḍalu, a non-feminine noun, and kuṇḍī denote a water-pot; bṛsī is a seat for vow-observers.

children.text: ajinaṃ carma kṛttiḥ strī bhaikṣaṃ bhikṣākadambakam
children.translated_text: Ajina, carman, and kṛtti, the last feminine, mean hide or skin; bhaikṣa is a collection of alms.

children.text: svādhyāyaḥ syājjapaḥ sutyābhiṣavaḥ savanaṃ ca sā ||
children.translated_text: Svādhyāya and japa mean recitation; sutyā, abhiṣava, and savana denote the Soma-pressing.
Aghamarṣaṇa, used in all three genders, is a recitation that destroys all sins.
Darśa and paurṇamāsa are the two separate sacrifices performed at the ends of the lunar fortnights.
Yama is a regular practice that depends on bodily discipline.
Niyama is that regular practice which depends on an additional or occasional means.

children.text: kṣauram tu bhadrākaraṇaṃ muṇḍanaṃ vapanaṃ triṣu
children.translated_text: Kṣaura, bhadrākaraṇa, muṇḍana, and vapana, used in all three genders, mean shaving or tonsure.

children.text: kakṣāpaṭī ca kaupīnaṃ śāṭī ca strīti lakṣyataḥ ||
children.translated_text: Kakṣāpaṭī, kaupīna, and śāṭī, the last marked as feminine, denote a loincloth.
Upavīta and brahmasūtra denote the sacred thread when the right arm is drawn out from under it.
When arranged over the other side it is prācīnāvīta; when hanging from the neck it is nivīta.
At the tips of the fingers is the daiva tīrtha; at the base of the little finger is the kāya tīrtha.
In the middle between thumb and fingers is the pitrya tīrtha, while at the base of the thumb is the brāhma tīrtha.
Brahmabhūya, brahmatva, and brahmasāyujya all denote becoming one with Brahman or attaining Brahmanhood.
Devabhūya and similar words are formed in the same way; kṛcchra denotes penances such as sāntapana.
Prāya, a masculine noun, denotes fasting undertaken with renunciation unto death; next comes vīrahā.
Vīrahā is one whose sacred fire has been lost; kuhanā is the false fabrication of a religious mode of life out of greed.
A vrātya is one lacking the saṃskāras; asvādhyāya and nirākṛti denote absence of Vedic study or proper formation.
Dharmadhvajin and liṅgavṛtti mean a hypocritical wearer of religious marks; avakīrṇin and kṣatavrata mean one whose vow has been broken.

children.text: supte yasmin astameti supte yasmin udeti ca
children.translated_text: When the sun sets while one is asleep, and when it rises while one is asleep,
those two states are called abhinirmukta and abhyudita, respectively, with reference to the sun.
A younger brother who takes a wife while his elder brother remains unmarried is a parivettṛ.
The elder brother passed over by him is parivitti; vivāha and upayama are equivalent words for marriage.
Likewise, pariṇaya, udvāha, upayāma, and pāṇipīḍana are words for marriage.
Vyavāya, grāmyadharma, maithuna, nidhuvana, and rata are words for sexual intercourse.
Trivarga is the triad of dharma, kāma, and artha; caturvarga is the same set together with mokṣa.
The affectionate companions of the bridegroom are called janya; together with those armed attendants the group is called caturbhadra.
Mūrdhābhiṣikta, rājanya, bāhuja, kṣatriya, and virāṭ denote a consecrated royal Kṣatriya.
Rājā, rāṭ, pārthiva, kṣmābhṛt, nṛpa, bhūpa, and mahīkṣit are words for a king.
A king before whom all vassal rulers bow is called an adhīśvara, an overlord.
Cakravartin and sārvabhauma denote a universal king; another, more limited ruler is a maṇḍaleśvara.
One by whom the rājasūya sacrifice has been performed, and who is lord of a realm,

children.text: śāsti yaścājñayā rājñaḥ sa samrāḍatha rājakam ||
children.translated_text: and who rules by royal command is a samrāṭ; next come rājaka and rājanyaka.
Rājaka and rājanyaka are collective terms for kings and Kṣatriyas, respectively.
Mantrin, dhīsaciva, and amātya denote a counsellor or minister; other officials are karmasacivas, ministers of action.
Mahāmātra and pradhāna denote high officers or chief ministers; purodhā and purohita denote the royal priest.
Prāḍvivāka and akṣadarśaka are names for the overseer or judge of legal proceedings.
Pratīhāra, dvārapāla, dvāstha, dvāsthita, and darśaka are terms for a doorkeeper or gate attendant.
The class of guards is called anīkastha; adhyakṣa and adhikṛta are equivalent terms for a superintendent or appointed officer.
An appointed official in a village is a sthāyuka; over many villages he is a gopa.
The superintendent of gold is called bhaurika; the superintendent of silver is called naiṣkika.
A person appointed in the inner palace is an antarvaṃśika.
Sauvidalla, kañcukin, sthāpatya, and sauvida are terms for such inner-palace attendants.
Śaṇḍha and varṣavara are equivalent terms for a eunuch; sevaka, arthin, and anujīvin denote a servant or dependent.
The king immediately next to one's territory is an enemy; the king beyond him is a friend.
One still farther away is neutral, while the one behind is a pārṣṇigrāha, a rear attacker.
Ripu, vairin, sapatna, ari, dviṣat, dveṣaṇa, and durhṛd are words for an enemy.
Dviṭ, vipakṣa, ahita, amitra, dasyu, śātrava, and śatru likewise denote an enemy or hostile opponent.
Abhighāti, parārāti, pratyarthin, and paripanthin also mean an assailant, adversary, or obstructing enemy.

children.text: vayasyaḥ snigdhaḥ savayā atha mitraṃ sakhā suhṛt
children.translated_text: Vayasya, snigdha, and savayā denote an affectionate companion or peer; mitra, sakhā, and suhṛd mean friend.
Sakhya and sāptapadīna denote friendship; anurodha means compliance or following another's wish.
A spy who assumes a suitable appearance is called praṇidhi, apasarpa, cara, or spaśa.
Cāra and gūḍhapuruṣa are also words for a spy; āpta and pratyayita are equivalent terms for a trusted person.
Sāṃvatsara, jyautiṣika, daivajña, and gaṇaka are names for an astrologer or calculator.
Mauhūrtika, mauhūrta, jñānin, and kārtāntika are also terms for such astrologers and diviners of times.
A tāntrika is one who knows an established doctrine or technical system; satrin and gṛhapati are equivalent terms.
Lipikāra, akṣaracaṇa, and akṣaracuñcu are words for a scribe.
Lipi and libi, both feminine, denote the arrangement of written letters, that is, script or writing.
A bearer of messages is a dūta, a messenger; dūtya denotes the state or work belonging to that role.
Adhvanīna, adhvaga, adhvanya, pāntha, and pathika are words for a traveler.
The king, minister, ally, treasury, realm, fortress, and army
are the limbs of a kingdom, called prakṛtis, and the guilds of citizens are also so called.
Alliance, war, marching, remaining encamped, dual policy, and seeking shelter
are the six policies; the three powers arise from resources, energy, and counsel.

children.text: kṣayaḥ sthānaṃ ca vṛddhiśca trivargo nītivedinām ||
children.translated_text: Decline, stability, and increase are the threefold set recognized by experts in political policy.
That vigor born of treasury and force is called pratāpa and prabhāva.
Dissension, punishment or force, conciliation, and gifts are the four means of policy.

children.text: sāhasaṃ tu damo daṇḍaḥ sāma sāntvamatho samau
children.translated_text: Sāhasa, dama, and daṇḍa denote coercive punishment; sāma and sāntva are equivalent terms for conciliation.
Bheda and upajāpa mean sowing dissension; upadhā is testing a person by dharma and other inducements.
Aṣaḍakṣīṇa, used in all three genders, denotes what is outside the sight of a third person or others.
Vivikta, vijana, channa, niḥśalāka, and rahas likewise denote a secluded or private place.
Rahas and upāṃśu are ungendered expressions for secrecy or whispering; rahasya, used in all three genders, means connected with that secrecy.
Visrambha and viśvāsa are equivalent terms for trust; bhreṣa and bhraṃśa denote a lapse from what is proper.
Abhreṣa, nyāya, kalpa, deśarūpa, and samañjasa denote what is fitting, proper, or regular.
Yukta, aupayika, labhya, bhajamāna, and abhinītavat likewise mean suitable or appropriate.

children.text: nyāyyaṃ ca triṣu ṣaṭ saṃpradhāraṇā tu samarthanam
children.translated_text: Nyāyya too is used in all three genders for what is proper; saṃpradhāraṇā means confirmation or support.

children.text: avavādastu nirdeśo nideśaḥ śāsanaṃ ca saḥ ||
children.translated_text: Avavāda, nirdeśa, nideśa, and śāsana denote instruction, direction, or command.

children.text: śiṣṭiścājñā ca saṃsthā tu maryādā dhāraṇā sthitiḥ
children.translated_text: Śiṣṭi and ājñā also mean command; saṃsthā, maryādā, dhāraṇā, and sthiti denote an established rule or boundary.
Sudharaṇā, the feminine sudhārā, susthiti, sudaśā, and unnati denote good condition, prosperity, or elevation.
Āgas, aparādha, and mantu are equivalent words for an offense; uddāna and bandhana are equivalent words for binding.

children.text: dvipādyo dviguṇo daṇḍo bhāgadheyaḥ karo baliḥ ||
children.translated_text: Dvipādya and dviguṇa denote a doubled fine; bhāgadheya, kara, and bali denote tax or tribute.
Śulka, not feminine, is a toll payable at a landing-place and the like; prābhṛta means a presented gift.
Upāyana, upagrāhya, upahāra, and upadā are likewise terms for a present or offering.

children.text: yautakādi tu yaddeyaṃ sudāyo haraṇaṃ ca tat
children.translated_text: What is to be given, such as a marriage gift, is called sudāya and haraṇa.
The present time is called tadātva; a later or future time is āyati.
Sāndṛṣṭika denotes a result visible at once; udarka denotes a subsequent result.
For kings, unseen danger is that from fire, water, and the like; seen danger is that produced by one's own or another's army.
Ahi-bhaya is fear arising from one's own faction among rulers.
Prakriyā means authority or jurisdiction; cāmara and prakīrṇaka denote a yak-tail fan.
The seat of a king is called a bhadrāsana; it is also called a siṃhāsana, a lion-throne.

children.text: haimaṃ chatraṃ tvātapatraṃ rājñastu nṛpalakṣma tat ||
children.translated_text: A golden parasol is an ātapatra; for a king it is a royal emblem.
Bhadrakumbha and pūrṇakumbha denote an auspicious full vessel; bhṛṅgāra and kanakālukā denote a golden vessel.
Niveśa and śibira, both neuter, mean a camp; sajjana means guarding or protection.
Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry make up the fourfold division of an army.
Dantī, dantāvala, hastin, dvirada, anekapa, and dvipa are words for an elephant.

children.text: mataṅgajo gajo nāgaḥ kuñjaro vāraṇaḥ karī
children.translated_text: Mataṅgaja, gaja, nāga, kuñjara, vāraṇa, and karī likewise denote an elephant.
Ibha, stamberama, and padmī also mean elephant; yūthanātha and yūthapa mean the leader of a herd.
Madotkaṭa and madakala denote a rutting elephant; kalabha means an elephant calf.
Prabhinna, garjita, and matta denote a rutting or excited elephant; udvānta and nirmada denote one whose rut-fluid has passed.

children.text: hāstikaṃ gajatā vṛnde kariṇī dhenukā vaśā
children.translated_text: Hāstika and gajatā denote a herd or collection of elephants; kariṇī, dhenukā, and vaśā denote a female elephant.

children.text: gaṇḍaḥ kaṭo mado dānaṃ vamathuḥ karaśīkaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: Gaṇḍa and kaṭa denote the temples or cheeks; mada and dāna denote rut-fluid; vamathu and karaśīkara denote spray from the trunk.

children.text: kumbhau tu piṇḍau śirasastayormadhye viduḥ pumān
children.translated_text: Kumbha denotes the two protuberances of the elephant's head; the part between them is known as pumān.
Avagraha denotes the forehead; īṣikā is the eye-socket or eye-prominence.
Niryāṇa is the region at the outer corner of the eye; cūlikā is the root of the ear.
Vāhittha is what lies below the elephant's frontal swelling; pratimāna is what is below that.
Āsana is the shoulder-region, and padmaka is a network of spots.
Pakṣabhāga is the side portion, while dantabhāga is the part in front.
The two front and rear regions beginning with the legs are, in order, the lower parts of the body.
Totra and veṇuka denote a driving stick; ālāna is a tethering post; next, for a chain,
anduka and nigaḍa are non-feminine words for a fetter, while aṅkuśa is non-feminine and sṛṇi is feminine for a goad.

children.text: dūṣyā kakṣyā varatrā syātkalpanā sajjanā same ||
children.translated_text: Dūṣyā, kakṣyā, and varatrā denote straps or girths; kalpanā and sajjanā are equivalent words for equipment or harnessing.
Praveṇī, āstaraṇa, and varṇa denote a covering; paristoma and kutha are used in two genders.

children.text: vītaṃ tvasāraṃ hastyaśvaṃ vārī tu gajabandhanī ||
children.translated_text: Vīta denotes an unsound or worthless elephant or horse; vārī is a tether for an elephant.
For a horse, the words are ghoṭaka, vīti, turaga, turaṅga, aśva, and turaṅgama,
as well as vājin, vāha, arvan, gandharva, haya, saindhava, and sapti.
Ājāneya and kulīna denote well-born horses; vinīta denotes horses that carry well or are well trained.
<s>Vanāyuja</s>, <s>Pārasīka</s>, <s>Kāmboja</s>, and <s>Bāhlika</s> are horse breeds or regional kinds of horses.
Yayu is a horse for the horse-sacrifice; javana denotes one that is especially swift.

children.text: pṛṣṭhyaḥ sthaurī sitaḥ karko rathyo voḍhā rathasya yaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Sthaurī is a horse fit for riding on the back; karka means a white horse; rathya is one that draws a chariot.

children.text: bālaḥ kiśoro vāmyaśvā vaḍavā vāḍavaṃ gaṇe
children.translated_text: A young horse is bāla or kiśora; a mare is vāmyaśvā or vaḍavā; vāḍava denotes a herd.
Āśvīna, used in all three genders, means the distance that can be travelled by a horse in one day.

children.text: kaśyaṃ tu madhyamaśvānāṃ heṣā hreṣā ca nisvanaḥ
children.translated_text: Kaśya is a term for middling horses, while heṣā, hreṣā, and nisvana denote a horse's neighing sound.
Nigāla is the throat-region; aśvīya and āśva denote a herd of horses.
Āskandita, dhauritaka, recita, valgita, and pluta

children.text: gatayo 'mūḥ pañca dhārā ghoṇā tu prothamastriyām ||
children.translated_text: are those five gaits, called dhārās; ghoṇā and non-feminine protha denote the muzzle or snout.

children.text: kavikā tu khalīno 'strī śaphaṃ klībe khuraḥ pumān
children.translated_text: Kavikā and non-feminine khalīna denote the bridle or bit; śapha is neuter and khura masculine for the hoof.
Puccha is non-feminine, and lūma, lāṅgūla, vālahasta, and vāladhi are words for the tail.
Upāvṛtta and luṭhita, in all three genders, describe one that has repeatedly rolled over on the ground.

children.text: yāne cakriṇi yuddhārthe śatāṅgaḥ syandano rathaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For a wheeled vehicle meant for battle, the words are śatāṅga, syandana, and ratha.
That same wheeled vehicle, when not meant for battle, is a puṣparatha.

children.text: karṇīrathaḥ pravahaṇaṃ ḍayanaṃ ca samaṃ trayam ||
children.translated_text: Karṇīratha, pravahaṇa, and ḍayana are three equivalent terms for such a carriage.
Anas is neuter and śakaṭa non-feminine for a cart; gantrī and kambalivāhyaka denote conveyances,
while śibikā and yāpyayāna denote a palanquin, and dolā, preṅkhā, and similar words are feminine.
Dvaipa and vaiyāghra are both used for a chariot covered with leopard or tiger skin.
A chariot wrapped in a pale blanket is called pāṇḍukambalī.
Terms such as kāmbala and vāstra are used for a chariot covered with blankets, cloths, and the like.
Dvaipa and related words are used in all three genders; rathyā and rathakaḍyā denote a train or group of chariots.
Dhūḥ is feminine and yānamukha neuter for the front or pole of a vehicle; apaskara denotes a part of a chariot.

children.text: cakraṃ rathāṅgaṃ tasyānte nemiḥ strī syātpradhiḥ pumān ||
children.translated_text: Cakra and rathāṅga denote the wheel; at its rim, nemi is feminine and pradhi masculine.
Piṇḍikā and nābhi denote the hub; the peg at the end of the axle is aṇi, used in two genders.
Rathagupti and masculine varūtha denote the chariot-guard or railing; kūbara is the yugandhara, the yoke-bearing pole.
Anukarṣī is the lower wooden piece; prāsaṅga, masculine, is a yoke attached to another yoke.

children.text: sarvaṃ syādvāhanaṃ yānaṃ yugyaṃ patraṃ ca dhoraṇam ||
children.translated_text: Vāhana, yāna, yugya, patra, and dhoraṇa are all words for a vehicle or conveyance.
A relay conveyance, one vehicle after another, is called vainītaka, a non-feminine word.
Ādhoraṇa, hastipaka, hastyāroha, and niṣādin denote elephant-drivers or elephant-riders.

children.text: niyantā prājitā yantā sūtaḥ kṣattā ca sārathiḥ
children.translated_text: Niyantṛ, prājitṛ, yantṛ, sūta, kṣattṛ, and sārathi denote a driver or charioteer.
Savyeṣṭha and dakṣiṇastha are names for the left- and right-side members of a chariot crew.
Rathin and syandanāroha denote chariot-warriors; aśvāroha and sādin denote horsemen.
Bhaṭa, yodha, and yoddhṛ are fighters; senārakṣa and sainika denote soldiers.

children.text: senāyāṃ samavetā ye sainyāste sainikāśca te
children.translated_text: Those assembled in an army are called sainya, and they are also sainikas.
Those who have a force of a thousand are called sāhasra and sahasrin.
Paridhistha and paricara denote an attendant or guard; senānī and vāhinīpati denote an army commander.
Kañcuka and non-feminine vārabāṇa denote a coat of mail; what armored men tie around the middle
is sārasana. Adhikāṅga and śīrṣaka are armor terms connected with the upper body and head,

children.text: śīrṣaṇyaṃ ca śirastre 'tha tanutraṃ varma daṃśanam ||
children.translated_text: as is śīrṣaṇya for a head-guard; then tanutra, varman, and daṃśana denote armor.
Uraśchada, kaṅkaṭaka, jāgara, and non-feminine kavaca are words for armor or a breastplate.
Āmukta, pratimukta, pinaddha, and apinaddhavat mean put on, fastened, or equipped.
Saṃnaddha, varmita, sajja, daṃśita, and vyūḍhakaṅkaṭa mean armed, armored, or ready for battle.
Āmukta and the following terms are used in all three genders; kāvacika denotes a group of armor-wearers.
Padāti, patti, padaga, pādātika, and padāta are words for a foot-soldier,
as are padga and padika; pādāta denotes a body or collection of infantry.
For one who lives by weapons, kāṇḍapṛṣṭha, āyudhīya, and āyudhika are equivalent terms.
Kṛtahasta, suprayogaviśikha, and kṛtapuṅkhavat denote a skilled archer or one practiced in the use of weapons.
Aparāddhapṛṣatka is one whose arrow has missed, whose shaft has fallen away from the target.
Dhanvin, dhanuṣmat, dhānuṣka, non-feminine niṣaṅgin, and dhanurdhara denote a bowman.
Kāṇḍavat and kāṇḍīra denote one furnished with arrows; śāktīka and śaktihetika denote one armed with a spear.
Yāṣṭīka and pāraśvadhika denote one whose weapons are a staff and an axe, respectively.
Naistriṃśika and asiheti denote one armed with a sword; prāsika and kauntika are equivalent terms for a lance-bearer.
Carmī is one with a shield in hand; patākī and vaijayantika denote a banner-bearer.
Anuplava, sahāya, anucara, and abhicara are equivalent words for a companion or follower.
Purogā, agresara, praṣṭha, agrataḥsara, and puraḥsara denote one who goes in front.
Purogama and purogāmī likewise mean one who goes ahead; mandagāmī and manthara mean slow-going.
Jaṅghāla and atijava are equivalent for very swift; jaṅghākarika and jāṅghika are also such speed terms.

children.text: tarasvī tvarito vegī prajavī javano javaḥ
children.translated_text: Tarasvin, tvarita, vegin, prajavin, javana, and java denote one who is swift or rapid.

children.text: jayyo yaḥ śakyate jetuṃ jeyo jetavyamātrake ||
children.translated_text: Jayya is what can be conquered; jeya is simply something to be conquered.

children.text: jaitrastu jetā yo gacchatyalaṃ vidviṣataḥ prati
children.translated_text: Jaitra denotes a conqueror; one who advances adequately against enemies
is also called abhyamitra, abhyamitrīya, and abhyamitrīṇa.
Ūrjasvala and ūrjasvin describe one endowed with an excess of vigor.
Urasvān and urasila mean broad-chested; rathika, rathira, and rathin denote a chariot-warrior.
Kāmagāmin and anukāmin mean one who goes as he wishes; atyantīna and bhṛśa mean extreme or excessive.

children.text: śūro vīraśca vikrānto jetā jiṣṇuśca jitvaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: Śūra, vīra, and vikrānta mean a hero or brave man; jetṛ, jiṣṇu, and jitvara mean a conqueror.
Sāṃyugīna means skilled in battle; śastrajīvin and similar words are used in all three genders.
Dhvajinī, vāhinī, senā, pṛtanā, anīkinī, and camū are words for an army.
Varūthinī, bala, sainya, cakra, and non-feminine anīka also denote an army or military force.
Vyūha is the arrangement of an army; in war its varieties are daṇḍa and the like.
Pratyāsāra and vyūhapārṣṇi denote the rear of a battle array; pratigraha is the rear part of an army.
A patti consists of one elephant, one chariot, three horses, and five foot-soldiers.
When all the elements of a patti are successively tripled, the following names are used in order.
They are senāmukha, gulma, gaṇa, vāhinī, pṛtanā, and camū.
Then come anīkinī and, from ten anīkinīs, an akṣauhiṇī. Next, under prosperity:
Saṃpatti, śrī, and lakṣmī mean prosperity; in adversity the terms are vipatti, vipad, and āpad.
Āyudha, praharaṇa, śastra, and astra are words for a weapon.
Dhanuṣ, cāpa, dhanvan, śarāsana, kodaṇḍa, and kārmuka are words for a bow.
Iṣvāsa is also a bow; the bow of <s>Karṇa</s> is called <s>Kālapṛṣṭha</s>.
The bow of <s>Kapidhvaja</s> is called <s>Gāṇḍīva</s> or <s>Gāṇḍiva</s>, in masculine and neuter forms.
Koṭi and aṭanī denote the ends of the bow; godhā and tala are guards against the blow of the bowstring.

children.text: lastakastu dhanurmadhyaṃ maurvī jyā śiñjinī guṇaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Lastaka is the middle of a bow; maurvī, jyā, śiñjinī, and guṇa are words for the bowstring.
Pratyālīḍha, ālīḍha, and the like form the five stances.

children.text: lakṣyaṃ lakṣaṃ śaravyaṃ ca śarābhyāsa upāsanam ||
children.translated_text: Lakṣya, lakṣa, and śaravya mean a target; upāsana is practice with arrows.
Pṛṣatka, bāṇa, viśikha, ajihmaga, khaga, and āśuga are words for an arrow.
Kalamba, mārgaṇa, śara, patrī, ropa, and iṣu also denote an arrow, with iṣu used in two genders.
Prakṣveḍana and nārāca denote particular arrows; pakṣa and vāja denote feathering, and the following adjectives are used in all three genders.
An arrow that has been sent forth is nirasta; one smeared with poison is viṣākta, digdha, or lipta.
Tūṇa, upāsaṅga, tūṇīra, niṣaṅga, and iṣudhi, the last in two genders, are words for a quiver.
Tūṇī is feminine; for a sword, the words are nistriṃśa, candrahāsa, asi, and riṣṭi.
Kaukṣeyaka, maṇḍalāgra, karavāla, and kṛpāṇa are also sword terms.
Tsaru is the hilt of a sword or similar weapon, and mekhalā is the fastening for it.

children.text: phalako 'strī phalaṃ carma saṃgrāho muṣṭirasya yaḥ
children.translated_text: Phalaka, non-feminine, along with phala and carman, denotes a shield; saṃgrāha is its handgrip.
Drughaṇa, mudgara, and ghana are words for a mace or hammer; īlī and karavālikā denote a small blade.
Bhindipāla and sṛga are equivalent terms; parigha and parighātin denote a heavy club or iron bar.
Kuṭhāra, used in two genders, along with svadhiti, paraśu, and paraśvadha, denotes an axe.
Śastrī, asiputrī, churikā, and asidhenukā are words for a knife or dagger.

children.text: vā puṃsi śalyaṃ śaṅkurnā sarvalā tomaro 'striyām ||
children.translated_text: Śalya may be masculine; śaṅku is masculine, while sarvalā and non-feminine tomara denote a dart or lance.
Prāsa and kunta are words for a spear; koṇa, and the feminine words pāli, aśri, and koṭi, denote an edge or point.
Sarvābhisāra and sarvaugha signify complete arming or the whole equipment of forces.
Lohābhisāra is the nīrājana rite performed for weapon-bearers or for kings.
The advance against an enemy with an army is called abhiṣeṇana.
Yātrā, vrajyā, abhiniryāṇa, prasthāna, gamana, and gama are terms for a march or departure.
Āsāra, prasaraṇa, and pracakra signify movement or setting out.
Abhikrama is the fearless advance in battle against enemies.
Vaitālikas are awakeners, and cākrikas are the same as ghāṇṭikas, bellmen.
Māgadhas, Magadhas, and bandins are reciters of praise.
Saṃśaptakas are those who, by agreement or vow, do not turn back from battle.

children.text: reṇurdvayoḥ striyāṃ dhūliḥ pāṃsurnā na dvayo rajaḥ
children.translated_text: Reṇu is used in two genders, dhūli is feminine, pāṃsu masculine, and rajas neuter; all mean dust.
Kṣoda means powder; samutpiñja and piñjala describe something extremely disturbed or confused.
Patākā and vaijayantī denote a banner; ketana and non-feminine dhvaja also mean a standard or flag.
That banner is called vīrāśaṃsana; yuddhabhūmi is the battlefield, fear-giving to those who approach it.
Ahaṃpūrvikā, feminine, is the rivalry expressed by saying, 'I first, I first.'
Āhopuruṣikā is self-estimation arising from pride.

children.text: ahamahamikā tu sā syāt parasparaṃ yo bhavatyahaṅkāraḥ
children.translated_text: Ahamahamikā is the mutual egoism in which each says, 'I, I.'

children.text: draviṇaṃ taraḥ sahobalaśauryāṇi sthāma śuṣmaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Draviṇa, taras, sahas, bala, śaurya, sthāman, and śuṣman are words for strength or valor.
Śakti, parākrama, prāṇa, and vikrama denote exceptional power or prowess.

children.text: vīrapāṇaṃ tu yatpānaṃ vṛtte bhāvini vā raṇe ||
children.translated_text: Vīrapāṇa is the drinking performed after a battle or before one still to come.
Yuddha, āyodhana, janya, praghana, and pravidāraṇa are words for battle.
Mṛdha, āskandana, saṃkhya, samīka, and sāṃparāyika also denote battle.
Non-feminine samara and anīkaraṇa, along with kalaha and vigraha, are terms for battle or conflict.
Saṃprahāra, abhisaṃpāta, kali, saṃsphoṭa, and saṃyuga are further words for combat.
Abhyāmarda, samāghāta, saṃgrāma, abhyāgama, and āhava also denote battle or hostile encounter.
Samudāya denotes an assemblage; the feminine words saṃyat, samiti, āji, samit, and yudh are also battle terms.
Niyuddha is hand-to-hand combat; tumula means a battle-confusion or tumult.

children.text: kṣveḍā tu siṃhanādaḥ syāt kariṇāṃ ghaṭanā ghaṭā ||
children.translated_text: Kṣveḍā is a lion-like battle-cry; a gathering of elephants is called ghaṭā.
Krandana is the collective shout of warriors, and bṛṃhita is the roaring or trumpeting of elephants.
Visphāra is the sound of a bow; paṭaha and āḍambara are equivalent drum terms.

children.text: prasabhaṃ tu balātkāro haṭho 'tha skhalitaṃ chalam
children.translated_text: Prasabha, balātkāra, and haṭha mean force or compulsion; skhalita and chala mean a slip or trick.
Ajanya, neuter, together with utpāta and upasarga, are three equivalent words for a calamity or portent.
Mūrchā, kaśmala, and moha mean fainting or bewilderment; avamarda means crushing or oppression.
Abhyavaskandana and abhyāsādana mean assault; vijaya and jaya mean victory.
Vairaśuddhi, pratīkāra, and vaira-niryātana mean requital or vengeance for enmity.
Pradrāva, uddrāva, saṃdrāva, saṃdāva, vidrava, and drava are words for rout or flight.
Apakrama and apayāna mean retreat; bhaṅga in battle and parājaya mean defeat.
Parājita and parābhūta mean defeated, in all three genders; naṣṭa and tirohita mean lost or vanished.
Pramāpaṇa, nibarhaṇa, nikāraṇa, and viśāraṇa are words for destruction or killing.
Pravāsana, parāsana, niṣūdana, and nihiṃsana likewise denote driving off, overthrowing, or killing.
Nirvāsana, saṃjñapana, nirgranthana, and apāsana are words for driving away, removal, or putting an end to something.
Nistarhaṇa, nihanana, kṣaṇana, and parivarjana likewise denote expulsion, striking down, destruction, or avoidance.
Nirvāpaṇa, viśasana, māraṇa, and pratighātana are terms for extinguishing, slaughtering, killing, and counter-striking.
Udvāsana, pramathana, krathana, and ujjāsana are also included among such words.
Ālambha, piñja, viśara, ghāta, unmātha, and vadha too are terms for seizure, breaking, striking, overthrowing, or killing.
Pañcatā, kāladharma, diṣṭānta, pralaya, and atyaya denote death, the destined end, dissolution, or passing away.

children.text: anto nāśo dvayor mṛtyur maraṇaṃ nidhano 'striyām
children.translated_text: Anta and nāśa mean end or destruction; mṛtyu, maraṇa, and the non-feminine nidhana are words for death.
Parāsu, prāptapañcatva, pareta, preta, and saṃsthita describe one who is dead or departed.

children.text: mṛtapramītau triṣvete citā cityā citiḥ striyām
children.translated_text: Together with mṛta and pramīta, these are used in all three genders; citā, cityā, and citi are feminine words for a funeral pyre.
Kabandha, not feminine, denotes a headless trunk or body that is still connected with action.
Śmaśāna and pitṛvana denote a cremation ground; kuṇapa and the non-feminine śava denote a corpse.
Pragraha and upagraha denote confinement or seizure; kārā is a prison, a house of bondage.
In the masculine plural, asu and prāṇa mean the vital breaths; likewise jīva and asudhāraṇa denote life or the sustaining of breath.
Āyus is the span of life, the time of living; jīvātu denotes a medicine that preserves or restores life.

children.text: ūravya ūrujā aryā vaiśyā bhūmispṛśo viśaḥ
children.translated_text: Ūravya, ūruja, ārya, vaiśya, bhūmispṛś, and viś are names for a member of the Vaiśya class.
Ājīva, jīvikā, vārtā, and vṛtti are words for livelihood, maintenance, or a way of living.

children.text: striyāṃ kṛṣiḥ pāśupālyaṃ vāṇijyaṃ ceti vṛttayaḥ
children.translated_text: In the feminine, kṛṣi, pāśupālya, and vāṇijya, agriculture, cattle-keeping, and trade, are occupations or means of livelihood.
Sevā is called the dog's livelihood; agriculture is anṛta, while gleaning ears and grains is ṛta.
For what is obtained by asking and what is not obtained by asking, the two terms are respectively mṛta and amṛta.
The state of a merchant is satyānṛta, a mixture of truth and untruth; ṛṇa denotes debt or borrowing.
Uddhāra is the lending or employment of money, while kusīda is livelihood by interest.
What is obtained by request is yācitaka; what is obtained by exchange or barter is āpamityaka.
Uttamarṇa and adhamarṇa are respectively the lender or creditor and the receiver or debtor.
Kusīdika, vārdhuṣika, vṛddhyājīva, and vārdhuṣi denote a money-lender, one who lives on interest.
Kṣetrājīva, karṣaka, kṛṣika, and kṛṣīvala are words for a farmer, one who lives by fields.
A field suitable for producing vrīhi rice or śāli rice is called vraiheya or śāleya.

children.text: yavyaṃ yavakyaṃ ṣaṣṭikyaṃ yavādibhavanaṃ hi yat
children.translated_text: Yavya, yavakya, and ṣaṣṭikya denote land in which barley and similar crops, including ṣaṣṭika rice, are produced.
For sesame fields, forms such as tilya and tailīna are used; for crops such as māṣa, umā, aṇu, and bhaṅgā there is a twofold formation.
For land capable of producing the remaining grains, forms such as maudgīna and kaudravīṇa are used.
For vegetable fields and the like, the expressions are śāka, śākata, and śākaśākin.

children.text: bījākṛtaṃ tūptakṛṣṭe sītyaṃ kṛṣṭaṃ ca halyavat
children.translated_text: When a field has been sown and ploughed it is bījākṛta; sītya, kṛṣṭa, and halyavat denote ploughed land.
In that case, when it has been worked three times, it is called triguṇākṛta, tṛtīyākṛta, trihalya, and trisītya.
For land worked twice, the corresponding earlier expressions are used, and śambākṛta is also mentioned here.
For sowing-measures beginning with a droṇa or an āḍhaka, words such as drauṇika and āḍhakika are used.
A khārī-vāpa field is called khārīka; terms beginning with uttamarṇa are used in all three genders.
Vapra is masculine and neuter; kedāra denotes a field or cultivated plot.

children.text: kaidārakaṃ syāt kaidāryaṃ kṣetraṃ kaidārikaṃ gaṇe
children.translated_text: What belongs to a kedāra is kaidāraka or kaidārya; a group of such fields is kaidārika.
Loṣṭa and the masculine leṣṭu denote clods; koṭiśa is an implement for breaking clods.
Prājana, todana, and totra are goads, while khanitra is an implement for digging or splitting the earth.
Dātra and lavitra denote a sickle; ābandha, yotra, and yoktra denote a fastening or yoke-strap, and phala is the ploughshare.

children.text: nirīṣaṃ kuṭakaṃ phālaḥ kṛṣako lāṅgalaṃ halam
children.translated_text: Nirīṣa, kuṭaka, and phāla are further words for the ploughshare; lāṅgala and hala denote the plough.

children.text: godāraṇaṃ ca sīro 'tha śamyā strī yugakīlakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Godāraṇa and sīra are also plough terms; śamyā is feminine and denotes the peg of a yoke.
Īṣā is the shaft of a plough, while sītā is the line or furrow made by the plough.

children.text: puṃsi medhiḥ khale dāru nyastaṃ yat paśubandhane ||
children.translated_text: Medhi, masculine, is the wooden post set in the threshing floor for tying animals.
Āśu and vrīhi are rice terms; pāṭala is another grain name, and śitaśūka and yava are equivalent terms for barley.

children.text: tokmas tu tatra harite kalāyas tu satīnakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Tokma denotes the green form of that grain; kalāya is the same as satīnaka, the pea.
Hareṇu and reṇuka are terms in this same pulse group; koradūṣa is the same as kodrava millet.
Maṅgalyaka is masūra, the lentil; then makuṣṭhaka and mayuṣṭaka are a pair of equivalent names.
Vanamudga denotes wild mung; in the case of mustard, tantubha and kadambaka are the two names.

children.text: siddhārthas tveṣa dhavalo godhūmaḥ sumanaḥ samau ||
children.translated_text: Siddhārtha denotes the white variety of this; godhūma and sumana are equivalent words for wheat.

children.text: syād yāvakas tu kulmāṣaś caṇako harimanthakaḥ
children.translated_text: Yāvaka is kulmāṣa; caṇaka, the chickpea, is also called harimanthaka.

children.text: dvau tile tilapejaś ca tilapiñjaś ca niṣphale ||
children.translated_text: For sesame without fruit, the two names are tilapeja and tilapiñja.
Kṣava is a sneeze-producing plant; rājikā, kṛṣṇikā, and āsurī are mustard names.

children.text: striyau kaṅgupriyaṅgū dve atasī syādumā kṣumā ||
children.translated_text: Kaṅgu and priyaṅgu are two feminine words; atasī, flax, is also called umā and kṣumā.

children.text: mātulānī tu bhaṅgāyāṃ vrīhibhedas tvaṇuḥ pumān
children.translated_text: Mātulānī is used for bhaṅgā, hemp; aṇu, masculine, is a variety of rice.
Kiṃśāru is the awn of grain; kaṇiśa denotes the ear or cluster of grain.

children.text: dhānyaṃ vrīhiḥ stambakariḥ stambo gucchas tṛṇādinaḥ
children.translated_text: Dhānya and vrīhi denote grain or paddy; stamba and guccha denote a clump, as of grass and similar plants.

children.text: nāḍī nālaṃ ca kāṇḍo 'sya palālo 'strī sa niṣphalaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Nāḍī, nāla, and kāṇḍa denote its stalk; palāla, not feminine, is straw when the grain is gone.

children.text: kaḍaṅgaro busaṃ klībe dhānyatvaci tuṣaḥ pumān
children.translated_text: Kaḍaṅgara and neuter busa denote chaff; tuṣa, masculine, is the husk or skin of grain.
Śūka, not feminine, is an awn with a smooth and sharp tip; śamī and śimbā, in the later usage, are used in all three genders.
Ṛddha and āvasita describe mature or ripened grain; pūta means grain that has been cleaned and made abundant.
Māṣa and similar pulses are śamīdhānya, leguminous grains; yava and similar grains are śūkadhānya, awned grains.

children.text: śālayaḥ kalamādyāś ca ṣaṣṭikādyāś ca puṃsyamī
children.translated_text: Śāli varieties such as kalama, and ṣaṣṭika varieties and the like, are masculine in gender.
Nīvāra grains are grass-grains; gavedhu and gavedhukā are feminine names for a grain of that class.
Ayogra and the non-feminine musala denote a pestle; udūkhala and ulūkhala denote a mortar.
Prasphoṭana and the non-feminine śūrpa denote a winnowing basket; cālanī and masculine titau denote a sieve.
Syūta and praseva denote bags or sewn containers; kaṇḍola and piṭa denote baskets, and kaṭa and kiliñjaka denote mats.
Rasavatī and mahānasa are equivalent words for the cooking place, the kitchen.
Paurogava is the superintendent of it; sūpakāra and ballava denote cooks.
Ārālika, āndhasika, sūda, audanika, and guṇa are also words for cooks or food-preparers.
Āpūpika, kāndavika, and bhakṣyakāra denote makers of cakes, confections, or prepared foods; these words are used in all three genders.
Aśmant, uddhāna, adhiśrayaṇī, culli, and antikā are words for a hearth or cooking stove.
Aṅgāradhānikā, aṅgāraśakaṭī, and hasantī are also names for a charcoal pan or brazier.
Hasanī is another such word; aṅgāra, not feminine, along with alāta and ulmuka, denotes charcoal or a firebrand.

children.text: klībe 'mbarīṣaṃ bhrāṣṭro nā kandur vā svedanī striyām
children.translated_text: Ambarīṣa is neuter; bhrāṣṭra, masculine, kandu, and feminine svedanī denote ovens, roasting pans, or steaming vessels.
Aliñjara, maṇika, karkayālu, and galantikā are names for household or kitchen vessels.

children.text: piṭharaḥ sthālyukhā kuṇḍaṃ kalaśas tu triṣu dvayoḥ
children.translated_text: Piṭhara, sthālī, ukhā, and kuṇḍa are names for vessels; kalaśa is used in three genders and also in two.
Ghaṭa denotes a jar; kuṭanī and pāvī are feminine, and śarāva and vardhamānaka denote bowls or dishes.
Ṛjīṣa and piṣṭapacana denote a vessel for baking flour-cakes; kaṃsa, non-feminine, is a drinking vessel.

children.text: kutūḥ kṛtteḥ snehapātraṃ saivālpā kutupaḥ pumān ||
children.translated_text: Kutū is an oil-vessel made of hide; when that same vessel is small, it is the masculine word kutupa.
Bhāṇḍa is any receptacle, and bhājana is used for any kind of vessel or container.

children.text: darviḥ kambiḥ khajākā ca syāt tardūrdāruhastakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Darvi, kambi, and khajākā denote ladles, and tardū is a wooden hand-implement.

children.text: astrī śākaṃ haritakaṃ śigrurasya tu nāḍikā
children.translated_text: Śāka and haritaka, non-feminine words, denote greens or vegetables; nāḍikā is the pod of the śigru tree.

children.text: kalambaś ca kadambaś ca vesavāra upaskaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: Kalamba and kadamba are vegetable names, while vesavāra and upaskara denote seasoning or condiment.

children.text: tintiḍīkaṃ ca cukraṃ ca vṛkṣāmlamatha vellajam
children.translated_text: Tintiḍīka, cukra, and vṛkṣāmla are names for tamarind or sour fruit; next comes vellaja,
and marīca, kolaka, kṛṣṇa, ūṣaṇa, and dharmapattana are names for black pepper.

children.text: jīrako jaraṇo 'jājī kaṇā kṛṣṇe tu jīrake
children.translated_text: Jīraka, jaraṇa, and ajājī denote cumin; for black cumin the term kaṇā is used,
as are suṣavī, kāravī, pṛthvī, pṛthu, and kālopakuñcikā.
Ārdraka and śṛṅgavera denote fresh ginger; then chattrā and vitunnaka denote the mushroom-like plant.
Kustumburu and dhānyāka denote coriander; śuṇṭhī and mahauṣadha denote dried ginger.
Viśva, used as feminine or neuter, together with nāgara and viśvabheṣaja, is another name for ginger.
Āranālaka, sauvīra, kulmāṣa, and abhiṣuta,
as well as avanti, soma, dhānyāmla, and kuñjala, are names for kāñjika, sour fermented gruel.
Sahasravedhi, jatuka, bāhlīka, hiṅgu, and rāmaṭha are names for asafoetida.

children.text: tatpattrī kāravī pṛthvī bāṣpikā kabarī pṛthuḥ
children.translated_text: Tatpattrī, kāravī, pṛthvī, bāṣpikā, kabarī, and pṛthu are names for that aromatic spice.
Niśā, kāñcanī, pītā, haridrā, and varavarṇinī are names for turmeric.

children.text: sāmudraṃ yat tu lavaṇamakṣīvaṃ vaśiraṃ ca tat
children.translated_text: Sea-salt is called sāmudra-lavaṇa, and also akṣīva and vaśira.
Saindhava, non-feminine, śītaśiva, and māṇimantha are names for salt produced in <s>Sindhu</s>.

children.text: raumakaṃ vasukaṃ pākyaṃ biḍaṃ ca kṛtake dvayam
children.translated_text: Raumaka, vasuka, pākya, and biḍa are two sets of names for prepared or artificial salt.
For sauvarcala salt, and especially its dark variety, the names akṣarucaka and tilaka are used.
Matsyaṇḍī and phāṇita denote boiled sugarcane syrup; when it is transformed into lumps, it is śarkarā or sitā, sugar.
Kūrcikā is a preparation of milk, while rasālā is the cleaned or refined form called mārjitā.
Temana is called niṣṭhāna; the terms beginning with vāsita and ending with avadhi are used in all three genders.

children.text: śūlākṛtaṃ bhaṭitraṃ ca śūlyamukhyaṃ tu paiṭharam ||
children.translated_text: Śūlākṛta and bhaṭitra denote something roasted on a spit, while the chief spit-roasted preparation is paiṭhara.
Praṇīta, upasaṃpanna, prayasta, and susaṃskṛta all mean well prepared or well cooked.

children.text: syātpicchilaṃ tu vijilaṃ saṃmṛṣṭaṃ śodhitaṃ same ||
children.translated_text: Picchila and vijila mean slimy or sticky; saṃmṛṣṭa and śodhita are equivalent terms for cleaned or purified.
Cikkaṇa, masṛṇa, and snigdha are alike in meaning smooth or unctuous; bhāvita and vāsita likewise mean infused or scented.
Āpakva, pauli, and abhyūṣa denote parched or partly cooked grain; lājāḥ and akṣatāḥ denote puffed or unbroken grains.
Pṛthuka and cipiṭaka denote flattened grain, while dhānā, feminine plural, denotes roasted barley or grain.
Pūpa, apūpa, and piṣṭaka are cakes; karambha is meal mixed with curds.
Bhissā is feminine; bhakta, andha, anna, odana, and dīdivi are words for boiled rice or food.
Bhissaṭā and dagdhikā denote a scorched food-preparation, and maṇḍa, non-feminine, is the first thin essence of cooked food.
Māsara, ācāma, and nisrāva are names for maṇḍa, the watery gruel arising from boiled rice.

children.text: yavāgūruṣṇikā śrāṇā vilepī taralā ca sā ||
children.translated_text: Yavāgū, uṣṇikā, śrāṇā, vilepī, and taralā are names for that thin gruel.
For smearing and anointing, the oil is taila; kṛsara is rice cooked with sesame.

children.text: gavyaṃ triṣu gavāṃ sarvaṃ goviḍ gomayam astriyām ||
children.translated_text: Gavya, used in all three genders, denotes everything derived from cows; goviḍ and gomaya, non-feminine, denote cow-dung.

children.text: tattu śuṣkaṃ karīṣo 'strī dugdhaṃ kṣīraṃ payaḥ samam
children.translated_text: When that cow-dung is dry it is karīṣa, non-feminine; dugdha, kṣīra, and payas are equivalent words for milk.
Payasya covers ghee, curds, and the like; trapsya is the non-solid, thin part of curds.
Ghṛta, ājya, havis, and sarpis denote ghee; navanīta and navoddhṛta denote freshly churned butter.
Haiyaṅgavīna is the ghee that is produced from freshly drawn milk.
Daṇḍāhata, kālaśeya, and ariṣṭa too are terms among preparations of cow's milk.

children.text: takraṃ hyudaśvin mathitaṃ pādāmbv ardhāmbu nirjalam ||
children.translated_text: Takra, also called udaśvin and mathita, is buttermilk, whether mixed with a quarter water, half water, or no water.
Mastu is the whey or liquid part produced from curds, while pīyūṣa is fresh milk or first milk.

children.text: aśanāyā bubhukṣā kṣud grāsastu kavalaḥ pumān ||
children.translated_text: Aśanāyā, bubhukṣā, and kṣud denote hunger; grāsa and the masculine kavala denote a mouthful.

children.text: sapītiḥ strī tulyapānaṃ sagdhiḥ strī sahabhojanam
children.translated_text: Sapīti, feminine, is drinking together; sagdhi, feminine, is eating together.

children.text: udanyā tu pipāsā tṛṭ tarpo jagdhistu bhojanam ||
children.translated_text: Udanyā, pipāsā, and tṛṭ denote thirst; tarpa, jagdhi, and bhojana denote eating or a meal.

children.text: jemanaṃ leha āhāro nighāso nyāda ityapi
children.translated_text: Jemana, leha, āhāra, nighāsa, and nyāda are also words for eating or food.
Sauhitya, tarpaṇa, and tṛpti denote satiety; phelā is what has been left over after eating.
Kāmam, prakāmam, paryāptam, nikāmam, iṣṭam, and yathepsitam all mean at will, sufficiently, or as desired.
Gopa, gopāla, gosaṃkhya, goduh, ābhīra, and vallava are names for a cowherd or milker.
Pādabandhana is a fetter for cows, buffaloes, and the like; gomān and gomī are two names for a possessor of cattle,

children.text: gomān gomī gokulaṃ tu godhanaṃ syātgavāṃ vraje ||
children.translated_text: while gokula and godhana denote a herd or wealth of cows gathered in a cattle-station.
Āśitaṃgavīna, used in all three genders, denotes a place where cows have formerly grazed.

children.text: ukṣā bhadro balīvarda ṛṣabho vṛṣabho vṛṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Ukṣan, bhadra, balīvarda, ṛṣabha, vṛṣabha, and vṛṣa are names for a bull or ox.
Anaḍvān, saurabheya, and gauḥ denote an ox, and a collection of bulls is called aukṣaka.
Gavyā and gotrā denote a herd of cows; vātsaka and dhainuka denote groups of calves and milch cows.
A great bull is called mahokṣa, while an old bull is called jaradgava.

children.text: utpanna ukṣā jātokṣaḥ sadyo jātastu tarṇakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: A bull that has come into being as such is jātokṣa, and one just born is tarṇaka.
A calf is called śakṛtkari; damya and vatsatara are equivalent terms for a young ox to be trained.
Ārṣabhya denotes one fit for castration as a bull; ṣaṇḍa, gopati, and iṭcara are names for a castrated or breeding bull.

children.text: skandhadeśe svasya vahaḥ sāsnā tu galakambalaḥ
children.translated_text: The shoulder region that bears the animal's load is vaha; sāsnā is the dewlap, the hanging fold at the throat.
Nastita or nasyota denotes an animal pierced or tied through the nose; praṣṭhavāh is one yoked at the side of the yoke.
Yugya, prāsaṅgya, and śākaṭa are names for animals that bear yokes and the like.
Hālika and sairika denote the plough-ox, the bearer of the implement with which one ploughs.
For one that bears the yoke, the words are dhurya, dhaureya, dhurīṇa, and dhurandhara.
Ekadhurīṇa, ekadhura, and ekadhurāvaha are equivalent terms for one bearing a single yoke.

children.text: sa tu sarvadhurīṇaḥ syādyo vai sarvadhurāvahaḥ
children.translated_text: One who truly bears every yoke or burden is called sarvadhurīṇa.

children.text: māheyī saurabheyī gaurusrā mātā ca śṛṅgiṇī ||
children.translated_text: Māheyī, saurabheyī, gauḥ, usrā, mātā, and śṛṅgiṇī are names for a cow.
Arjunī, aghnyā, and rohiṇī are cow-names, and the best among cows is called naucikī.
According to distinctions such as color, names like śabalī, 'spotted,' and dhavalā, 'white,' are used.
A two-year-old cow is dvihāyanī or dvivarṣā, while a one-year-old is ekābdā or ekahāyanī.
A four-year-old cow is called caturabdā or caturhāyaṇī; in the same way a three-year-old is tryabdā or trihāyaṇī.
Vaśā and vandhyā mean a barren cow; avatokā is one whose fetus slips away, and sandhinī
is a cow that has been mounted by a bull; vehat is one that injures or loses the fetus.
At the time of calving she is kālyā or upasaryā; praṣṭhauhī means one pregnant while still young.
A cow that is not fierce is sukarā; one that bears often is bahusūti or pareṣṭukā.
A cow that calved long ago is baṣkayaṇī; a dhenu is a cow that has newly calved.
Suvratā and sukhasandohyā denote one easy to milk; pīnodhnī and pīvarastanī denote one with full udders.
Droṇakṣīrā and droṇadugdhā denote a cow yielding a droṇa of milk; dhenuṣyā denotes one standing in the stall or tethering place.
That same cow, when it calves every year, is called samāṃsamīnā.
The udder is neuter: ūdhaḥ or āpīna; śivaka and kīlaka are equivalent words for a tethering peg.

children.text: na pumsi dāma sandānaṃ paśurajjustu dāmanī ||
children.translated_text: Dāma and sandāna are neuter words for a bond, while dāmanī is the rope for an animal.
Vaiśākha, mantha, manthāna, and manthāna denote the churning-stick.
Kuṭhara and daṇḍaviṣkambha denote its crossbar; manthanī and gargarī are equivalent words for the churning vessel.
For a camel the words are uṣṭra, kramelaka, maya, and mahāṅga; karabha is the young camel.
Karabhā and śṛṅkhalakā denote wooden fetters or foot-bonds.
Ajā, chāgī, chāga, basta, and chagalaka are words for a goat.
Meḍhra, urabhra, uraṇa, ūrṇāyu, meṣa, vṛṣṇa, and eḍaka are words for a sheep or ram.
A herd of camels, sheep, or goats is respectively called auṣṭraka, aurabhraka, or ājaka.
Cakrīvant, vāleya, rāsabha, gardabha, and khara are words for an ass.
Vaidehaka, sārthavāha, naigama, vāṇija, and vaṇik denote a merchant or trader.
Paṇyājīva, āpaṇika, and krayavikrayika also denote one who lives by buying and selling.
A seller is vikretṛ or vikrayika; krāyika and krayika are equivalent words for a buyer.

children.text: vāṇijyaṃ tu vaṇijyā syān mūlyaṃ vasno 'pyavakrayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Trade is vāṇijya or vaṇijyā; price is mūlya, and also vasna or avakraya.
Nīvī, paripaṇa, and mūladhana denote capital; lābha, adhika, and phala denote profit.
Paridāna, parīvarta, naimeya, and niyama are also words for exchange or barter.
Upanidhi, masculine, and nyāsa denote a deposit; pratidāna is its return, the handing back of it.
In a purchase, what has been put forth for buying is krayya, kreya, or simply kretavya.
What is to be sold is vikreya, paṇitavya, or paṇya; words such as krayya are used in all three genders.
Satyāpana is neuter for the confirmation of a bargain; satyaṅkāra and feminine satyākṛti have the same sense.

children.text: vipaṇo vikrayaḥ saṃkhyāḥ saṃkhyeye hyādaśa triṣu
children.translated_text: Vipaṇa and vikraya mean sale; numerals up to ten, when used with things counted, occur in all three genders.
Numerals beginning with twenty are always singular, whether denoting a number or the things counted.

children.text: saṃkhyārthe dvibahutve stas tāsu cānavateḥ striyaḥ
children.translated_text: When they are used in the numerical sense they may have dual and plural forms, and among them those up to ninety are feminine.
Beginning with paṅkti, the series such as hundred and thousand increases successively by a factor of ten.
Yautava, druvaya, and pāyya are the three words that have the sense of a measure.
Māna, measurement, is by balance, finger-breadth, and prastha-measure; five guñjā berries make a māṣaka.
Sixteen of these make an akṣa or karṣa, which is not feminine; four karṣas make a pala.
For gold, an akṣa is called suvarṇa or bista; a pala of it is called kurubista.
A tulā, feminine, is one hundred palas; a bhāra is twenty tulās.

children.text: ācito daśa bhārāḥ syuḥ śākaṭo bhāra ācitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Ten bhāras make an ācita; śākaṭa, bhāra, and ācita are load-measures.

children.text: kārṣāpaṇaḥ kārṣikaḥ syāt kārṣike tāmrike paṇaḥ
children.translated_text: A coin or weight of a karṣa is kārṣāpaṇa or kārṣika; when the kārṣika is copper it is a paṇa.
Āḍhaka and droṇa are non-feminine capacity measures; khārī, vāha, and nikuñcaka are also such measures.
Kuḍava, prastha, and the like separately denote measures of quantity or capacity.
Pāda, turīya, and bhāga denote a quarter; aṃśa and bhāga denote a share in a division.

children.text: dravyaṃ vittaṃ svāpateyaṃ rikthamṛkthaṃ dhanaṃ vasu
children.translated_text: Dravya, vitta, svāpateya, riktha, mṛktha, dhana, and vasu are words for property or wealth.
Hiraṇya, draviṇa, dyumna, artha, rai, and vibhava are also words for wealth.
Kośa and hiraṇya denote gold and silver, whether worked or unworked.

children.text: tābhyāṃ yadanyat tatkupyaṃ rūpyaṃ tad dvayamāhatam ||
children.translated_text: What is other than those two is kupya; that pair, when stamped or struck, is rūpya.
Gārutmata, marakata, aśmagarbha, and harinmaṇi are words for emerald.
Śoṇaratna, lohitaka, and padmarāga are words for ruby; next, mauktika means pearl.
Muktā also means pearl; vidruma is masculine for coral, while pravāla is masculine and neuter.
Ratna and maṇi are used for stone-born gems and also for pearls and the like.
Svarṇa, suvarṇa, kanaka, hiraṇya, heman, and kāṭaka are words for gold.
Tapanīya, śātakumbha, gāṅgeya, bharma, and karvura are also words for gold.
Cāmīkara, jātarūpa, mahārajata, and kāñcana likewise denote gold.
Rukma, kārtasvara, jāmbūnada, and aṣṭāpada, non-feminine, are also words for gold.
Gold used for ornaments is called śṛṅgīkanaka.
Durvarṇa, rajata, rūpya, kharjūra, and śveta are words for silver.
Rīti is feminine and ārakūṭa is not feminine; then tāmraka,
śulba, mlecchamukha, dvyaṣṭa, variṣṭa, and udumbara are words for copper or copper-alloy metal.
Loha, not feminine, śastraka, tīkṣṇa, piṇḍa, kālāyasa, and ayas are words for iron.
Aśmasāra is also iron; maṇḍūra and siṃhāṇa denote its rust or impurity.

children.text: sarvaṃ ca taijasaṃ lauhaṃ vikārastvayasaḥ kuśī
children.translated_text: Anything made of metal is taijasa or lauha; kuśī is a product or modification of iron.

children.text: kṣāraḥ kāco 'tha capalo rasaḥ sūtaśca pārade ||
children.translated_text: Kṣāra means alkali and kāca means glass; mercury is capala, rasa, sūta, or pārada.
Gavala, māhiṣa, and śṛṅga denote buffalo horn; abhraka is mica, the impurity of the mountain-born ore.
Srotoñjana is mauvīra; kāpotāñjana and yāmuna are further names for collyrium.
Tutthāñjana, śikhigrīva, vitunnaka, and mayūraka are names in the class of mineral collyria.
Karparī, dāviṅkā, mine-born tuttha, and rasāñjana are further mineral substances or collyria.
Rasagarbha and tārkṣyaśaila are equivalent names; for gandhāśman the word is gandhika.
Saugandhika and cakṣuṣya are also its names; kulālī and kulatthikā are equivalent.
Rītipuṣpa, puṣpaka, and kusumāñjana are terms in the class called puṣpaka.
Piñjara, pītana, tāla, and āla are words for haritāla, or orpiment.
Gaireya, arthya, girija, and aśmaja are words for śilājatu, mineral pitch.
Vola, gandharasa, prāṇa, piṇḍa, and goparasa are equivalent names for fragrant resin.
Ḍiṇḍīra, abdhikapha, and phena are words for sea-foam; sindūra is produced from lead.
Nāga and sīsaka denote lead; piñcaṭa is used in all three genders for a desired lead compound.
Raṅga and vaṅga denote tin; then picu and tūla denote cotton, and next kamalottara is introduced.
Kusumbha is also called vahniśikha and mahārajana.
Meṣakambala and ūrṇāyu denote wool or a wool-bearing sheep; śaśorṇa and śaśaloman denote hare's fur.

children.text: madhu kṣaudraṃ mākṣikādi madhūcchiṣṭaṃ tu sikthakam ||
children.translated_text: Madhu, kṣaudra, mākṣika, and similar words denote honey, while madhūcchiṣṭa is sikthaka, beeswax.
Manaḥśilā, realgar, is called manoguptā, manohvā, and nāgajihvikā.
Naipālī, kunaṭī, and golā are further names for it; yavakṣāra, barley-alkali, is also yavāgraja.
Yavakṣāra is also pākya; sarjikākṣāra is called kāpota and sukhavarcaka.
Sauvarcala is rucaka, and tvakkṣīrī is vaṃśarocanā.
Śigruja is śvetamārica, white pepper; moraṭa is sugarcane root.
Granthika and caṭikāśira are also names for pippalīmūla, the root of long pepper.
Golomī is also the masculine bhūtakeśa; patrāṅga is red sandalwood.

children.text: trikaṭu tryūpaṇaṃ vyopaṃ triphalā tu phalatrikam ||
children.translated_text: Trikaṭu, tryūpaṇa, and vyopa are the three pungents; triphalā is phalatrika, the three fruits.

children.text: śūdrāś cāvaravarṇāś ca vṛṣalāś ca jaghanyajāḥ
children.translated_text: Śūdras are also called avaravarṇa, vṛṣala, and jaghanyaja.
Those down to the caṇḍāla, such as ambaṣṭha and karaṇa, are the saṃkīrṇa, mixed classes.
Karaṇa is the mixed offspring of a Vaiśya and a Śūdra woman, and ambaṣṭha of a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya woman.
Ugra is from a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra woman, while Māgadha is from a Vaiśya and a Kṣatriya woman.
Māhiṣa is from an āryā and a Kṣatriya; kṣattṛ is the son of an āryā and a Śūdra.

children.text: brāhmaṇyāṃ kṣatriyāt sūtas tasyāṃ vaidehako viśaḥ ||
children.translated_text: A sūta is born in a Brāhmaṇī from a Kṣatriya; in that same woman, from a Vaiśya, is a vaidehaka.

children.text: rathakāras tu māhiṣyāt karaṇyāṃ yasya saṃbhavaḥ
children.translated_text: Rathakāra is one whose birth is from a māhiṣa father in a karaṇī woman.

children.text: syāc caṇḍālas tu janito brāhmaṇyāṃ vṛṣalena yaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Caṇḍāla is one born in a Brāhmaṇī by a vṛṣala, a Śūdra.

children.text: kāruḥ śilpī saṃhatais tair dvayoḥ śreṇiḥ sajātibhiḥ
children.translated_text: Kāru and śilpin mean artisan; a śreṇi is an association of such people, or of members of the same class.

children.text: kulakaḥ syāt kulaśreṣṭhī mālākāras tu mālikaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Kulaka is a kulaśreṣṭhin, a head of a family or guild; a mālākāra is a mālika, a garland-maker.

children.text: kumbhakāraḥ kulālaḥ syāt palagaṇḍas tu lepakaḥ
children.translated_text: Kumbhakāra is kulāla, a potter, while palagaṇḍa is lepaka, a plasterer.

children.text: tantuvāyaḥ kuvindaḥ syāt tunnavāyas tu saucikaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Tantuvāya is kuvinda, a weaver, while tunnavāya is saucika, a sewer or tailor.
Raṅgājīva is citrakara, a painter; śastramārja is an asi-dhāvaka, a sword-cleaner.
Pādakṛt is carmakāra, a leatherworker or shoemaker, and vyokāra is lohakāraka, an ironworker.
Nāḍindhama, svarṇakāra, kalāda, and rukmakāraka are names for a goldsmith.
Śāṅkhika and kāmbavika denote a worker in conch-shell, while śaulbika is a tāmrakuṭṭaka, a copper-beater.

children.text: takṣā tu vardhakis tvaṣṭā rathakāraś ca kāṣṭhataṭ
children.translated_text: Takṣan, vardhaki, tvaṣṭṛ, rathakāra, and kāṣṭhataṭ are terms for a carpenter or woodworker.
A village-dependent carpenter is a grāmatakṣa, while an independent one is a kauṭatakṣa.
Kṣurī, muṇḍī, divākīrti, nāpita, and antāvasāyin are terms for a barber.
Nirṇejaka is rajaka, a washerman; śauṇḍika is maṇḍahāraka, a distiller or liquor-seller.
Jābāla is one who lives by goats; devājīva is devala, one who lives by temple service.

children.text: syān māyā śāmbarī māyākāras tu pratihārakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Māyā is śāmbarī, magic, and a māyākāra is a pratihāraka, a conjurer.
Śailālina, śailūṣa, jāyājīva, and kṛśāśvin are terms for performers.

children.text: bharatā ityapi naṭāś cāraṇās tu kuśīlavāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Bharata is also a term for an actor, and cāraṇa and kuśīlava denote bards or performers.
Mārdaṅgika and maurajika are drummers, while pāṇivāda and pāṇigha denote hand-percussion players.

children.text: veṇudhmāḥ syur vaiṇavikā vīṇāvādās tu vaiṇikāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Veṇudhma and vaiṇavika are flute-players, while vīṇāvāda and vaiṇika are lute-players.
Jīvāntaka and śākunika denote a fowler or bird-killer; vāgurika and jālika are two terms for a netter.

children.text: vaitaṃsikaḥ kauṭikaś ca māṃsikaś ca samaṃ trayam ||
children.translated_text: Vaitaṃsika, kauṭika, and māṃsika are three equivalent terms for a trapper or meatman.
Bhṛtaka, bhṛtibhuj, karmakara, and vaitanika all denote a hired worker.
Vārtāvaha is vaivadhika, a carrier, and bhāravāha is bhārika, a porter.

children.text: vivarṇaḥ pāmaro nīcaḥ prākṛtaś ca pṛthagjanaḥ
children.translated_text: Vivarṇa, pāmara, nīca, prākṛta, and pṛthagjana denote a low or common person.

children.text: nihīno 'pasado jālmaḥ kṣullakaś cetaraś ca saḥ ||
children.translated_text: Nihīna, apasada, jālma, kṣullaka, and itara are also terms for such a base person.
For a servant, the words are dāsera, dāseya, dāsagopyaka, and ceṭaka.
Niyojya, kiṅkara, praiṣya, bhujiṣya, and paricāraka are also names for a servant or attendant.
Parācita, pariskanda, parajāta, and paraidhita are further terms for one dependent on another.
Mānda, tundaparimṛja, ālasya, śītaka, alasa, and anuṣṇa denote a lazy person.

children.text: dakṣe tu caturapeśalapaṭavaḥ sūtthāna uṣṇaś ca
children.translated_text: For a capable person, the terms are catura, peśala, paṭu, sūtthāna, and uṣṇa.
Caṇḍāla, plava, mātaṅga, divākīrti, and janaṅgama are names for outcaste groups.
Nipāda, śvapaca, antevāsin, caṇḍāla, and pukkasa are likewise such distinctions.
The <s>Kirāta</s>, <s>Śabara</s>, and <s>Pulinda</s> are mleccha peoples.
Vyādha, mṛgavadhājīvin, mṛgayu, and lubdhaka are terms for a hunter who lives by killing animals.
Kauleyaka, sārameya, kukkura, and mṛgadaṃśaka are names for a dog.

children.text: śunako bhapakaḥ śvā syādalarkas tu sa yogitaḥ
children.translated_text: Śunaka, bhapaka, and śvā also denote a dog; when mad or rabid it is alarka.
Viśvakadru is a dog skilled in hunting; <s>Saramā</s> and śunī denote a bitch.

children.text: viṭcaraḥ sūkaro grāmyo varkaras taruṇaḥ paśuḥ
children.translated_text: Viṭcara, sūkara, and grāmya denote a domestic pig; varkara is a young animal.
Ācchodana, mṛgavya, ākheṭa, and the feminine mṛgayā denote hunting.
Dakṣiṇāru and dakṣiṇermā, through association with a hunter, denote a small antelope, a kuraṅgaka.
Caura, ekāgārika, stena, dasyu, taskara, and mopaka are terms for a thief.
Pratirodhin, parāskandin, pāṭaccara, and malimluca are further words for a robber.

children.text: caurikā stainyacaurye ca steyaṃ loptraṃ tu taddhane ||
children.translated_text: Caurikā, stainya, caurya, and steya denote theft; loptra denotes the stolen property.
Vītaṃsa is an implement for binding or catching animals and birds.
Unmātha is a cunning trap-device, and vāgurā is a snare for catching animals.

children.text: śulbaṃ varāṭakaṃ strī tu rajjus triṣu vaṭī guṇaḥ
children.translated_text: Śulba and varāṭaka denote rope; rajju is feminine, while vaṭī and guṇa are used in all three genders.
Udghāṭana, ghaṭīyantra, and salilodvāhana denote a water-lifting device.

children.text: puṃsi vemā vāyadaṇḍaḥ sūtrāṇi nari tantavaḥ
children.translated_text: Vemā, masculine, is the weaver's rod; sūtra and tantu denote threads.

children.text: vāṇir vyūtiḥ striyau tulye pustaṃ lepyādikarmaṇi ||
children.translated_text: Vāṇi and vyūti, both feminine, are equivalent weaving terms; pusta denotes work made by plastering and similar crafts.
Pāñcālikā is a puttrikā, a doll or small figure made from cloth, ivory, and the like.
For products made from lac and tin, jātupa and trāpuṣa are used in all three genders.
Piṭaka, peṭaka, peṭā, and mañjūṣā are names for a box or basket; then vihaṅgikā follows.
Vihaṅgikā is a load-carrying pole; śikya is what hangs from it, kāca is another such sling, and next come sandals.
Pādukā, pādū, and the feminine upānat denote footwear; the same, when extending along the foot, is anupadīnā.

children.text: naddhnī vardhnī varatrā syādaśvādes tāḍanī kaśā ||
children.translated_text: Naddhnī, vardhnī, and varatrā denote straps or thongs; kaśā is a whip for striking horses and the like.
Cāṇḍālikā, kaṇḍola-vīṇā, and caṇḍālavallakī denote a lute associated with caṇḍālas.

children.text: nārācī syādeṣaṇikā śāṇas tu nikaṣaḥ kaṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Nārācī is eṣaṇikā, a probe or awl; śāṇa, nikaṣa, and kaṣa denote a whetstone or touchstone.
Vraścana, patraparaśu, ṛpikā, and tūlikā are equivalent names for a cutting implement.
Taijasāvartanī is a metal-mould, mūṣā is a crucible, and bhastrā is a leather bellows.
Āsphoṭanī, vedhanikā, kṛpāṇī, and kartarī are equivalent names for shears or a cutting instrument.
Vṛkṣādanī and vṛkṣabhedin are tree-cutting implements; ṭaṅka is a stone-splitting tool.
Krakaca, of non-feminine gender, and karapatra denote a saw; ārā is the leather-piercing tool.
Sūrmī and sthūṇā denote an iron figure or post; śilpa means craft, work beginning with the arts.
Pratimāna, pratibimba, pratimā, pratiyātanā, and praticchāyā are terms for a likeness, image, or reflection.
Pratikṛti and arcā, masculine pratinidhi, and upamā or upamāna likewise denote a representation, counterpart, or standard of comparison.

children.text: vācyaliṅgāḥ samas tulyaḥ sadṛkṣaḥ sadṛśaḥ sadṛk
children.translated_text: The words sama, tulya, sadṛkṣa, sadṛśa, and sadṛk take the gender of the noun they describe.
Sādhāraṇa and samāna are the same; but as the final member of a compound, the following words are used.
These are nibha, saṃkāśa, nīkāśa, pratīkāśa, upama, and the like, all meaning 'resembling' or 'similar to.'
For wages or payment connected with work, the terms are vidhā, bhṛtyā, ābhṛti, bharma, and vetana.

children.text: bharaṇyaṃ bharaṇaṃ mūlyaṃ nirveśaḥ paṇa ityapi
children.translated_text: Bharaṇya, bharaṇa, mūlya, nirveśa, and paṇa are also terms for hire, price, or payment.
Surā, halipriyā, hālā, parisrut, and varuṇātmajā, 'daughter of <s>Varuṇa</s>,' are names for liquor.
Gandhottamā, prasannā, erā, kādambarī, and parisrutā are further names for fermented or clarified liquor.
Madirā, kaśya, and madya are also words for liquor; avadaṃśa, however, means food or a bite to eat with it.
Śuṇḍāpāna and madasthāna denote a drinking-house; madhuvāra and madhukrama are names of honey-liquor.
Madhvāsava, mādhavaka, madhu, and mādhvīka also denote mead or honey-based liquor, the last two being used in two genders.
Maireya, āsava, and sīdhu are kinds of liquor; mandaka and jagala are equivalent terms.

children.text: sandhānaṃ syādabhiṣavaḥ kiṇvaṃ puṃsi tu nagnahūḥ ||
children.translated_text: Sandhāna and abhiṣava denote fermentation or brewing; kiṇva, masculine, is also called nagnahū, a ferment or leaven.
Kārottara and surāmaṇḍa denote the froth, essence, or sediment of liquor; āpāna and pānaghoṣṭhikā denote a drinking gathering or tavern.
Capaka, non-feminine, and pānapātra are drinking vessels; saraka too is a cup, and anutarṣaṇa means a follow-up drink.
Dhūrta, akṣadevin, kitava, akṣadhūrta, and dyūtakṛt are equivalent names for a gambler or dice-player.
Lagnaka, pratibhu, sabhika, and dyūtakāraka are terms for people involved in gambling, such as stake-holders, sureties, or gaming-house officials.
Dyūta, in a non-feminine gender, akṣavatī, kaitava, and paṇa are also names for gambling.

children.text: paṇo 'kṣeṣu glaho 'kṣās tu devanāḥ pāśakāś ca te ||
children.translated_text: In dice-play, the stake is called paṇa or glaha; the dice themselves are akṣa, devana, and pāśaka.
Pariṇāya, non-feminine, is the moving of board-game pieces all around.
Aṣṭāpada, śāriphala, prāṇivṛtta, and samāhvaya are terms for the gaming board or board game.
Some derivative terms have been stated here in one gender because that is their common usage.
When used elsewhere through possession of the same property, those terms should be understood even in another gender.
